topics.title: What makes something living, and how diverse is life?

learn.hook: A crystal of salt grows in brine and a mule cannot reproduce. So which of them is alive? Biology starts by answering exactly this.
points: Living organisms show growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation and response to surroundings (consciousness). Metabolism and cellular organisation are the defining features.
Growth alone cannot define life: non-living mountains, sand mounds and crystals also grow, by accumulation of material on the outer surface. Living organisms grow from inside.
Reproduction alone cannot define life: mules, sterile worker bees and infertile couples do not reproduce, yet they are alive.
Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions in the body. No non-living object shows metabolism, so it is a defining property of life.
Biodiversity means the number and variety of organisms on Earth. About 1.7 to 1.8 million species have been described so far, and many more are still unknown.

example.q: Explain why a sterile worker honeybee is classed as living even though it never reproduces.
steps: Reproduction is not shown by every living individual, so it cannot be a defining feature.
The worker bee shows metabolism: it digests nectar, respires and builds wax.
It also shows cellular organisation and responds to stimuli such as light and smell.
Metabolism and cellular organisation are defining features of life.
example.answer: It is living because it has cellular organisation and metabolism; reproduction is not a defining property.

learn.reallife: India is one of the world's 17 megadiverse countries. The Western Ghats and the north-east alone hold thousands of plant and animal species, many found nowhere else.

quiz.explain: No non-living object shows metabolism, so it can be used to define life. Growth and reproduction fail this test.
steps: Asked: which feature can define life, i.e. is shown by no non-living thing.
Growth is shown by crystals; reproduction is absent in mules and worker bees.
Metabolism (all chemical reactions in the body) is shown by no non-living object.
So the defining feature is Metabolism.
Answer: Metabolism

quiz.q: Why is growth NOT taken as a defining property of living things?
quiz.explain: Crystals and sand mounds increase in size by accumulation of material on the surface, so growth is not unique to life.
steps: Asked: why growth fails as a defining feature of life.
Mountains, sand mounds and crystals also grow, by adding material on the outer surface.

Answer: Non-living objects such as crystals and mountains also grow

quiz.q: A worker bee, a mule and an infertile human have one thing in common. What is it?
quiz.explain: All three are alive but cannot produce offspring, which shows reproduction is not a defining feature of life.
steps: List what each lacks: a worker bee, a mule and an infertile human all cannot produce offspring.
Yet all three metabolise, are made of cells and respond to stimuli, so they are alive.
Common feature: they are living but do not reproduce.
Answer: They are living but do not reproduce
quiz.mistake: Assumes anything that cannot reproduce must be non-living
options: They are living but do not reproduce
They are not made of cells

quiz.q: How does growth in living organisms differ from growth in a salt crystal?
quiz.explain: Living organisms grow by cell division and increase in mass from within, while non-living things grow by external accumulation.
steps: Living organisms grow from inside, by cell division and increase in mass.
A salt crystal grows only by accumulation of material on its outer surface.
So: organisms grow from inside; the crystal grows by adding material on its outer surface.
The reversed statement (organisms on the surface, crystal from inside) is wrong.
Answer: Organisms grow from inside; the crystal grows by adding material on its outer surface
quiz.mistake: Thinks all growth is the same process
options: Organisms grow only on the surface; the crystal grows from inside
Organisms grow from inside; the crystal grows by adding material on its outer surface
Both grow in exactly the same way

quiz.q: About how many species have been described so far on Earth?
quiz.explain: Taxonomists have named and described roughly 1.7 to 1.8 million species; many more remain undiscovered.
steps: Recall the figure from the lesson: about 1.7 to 1.8 million species have been described.
Check the unit: million, not thousand or hundreds of millions.
Answer: 1.7 to 1.8 million
quiz.mistake: Slips by a factor of a thousand or ten when recalling the figure

quiz.q: The term biodiversity refers to:
quiz.explain: Biodiversity is the variety and number of living organisms in an area or on Earth as a whole.
steps: Biodiversity = the number and variety (types) of organisms on Earth.
It covers all organisms, not only plants, and is not about fossils or mass.
Answer: The number and types of organisms present on Earth
quiz.mistake: Restricts biodiversity to one group of organisms
options: Only the number of plant species
The number and types of organisms present on Earth
The total mass of all animals

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Reproduction cannot be an all-inclusive defining feature of living organisms. Reason (R): Many living organisms, such as mules and sterile worker bees, do not reproduce.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, and the existence of living but non-reproducing organisms is exactly why reproduction cannot define life.
steps: A: reproduction cannot define all living things. True.
R: mules and sterile worker bees are alive but do not reproduce. True.
R gives the exact reason A holds, so both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Fails to see the reason directly explains the assertion

quiz.q: A student says, 'A candle flame grows, uses oxygen and gives out CO₂, so it is alive.' What is the best reply?
quiz.explain: Life is defined by cellular organisation and metabolism inside cells. A flame shows neither, even if it looks like it grows and 'breathes'.
steps: Test the flame against the defining features: cellular organisation and metabolism.
A flame has no cells and no metabolism; its 'growth' and gas use are not defining features.
So the flame is not alive; the student is wrong.
Answer: A flame has no cells and no metabolism; the features it shows are not defining features of life
quiz.mistake: Confuses look-alike features with the defining features of life
options: A flame is alive because it grows
A flame has no cells and no metabolism; the features it shows are not defining features of life
Flames are alive only while burning
The student is right because it uses oxygen

teach.ask: Gappu holds up a growing sugar crystal: 'It grows, so it is alive, right? Tell me what really makes something living!'
teach.praise: Tweet! So growth fools us, but metabolism and cells never lie. Got it!
teach.nudge: Hmm, crystals grow too. What feature do only living things have?

revise.summary: Living things show growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation and response, but only metabolism and cellular organisation define life. Biodiversity is the number and variety of organisms; about 1.7–1.8 million species are described.
focus: Why growth and reproduction are not defining features of life
Metabolism and cellular organisation as the defining features
Difference between growth from inside and growth by surface accumulation
Meaning of biodiversity and the number of described species
remember: Defining features of life: metabolism and cellular organisation
Metabolism = sum of all chemical reactions in the body
Described species: about 1.7 to 1.8 million
traps: Don't call growth a defining feature: crystals and mountains also grow
Don't say non-reproducing organisms (mule, worker bee) are non-living

topics.title: Why scientific names? Identification and nomenclature

learn.hook: Brinjal, baingan, vankaya, kathirikai, aubergine, eggplant: six names for one vegetable. A scientist in Chennai and one in Berlin need one name they both trust.
points: Local names of the same organism differ from place to place, even within one country, so a standard name is needed worldwide.
Identification: describing an organism correctly so that we know exactly which organism it is. It comes before naming.
Nomenclature: giving a correct scientific name to an organism that has been identified.
Scientific names follow international codes: ICBN (International Code for Botanical Nomenclature) for plants and ICZN (International Code of Zoological Nomenclature) for animals.
These codes make sure each organism has only one correct name, and that no name is used for two different organisms.

example.q: Put the steps in order: a new plant found in Meghalaya must be given a scientific name.
steps: First describe its features accurately (identification).
Check it against known plants to confirm it is new.
Name it following the rules of ICBN (nomenclature).
example.answer: Identification first, then nomenclature under ICBN.

learn.reallife: When AIIMS doctors report a fungal infection, or the Botanical Survey of India lists a new orchid from Arunachal Pradesh, they use scientific names so labs anywhere can understand them.

games.title: Match the term to its meaning

quiz.q: Why do biologists need scientific names instead of local names?
quiz.explain: The same organism has many local names, and the same local name may refer to different organisms. A standard name avoids confusion.
steps: The same organism has different local names in different places.
The same local name may even refer to different organisms, causing confusion.
So a standard scientific name is needed: local names differ from place to place and cause confusion.
Answer: Local names differ from place to place and cause confusion
quiz.mistake: Thinks the issue is length or pronunciation rather than confusion
options: Local names are always too long
Local names differ from place to place and cause confusion
Scientific names are easier to pronounce

quiz.q: Which process must come first before an organism can be named?
quiz.explain: You can only name an organism once you have described it correctly and know what it is.

Nomenclature (naming) can only follow once the organism is identified.
So identification must come first.
Answer: Identification
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of identification and nomenclature

quiz.q: ICZN provides rules for naming:

'Zoological' refers to animals.

Full form: International Code for Botanical Nomenclature.
Answer: International Code for Botanical Nomenclature
quiz.mistake: Guesses a full form from the letters without knowing it

quiz.q: Nomenclature means:
quiz.explain: Nomenclature is naming. Grouping is classification and relationships are part of systematics.

Grouping is classification, not nomenclature.
Answer: Giving a correct scientific name to an organism
options: Giving a correct scientific name to an organism

quiz.q: A biologist correctly describes the features of a new beetle so that it can be told apart from all others. This step is:
quiz.explain: Correct description of an organism is identification; naming comes after it.
steps: The biologist describes the beetle's features so it can be told apart from others.
Correct description of an organism is identification.
Naming (nomenclature) comes only after this, so the step is identification.
Answer: Identification
quiz.mistake: Thinks describing and naming are the same step

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Each organism can have only one correct scientific name. Reason (R): International codes such as ICBN and ICZN make sure a given name is used for only one organism.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

R: ICBN and ICZN ensure a name is used for one organism only. True.
The codes are why names are unique, so both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.q: Which statement about common names is correct?

They are not uniform, not in Latin and not governed by ICBN.

teach.ask: Gappu calls the same bird 'kauwa' in Delhi and 'kaka' in Kerala. 'Why can't scientists just use local names?' Explain!
teach.praise: Chirp! One name, one organism, decided by the codes. Neat!
teach.nudge: Good, but who makes the naming rules for plants and animals?

topics.title: Binomial nomenclature: writing scientific names right

learn.hook: A board examiner can cut marks for writing 'Mangifera Indica'. One wrong capital letter, and the name is wrong. Let's get it right forever.
points: Binomial nomenclature was proposed by Carolus Linnaeus. Every scientific name has two parts: the generic name (genus) and the specific epithet (species).
Names are in Latin or are latinised, whatever their origin.
When printed, the name is in italics; when handwritten, the two words are underlined separately to show their Latin origin.
The genus name begins with a capital letter and the specific epithet with a small letter. Example: Mangifera indica.
The name of the author who first described the species appears after the epithet in abbreviated form, e.g. Mangifera indica Linn. (Linn. = Linnaeus).

example.q: A student writes the human scientific name as 'Homo Sapiens' in her answer sheet with no underline. Correct it.
steps: Genus Homo starts with a capital: correct.
Specific epithet must start with a small letter: sapiens.
Handwritten names must be underlined, each word separately.
example.answer: Homo sapiens, with 'Homo' and 'sapiens' each underlined separately.

learn.reallife: The mango, India's national fruit, is Mangifera indica, and the peacock, the national bird, is Pavo cristatus. 'indica' itself honours India.

items: The specific epithet starts with a capital letter.
Only the genus name starts with a capital letter.
Handwritten scientific names are underlined separately.
Each word is underlined on its own to show Latin origin.
Binomial nomenclature was proposed by Carolus Linnaeus.

quiz.q: Who proposed binomial nomenclature?
quiz.explain: Carolus Linnaeus introduced the two-word naming system used for all organisms.
steps: Binomial nomenclature gives each organism a two-part name.
This system was proposed by Carolus Linnaeus.
Answer: Carolus Linnaeus
quiz.mistake: Confuses the founder of naming with the founder of the five-kingdom system

quiz.q: A magazine prints the lion's name as 'Panthera Leo'. Which rule does this break?
quiz.explain: Genus takes a capital letter and the epithet a small letter, so it should be Panthera leo (in italics in print).
steps: Rule: genus starts with a capital letter, specific epithet with a small letter.
'Panthera Leo' has a capital L in the epithet.
Correct form is Panthera leo, so the broken rule is: epithet must begin with a small letter.
Answer: The specific epithet must begin with a small letter
quiz.mistake: Capitalises the specific epithet as in an English proper noun
options: The specific epithet must begin with a small letter
The name must be underlined in print
The genus must begin with a small letter
The author's name must always be written

quiz.q: In Mangifera indica Linn., the word 'indica' is the:
quiz.explain: The second word of a binomial is the specific epithet.
steps: A binomial has two parts: genus (first word) and specific epithet (second word).
In Mangifera indica Linn., 'indica' is the second word.
So 'indica' is the specific epithet.
Answer: Specific epithet
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of the two parts

quiz.q: In Mangifera indica Linn., what does 'Linn.' tell us?
quiz.explain: The abbreviated author name follows the epithet; here it stands for Linnaeus.
steps: The author's name comes after the epithet in abbreviated form.
'Linn.' stands for Linnaeus, who first described the species.
So it tells us the scientist who first described the species.
Answer: The scientist who first described the species
quiz.mistake: Thinks the third word is part of the classification
options: The scientist who first described the species

quiz.q: How should a scientific name be written in a handwritten answer?
quiz.explain: Handwritten names are underlined, each word separately, to show their Latin origin.
steps: Printed names are in italics; handwritten names are underlined.
Each of the two words is underlined separately to show Latin origin.
Answer: Each of the two words underlined separately
options: With one line under both words together
Each of the two words underlined separately

quiz.q: Scientific names are taken from which language, or are made to fit it?
quiz.explain: Biological names are Latin or latinised, whatever their source.
steps: Scientific names are in Latin or are latinised, whatever their origin.
Answer: Latin
quiz.mistake: Thinks scientific names come from the discoverer's language

quiz.q: A textbook prints 'Solanum tuberosum' in italics. What does 'Solanum' denote?
quiz.explain: The first word, beginning with a capital letter, is the genus.
steps: In a binomial, the first word, starting with a capital letter, is the genus.
'Solanum' is the first word of Solanum tuberosum.
So Solanum denotes the genus.
Answer: The genus
quiz.mistake: Thinks the first word is the species

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The specific epithet in a binomial name begins with a small letter. Reason (R): The generic name always ends in '-ae'.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: The assertion is a correct rule. The reason is false: generic names such as Homo or Panthera do not end in '-ae'; the ending '-ae' is typical of plant family names.
steps: A: the specific epithet begins with a small letter. True rule.
R: generic names always end in '-ae'. False: Homo and Panthera do not.
So A is true but R is false.
Answer: A is true, but R is false
quiz.mistake: Accepts a made-up rule because it sounds technical

teach.ask: Gappu wrote 'Mangifera Indica' on his test and lost marks. Explain the rules of writing a scientific name!
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Capital genus, small epithet, italics or underline. Full marks next time!
teach.nudge: Almost! What about capital and small letters, and how is it shown in print or handwriting?

revise.summary: Linnaeus's binomial nomenclature gives every organism a two-part Latin name: genus (capital letter) and specific epithet (small letter), italicised in print or underlined separately by hand, with the author's name abbreviated after it.

Meaning of the author abbreviation such as Linn.

Genus: capital first letter; specific epithet: small first letter
Printed in italics; handwritten with each word underlined separately
Example: Mangifera indica Linn.

topics.title: Classification, taxon, taxonomy and systematics

learn.hook: Supermarkets put all dals in one aisle and all spices in another so you find things fast. Biologists do the same with 1.7 million species.
points: Classification: grouping organisms into convenient categories based on easily observable characters.
Taxon: a group at any level of classification. 'Plants', 'animals', 'mammals' and 'dogs' are all taxa.
Taxonomy includes characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature of organisms.
Bases of modern taxonomic studies: external and internal structure, cell structure, development process and ecological information.
Systematics (from Latin 'systema', systematic arrangement) studies the kinds and diversity of organisms and their evolutionary relationships. It is broader than taxonomy.

example.q: Is 'mammals' a taxon? Is 'wheat'? Explain.
steps: A taxon is any group at any level of classification.
Mammals form a group at class level, so they are a taxon.
Wheat refers to a group at species level, which is also a taxon.
example.answer: Yes, both are taxa; one at class level, the other at species level.

learn.reallife: Seed banks of the ICAR and the National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources in New Delhi store lakhs of crop samples. Without careful classification, finding the right rice variety would be impossible.

games.title: Is it a basis of modern taxonomic study?

quiz.q: A group of organisms at any level of classification is called a:
quiz.explain: Taxon is the general word for a group at any rank, from kingdom down to species.
steps: A taxon is a group at any level (rank) of classification.
It applies from kingdom down to species, not to one rank only.
Answer: Taxon
quiz.mistake: Thinks taxon means only one particular rank

quiz.q: Which word comes from the Latin 'systema'?
quiz.explain: Systematics comes from 'systema', meaning systematic arrangement of organisms.
steps: 'Systema' is Latin for systematic arrangement.
Systematics takes its name from this word.
Answer: Systematics
quiz.mistake: Links taxonomy to the Latin root

quiz.q: Systematics differs from taxonomy because it also includes:
quiz.explain: Systematics covers identification, nomenclature and classification and also takes account of evolutionary relationships.
steps: Taxonomy: characterisation, identification, classification, nomenclature.
Systematics also takes account of evolutionary relationships between organisms.
So the extra part is evolutionary relationships.
Answer: Evolutionary relationships between organisms
quiz.mistake: Treats taxonomy and systematics as identical

quiz.q: Which set lists the processes included in taxonomy?
quiz.explain: Taxonomy brings together characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature.
steps: Taxonomy includes four processes in the lesson.
They are characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature.
The other sets are life processes or evolution steps, not taxonomy.
Answer: Characterisation, identification, classification, nomenclature
quiz.mistake: Mixes up taxonomy with physiology or evolution

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a basis of modern taxonomic studies?
quiz.explain: Taxonomy uses structure, cells, development and ecology. Market price has nothing to do with relationships.
steps: Bases of modern taxonomy: external and internal structure, cell structure, development, ecology.
Commercial price says nothing about an organism's features or relationships.
So the commercial price is NOT a basis.
Answer: The commercial price of the organism
quiz.mistake: Picks a real character because it sounds unfamiliar
options: The commercial price of the organism

quiz.q: Grouping organisms into convenient categories based on easily observable characters is:
quiz.explain: This is the definition of classification.
steps: Grouping organisms into convenient categories on easily observable characters is the definition of classification.
Naming is nomenclature; describing is identification.
Answer: Classification

quiz.q: 'Dogs', 'mammals' and 'plants' are examples of:
quiz.explain: Each is a group at some level of classification, so each is a taxon.
steps: A taxon is a group at any level of classification.
Dogs, mammals and plants are groups at different levels.
So they are taxa at different levels.
Answer: Taxa at different levels
quiz.mistake: Thinks only a species can be a taxon
options: Common names with no scientific meaning

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Taxonomy is a broader study than systematics. Reason (R): Systematics also considers the evolutionary relationships between organisms.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: systematics is the broader study, not taxonomy. R is true: systematics adds evolutionary relationships to identification, naming and classification, which is exactly why it is broader.
steps: A says taxonomy is broader than systematics. False: systematics is broader.
R says systematics also considers evolutionary relationships. True.
So A is false, R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true
quiz.mistake: Judges the assertion true just because the reason is a correct fact

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'Taxon, taxonomy, systematics... aren't they all the same word?' Untangle them for him!
teach.praise: Chirp! A taxon is a group, taxonomy names and sorts, systematics adds family history. Clear!
teach.nudge: Nice! But what extra thing does systematics look at?

revise.summary: Classification groups organisms by observable characters; any group at any rank is a taxon. Taxonomy covers characterisation, identification, classification and nomenclature, while systematics also studies evolutionary relationships.
focus: Definitions of classification, taxon, taxonomy and systematics
Why systematics is broader than taxonomy
remember: Taxon = a group at any level of classification
Taxonomy = characterisation + identification + classification + nomenclature
Systematics (Latin 'systema') adds evolutionary relationships

topics.title: Taxonomic hierarchy: species and genus

learn.hook: Your address goes Country → State → City → Street → House. Each organism has a 'biological address' too, and species is the house number.
points: Taxonomic hierarchy: categories arranged in a step-like order, kingdom at the top and species at the bottom.
Each category (rank) is a unit of classification and represents a taxon at that level.
Species: a group of individuals with fundamental similarities. It is the basic unit of classification. Examples: leo (lion), tigris (tiger), pardus (leopard) in Panthera.
Genus: a group of related species with more characters in common than species of other genera. Panthera has lion, tiger and leopard; Solanum has potato (S. tuberosum) and brinjal (S. melongena).
Lion, tiger and leopard share many features, so they are placed in one genus, Panthera; the cat is in a different genus, Felis.

example.q: Why are potato and brinjal in the same genus but given different species names?
steps: Both share many fundamental features, so they belong to the genus Solanum.
They differ in key characters, so each is a separate species.
Hence potato is Solanum tuberosum and brinjal is Solanum melongena.
example.answer: Same genus Solanum, different species: tuberosum and melongena.

learn.reallife: The Bengal tiger in Sundarbans, the Asiatic lion in Gir and the leopards of Mumbai's Sanjay Gandhi National Park are all members of one genus: Panthera.

quiz.q: Which is the basic unit of classification?
quiz.explain: Species is the lowest category and the basic unit; all higher categories are built from species.
steps: The hierarchy runs from kingdom (top) to species (bottom).
Species is the lowest category and all higher ranks are built from species.
So the basic unit is species.
Answer: Species

topics.title: Family, order, class, phylum and kingdom

learn.hook: Going up the hierarchy is like zooming out on Google Maps: you see more and more places, but each one shows fewer shared details.
points: Family: a group of related genera. Felidae (Panthera, Felis), Canidae (dogs) and Solanaceae (Solanum, Petunia, Datura) are families.
Order: an assemblage of families with a few similar characters. Carnivora includes Felidae and Canidae; Polymoniales includes Solanaceae and Convolvulaceae.
Class: related orders. Mammalia includes orders such as Primata (monkey, gorilla, gibbon) and Carnivora (tiger, cat, dog). Dicotyledonae is a plant class.
Phylum (animals) or Division (plants): related classes. Chordata includes Mammalia, Aves, Reptilia and Amphibia. Kingdom is the highest category (Animalia, Plantae).
As we go up from species to kingdom, the number of common characters decreases, and the number of organisms in the group increases.

example.q: Arrange in ascending order (lowest first): Order, Species, Kingdom, Family, Class, Genus, Phylum.
steps: Ascending means from the lowest rank to the highest.
Lowest rank is species, then genus, family, order, class, phylum, and kingdom on top.
example.answer: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum → Kingdom

learn.reallife: Indian Railways groups its trains into zones, divisions and routes. Bigger units hold more trains but those trains share fewer specific features, just like higher taxa.

topics.title: From two kingdoms to five: history of classification

learn.hook: Linnaeus put mushrooms and mango trees in the same kingdom. It took two centuries and a microscope to fix that.
points: Aristotle made the earliest attempt: plants as trees, shrubs and herbs; animals as those with red blood and those without.
Linnaeus used two kingdoms, Plantae and Animalia. It did not separate prokaryotes from eukaryotes, unicellular from multicellular, or photosynthetic green algae from non-photosynthetic fungi.
R.H. Whittaker (1969) proposed five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
Whittaker's criteria: cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships.
A three-domain system (Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya) has also been proposed, which splits Monera into two domains and keeps all eukaryotes in the third.

example.q: Use the five-kingdom table to place an organism: eukaryotic, cell wall of chitin (no cellulose), heterotrophic by absorption.
steps: Eukaryotic rules out Monera.
A cell wall without cellulose rules out Plantae and Animalia (no wall).
Chitin walls and absorptive heterotrophy are features of Fungi.
example.answer: Kingdom Fungi

topics.title: Kingdom Monera: bacterial shapes, nutrition and archaebacteria

learn.hook: The gas cooking food in many Indian villages comes from cow dung. The real chefs are microbes living in the cow's stomach.
points: Bacteria are the most abundant microorganisms and live almost everywhere, from hot springs to deserts to the deep sea.
Shapes: coccus (spherical), bacillus (rod), vibrio (comma-shaped) and spirillum (spiral).
Nutrition: most are heterotrophs; some are autotrophs, either photosynthetic or chemosynthetic.

Archaebacteria live in extreme habitats: halophiles (very salty areas), thermoacidophiles (hot springs) and methanogens (marshy areas). Their cell wall structure is different from other bacteria, which helps them survive.
Methanogens live in the guts of ruminants such as cows and buffaloes and produce methane (biogas) from dung.

steps: Extreme habitat points to archaebacteria.

topics.title: Eubacteria: cyanobacteria and chemosynthetic bacteria

learn.hook: Rice farmers in Odisha add 'blue-green algae' to their paddies for free nitrogen. But these 'algae' are actually bacteria!
points: Eubacteria ('true bacteria') have a rigid cell wall and, if motile, a flagellum.
Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) have chlorophyll a like green plants and are photosynthetic autotrophs. They may be unicellular, colonial or filamentous, often with a gelatinous sheath.
Some cyanobacteria, such as Nostoc and Anabaena, fix atmospheric nitrogen in specialised cells called heterocysts.
Cyanobacteria often form blooms in polluted water bodies.

Chemosynthetic autotrophic bacteria oxidise inorganic substances such as nitrates, nitrites and ammonia and use the energy released to make ATP. They help recycle nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and sulphur.

example.q: A Nostoc filament shows a few larger, thick-walled cells. What are they and what do they do?

topics.title: Heterotrophic bacteria, reproduction and Mycoplasma

learn.hook: The dahi setting in your kitchen tonight and the cholera outbreak in a flooded town are both bacterial stories.
points: Heterotrophic bacteria are the most abundant in nature. Most are decomposers.
Helpful roles: making curd from milk, producing antibiotics and fixing nitrogen in legume roots.
Harmful roles: diseases such as cholera, typhoid and tetanus in humans, and citrus canker in plants.
Bacteria reproduce mainly by fission; under unfavourable conditions they form spores. A primitive DNA transfer from one bacterium to another is a sexual-like process.
Mycoplasma completely lack a cell wall. They are the smallest living cells known, can survive without oxygen, and many are pathogenic in plants and animals.

steps: Such antibiotics act on the bacterial cell wall.

topics.title: Protista: chrysophytes, dinoflagellates and euglenoids

learn.hook: Parts of India's coastline sometimes turn red and fish die off in large numbers. Tiny protists with armour plates are to blame.
points: Protista are single-celled eukaryotes, mostly aquatic. They have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles and form a link between plants, animals and fungi.

Chrysophytes include diatoms and desmids (golden algae). Diatom walls are two overlapping shells, like a soap box, embedded with silica. Deposits form diatomaceous earth, used in polishing and in filtering oils and syrups. Diatoms are the chief producers in the oceans.
Dinoflagellates are mostly marine and photosynthetic, with stiff cellulose plates on the outer wall and two flagella (one longitudinal, one transverse in a furrow).
Red dinoflagellates such as Gonyaulax multiply rapidly and cause red tides; their toxins can kill fishes.

Euglenoids (e.g. Euglena) live in stagnant fresh water, have no cell wall but a flexible, protein-rich pellicle and two flagella (one short, one long). They photosynthesise in light and behave as heterotrophs in the dark.

steps: No cell wall but a flexible body points to a pellicle.

These are features of euglenoids.
example.answer: Euglena, a euglenoid.

topics.title: Slime moulds and protozoans

learn.hook: Malaria still affects many Indians each year. The culprit is a single-celled protist that hides in mosquito saliva.
points: Slime moulds are saprophytic protists that creep over decaying twigs and leaves, engulfing organic matter.

In good conditions they form a plasmodium that can spread over several feet. In bad conditions the plasmodium forms fruiting bodies bearing spores with true walls; these spores are extremely resistant, survive for years and spread by air.
Protozoans are heterotrophs (predators or parasites), believed to be primitive relatives of animals.

Four groups: amoeboid (Amoeba; parasitic Entamoeba) with pseudopodia; flagellated (Trypanosoma, causes sleeping sickness); ciliated (Paramoecium, with a gullet and thousands of cilia); sporozoans (Plasmodium, causes malaria) with an infectious spore-like stage.

topics.title: Kingdom Fungi: structure, nutrition and reproduction

learn.hook: The bread in your tiffin, the penicillin in a hospital and the rust on a Punjab wheat field are all fungal stories.
points: Fungi are heterotrophs: saprophytes (absorb dead organic matter), parasites, or symbionts (with algae as lichens, with plant roots as mycorrhiza). Yeast makes bread and beer, Penicillium gives antibiotics, Puccinia causes wheat rust.

Except unicellular yeasts, fungi are filamentous. Thread-like hyphae form a network called mycelium. Coenocytic hyphae are continuous tubes with many nuclei; others have septa (cross walls). Cell walls contain chitin and polysaccharides.
Vegetative reproduction: fragmentation, fission, budding. Asexual spores: conidia, sporangiospores or zoospores. Sexual spores: oospores, ascospores, basidiospores, produced in fruiting bodies.
Sexual cycle: plasmogamy (fusion of protoplasms), karyogamy (fusion of nuclei) and meiosis in the zygote giving haploid spores.
In ascomycetes and basidiomycetes a dikaryotic stage (n + n, two nuclei per cell) comes between plasmogamy and karyogamy; this phase is the dikaryophase.

example.q: Order the sexual cycle of a basidiomycete.
steps: Two compatible haploid cells fuse their cytoplasm: plasmogamy.
Cells now have two separate nuclei: dikaryon (n + n).
The nuclei fuse: karyogamy, giving a diploid nucleus.
Meiosis produces haploid spores.
example.answer: Plasmogamy → dikaryon → karyogamy → meiosis

topics.title: Classes of fungi

learn.hook: Truffles sell for lakhs of rupees a kilo, while a smut fungus ruins a maize cob. Both belong to the fungal family album.
points: Phycomycetes: aquatic or on decaying wood in damp places, or obligate plant parasites. Mycelium aseptate and coenocytic. Asexual zoospores (motile) or aplanospores (non-motile) formed inside sporangia. Zygospore from fusion of gametes. Mucor, Rhizopus (bread mould), Albugo (parasite on mustard).

Ascomycetes (sac fungi): mostly multicellular (Penicillium), rarely unicellular (yeast, Saccharomyces). Septate, branched mycelium. Conidia formed exogenously on conidiophores; ascospores formed endogenously in asci, which are grouped in ascocarps. Aspergillus, Claviceps, Neurospora (used in genetics); morels and truffles are edible.

Basidiomycetes: mushrooms, bracket fungi, puffballs. Septate mycelium; asexual spores generally absent; sex organs absent. Plasmogamy by fusion of two somatic cells, a dikaryon forms, karyogamy and meiosis in the basidium give four basidiospores borne exogenously. Basidia lie in basidiocarps. Agaricus, Ustilago (smut), Puccinia (rust).

Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi): only asexual or vegetative phases known; reproduce by conidia; septate mycelium. Many are decomposers that help mineral cycling. Alternaria, Colletotrichum, Trichoderma. When sexual stages are found, they are moved to ascomycetes or basidiomycetes.

example.answer: Ascomycetes; the fruiting body is an ascocarp.

topics.title: Kingdoms Plantae and Animalia

learn.hook: The amarbel (Cuscuta) draped over hedges in Indian towns is a plant that has given up making most of its own food.
points: Plantae: eukaryotic, chlorophyll-containing organisms with prominent chloroplasts and cell walls mainly of cellulose. Includes algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms.
A few plants are partially heterotrophic: insectivorous plants such as bladderwort and Venus fly trap, and parasites such as Cuscuta.
Plant life cycles alternate between a diploid sporophytic phase and a haploid gametophytic phase. This is alternation of generations.
Animalia: heterotrophic, multicellular eukaryotes whose cells lack cell walls. They depend directly or indirectly on plants, show holozoic nutrition (ingestion) and store food as glycogen or fat.

Animals follow a definite growth pattern to reach a definite shape and size; most can move; higher forms have elaborate sensory and neuromotor systems; sexual reproduction is followed by embryological development.

topics.title: Viruses: discovery, structure and diseases

learn.hook: COVID-19 showed the world how something that is not even a cell can bring cities to a halt.
points: Viruses are non-cellular. Outside a living cell they are inert, crystalline particles; inside a host they take over its machinery to multiply. They are obligate parasites.

Pasteur coined 'virus' (venom or poisonous fluid). D.J. Ivanowsky (1892) found the agent of tobacco mosaic disease passed through bacteria-proof filters. M.W. Beijerinek (1898) called the infectious extract 'Contagium vivum fluidum'. W.M. Stanley (1935) crystallised viruses and showed the crystals were mainly protein.
A virus is a nucleoprotein: genetic material (RNA or DNA, never both) inside a protein coat called a capsid made of capsomeres, arranged in helical or polyhedral forms.
Plant viruses usually have single-stranded RNA. Animal viruses have single- or double-stranded RNA or double-stranded DNA. Bacteriophages usually have double-stranded DNA.
Human viral diseases: mumps, smallpox, herpes, influenza and AIDS. Plant symptoms: mosaic, leaf rolling and curling, yellowing and vein clearing, dwarfing and stunted growth.

example.q: A tobacco leaf extract still infects healthy plants after passing through a filter that stops bacteria. What does this show?
steps: The agent is smaller than bacteria.
It is not a bacterium.
This was Ivanowsky's 1892 observation, and Beijerinek later called it Contagium vivum fluidum.
example.answer: The agent is a filterable virus, smaller than bacteria.

topics.title: Viroids, prions and lichens

learn.hook: Some infections are caused by naked RNA, some by misfolded protein, and some 'single organisms' on tree bark are really two partners living together.
points: Viroids: discovered by T.O. Diener (1971); cause potato spindle tuber disease. They are free RNA with no protein coat, of low molecular weight, smaller than viruses.

Prions: infectious agents made of abnormally folded protein, similar in size to viruses. They cause bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE, mad cow disease) in cattle and its human analogue Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD).

Lichens: symbiotic (mutually useful) associations of an alga (phycobiont, autotrophic) and a fungus (mycobiont, heterotrophic). The alga makes food; the fungus gives shelter and absorbs water and minerals.
Lichens are very good pollution indicators: they do not grow in polluted areas.
Comparison: a virus has nucleic acid plus a protein coat; a viroid is nucleic acid only; a prion is protein only.

example.q: City A has lichens on its tree trunks; City B, beside a busy industrial belt, has none. What can you infer?
steps: Lichens do not grow in polluted air.

example.answer: City B's air is likely more polluted; lichens act as pollution indicators.

learn.reallife: Lichens are used to track air quality; some lichens are sold as the spice 'kalpasi' (stone flower) used in Chettinad cooking.

topics.title: Systems of plant classification

learn.hook: Imagine sorting your class only by height. Tall friends would be 'related'. Early plant classification made a similar mistake.
points: Artificial systems (e.g. Linnaeus) used only a few characters such as habit, colour, number and shape of leaves, or the androecium. They gave equal weight to vegetative and sexual characters, which is unacceptable because vegetative characters are easily affected by the environment.
Natural systems (e.g. Bentham and Hooker) are based on natural affinities and use many characters: external features and internal ones such as ultrastructure, anatomy, embryology and phytochemistry.
Phylogenetic systems are based on evolutionary relationships; they assume members of a taxon share a common ancestor.
Numerical taxonomy uses computers: all observable characters are coded as numbers and given equal importance, so hundreds of characters can be handled.
Cytotaxonomy uses chromosome number, structure and behaviour; chemotaxonomy uses the plant's chemical constituents.

example.q: Two plant groups look alike, but one has 2n = 14 and the other 2n = 24, and their alkaloids differ. Which branches of taxonomy use these clues?
steps: Chromosome number is cytological information: cytotaxonomy.
Chemical constituents such as alkaloids: chemotaxonomy.
example.answer: Cytotaxonomy (chromosomes) and chemotaxonomy (chemicals).

topics.title: Algae: forms, reproduction and importance

learn.hook: The agar in your school lab petri dish and in some ice creams comes from red seaweed off the coast. Algae are quietly everywhere.
points: Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, simple, thalloid, autotrophic and mostly aquatic. Forms range from unicellular (Chlamydomonas) and colonial (Volvox) to filamentous (Ulothrix, Spirogyra) and massive marine kelps.
Vegetative reproduction is by fragmentation; asexual reproduction is by spores, most commonly flagellated zoospores.

Sexual reproduction: isogamy (gametes similar in size; flagellated in Chlamydomonas, non-flagellated in Spirogyra), anisogamy (gametes dissimilar in size, e.g. species of Eudorina), oogamy (large non-motile female and small motile male gamete, e.g. Volvox, Fucus).
Algae carry out at least half of the total CO₂ fixation on Earth and are primary producers in aquatic food chains.

Uses: about 70 marine species are eaten, e.g. Porphyra, Laminaria, Sargassum. Algin (brown algae) and carrageen (red algae) are used commercially; agar (Gelidium, Gracilaria) is used to grow microbes and in jellies and ice creams; Chlorella, rich in protein, is a food supplement even for space travellers.

example.q: In an alga, a large non-motile egg is fertilised by a small motile male gamete. Name the type of sexual reproduction and give two examples.
steps: Gametes differ in size and motility.
Large non-motile female with small motile male is oogamy.
example.answer: Oogamy, e.g. Volvox and Fucus.

learn.reallife: Seaweed farming of Gracilaria and Kappaphycus along Tamil Nadu's Ramanathapuram coast gives coastal women's groups an income from agar and carrageenan.

topics.title: Classes of algae: green, brown and red

learn.hook: Why are some seaweeds red even when they live deep under the sea? The answer lies in a pigment that catches the light that reaches the depths.
points: Chlorophyceae (green algae): chlorophyll a and b; chloroplasts of many shapes; pyrenoids store protein and starch; food stored as starch (and oil); cell wall of inner cellulose and outer pectose; 2 to 8 equal apical flagella. Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix, Spirogyra, Chara.

Phaeophyceae (brown algae): mainly marine; chlorophyll a and c, carotenoids and xanthophylls (fucoxanthin); food as laminarin or mannitol; cellulose wall covered by gelatinous algin; body has holdfast, stipe and frond; 2 unequal lateral flagella. Ectocarpus, Dictyota, Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus.

Rhodophyceae (red algae): pigment r-phycoerythrin with chlorophyll a and d; mostly marine, near the surface and at great depths; food as floridean starch (like amylopectin and glycogen); wall of cellulose, pectin and polysulphate esters; no flagella. Polysiphonia, Porphyra, Gracilaria, Gelidium.
Red algae reproduce sexually by oogamy with complex post-fertilisation development; asexual spores are non-motile.

topics.title: Bryophytes: amphibians of the plant kingdom

learn.hook: After the monsoon, a green velvet covers old walls in Kerala. These mosses need land to live on but water to have babies, just like frogs.
points: Bryophytes live in soil but depend on water for sexual reproduction, so they are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom. They grow in damp, humid, shaded places and help plant succession on bare rocks and soil.
The plant body is thallus-like, prostrate or erect, attached by rhizoids. It has no true roots, stems or leaves. The main plant body is the haploid gametophyte.
Sex organs are multicellular. The antheridium produces biflagellate antherozoids; the flask-shaped archegonium has a single egg. Antherozoids swim through water to reach the egg.

The zygote forms a multicellular sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) that stays attached to the gametophyte and depends on it for food. Some sporophyte cells undergo meiosis to form haploid spores, which grow into new gametophytes.

Uses: food for herbivorous mammals and birds; Sphagnum gives peat, used as fuel and as packing material for living material because it holds water. Mosses with lichens are first colonisers of rocks, and moss mats reduce soil erosion.

example.q: Why does a moss plant fail to produce a sporophyte in a long dry spell?
steps: Antherozoids are flagellated and must swim to the archegonium.
Without water, they cannot reach the egg.
No fertilisation means no zygote, so no sporophyte.
example.answer: Fertilisation needs water; without it no zygote or sporophyte forms.

learn.reallife: Sphagnum peat moss is used by plant nurseries to pack and transport living saplings because it holds water so well.

topics.title: Liverworts and mosses

learn.hook: Marchantia carries tiny 'cups' full of green buds that splash away in rain drops to start new plants.
points: Liverworts grow in moist shady places such as stream banks, marshy ground, damp soil, tree bark and deep woods. The thalloid body of Marchantia is dorsiventral and closely pressed to the ground; leafy liverworts have tiny leaf-like parts in two rows.
Liverworts reproduce asexually by fragmentation or by gemmae: green, multicellular asexual buds formed in gemma cups on the thallus. Gemmae detach and grow into new plants.
In liverworts, male and female sex organs may be on the same or different thalli; the sporophyte has foot, seta and capsule, and spores form after meiosis.

Mosses: the gametophyte has two stages. The protonema grows directly from a spore and is creeping, green, branched and often filamentous. The leafy stage grows from the secondary protonema as a lateral bud, with upright axes bearing spirally arranged leaves and multicellular branched rhizoids; it bears the sex organs.

Mosses reproduce vegetatively by fragmentation and budding of the secondary protonema. Their sporophyte is more elaborate than in liverworts, with an elaborate mechanism of spore dispersal. Examples: Funaria, Polytrichum, Sphagnum.

example.q: A student sees a green filament growing from a moss spore. What is it and what will it give rise to?
steps: A creeping green filament growing directly from a spore is the protonema.
Lateral buds on it grow into the leafy stage that bears sex organs.
example.answer: Protonema; it gives rise to the leafy gametophyte stage.

learn.reallife: Polytrichum and Funaria carpet Himalayan slopes in Darjeeling and Sikkim, holding soil during heavy rains.

topics.title: Pteridophytes: the first vascular land plants

learn.hook: The lacy ferns in Ooty's gardens were the first plants to build 'plumbing pipes'. That's why they could stand taller than mosses.
points: Pteridophytes (horsetails and ferns) are the first terrestrial plants with vascular tissues, xylem and phloem. They mostly grow in cool, damp, shady places.
The main plant body is the diploid sporophyte with true roots, stems and leaves. Leaves may be small (microphylls, as in Selaginella) or large (macrophylls, as in ferns).
Sporangia are borne on leaf-like sporophylls. In some, sporophylls form compact strobili or cones (Selaginella, Equisetum). Spore mother cells undergo meiosis to form spores.
Spores grow into a small, multicellular, free-living, mostly photosynthetic thalloid gametophyte called the prothallus, which needs cool, damp, shady places.
The prothallus bears antheridia and archegonia; water is needed for antherozoids to reach the egg. The zygote grows into the well-differentiated sporophyte.

example.q: Fern spores on a dry concrete wall do not produce new ferns, but on wet soil near a stream they do. Explain.
steps: Spores grow into the prothallus, which needs cool, damp, shady places.
Fertilisation on the prothallus also needs water for antherozoids to swim.
example.answer: The prothallus and fertilisation both need moist conditions.

learn.reallife: Ferns like Adiantum (maidenhair fern) are popular ornamental plants in Indian homes and hill-station gardens.

topics.title: Heterospory and classes of pteridophytes

learn.hook: Selaginella makes two sizes of spores. That small step, keeping the female spore at home, set plants on the road to seeds.
points: Most pteridophytes are homosporous: they produce one kind of spore.
Selaginella and Salvinia are heterosporous: they produce large megaspores and small microspores, which grow into female and male gametophytes.
In heterosporous forms, the female gametophyte stays on the parent sporophyte for some time and the embryo develops inside it. This is a precursor to the seed habit, an important step in evolution.
Classes: Psilopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Selaginella, Lycopodium), Sphenopsida (Equisetum) and Pteropsida (Dryopteris, Pteris, Adiantum).
Uses: medicinal purposes, as soil binders, and as ornamentals.

example.q: Why is heterospory in Selaginella considered a step towards the seed habit?
steps: Megaspores and microspores form female and male gametophytes.
The female gametophyte is retained on the parent sporophyte.
The zygote develops into an embryo within it, as happens inside a seed.
example.answer: Retention of the female gametophyte and development of the embryo on the parent is a precursor to seeds.

learn.reallife: Pteris and Adiantum ferns grow on the walls of old forts in Rajasthan and the Western Ghats, and many ferns help bind soil on slopes.

topics.title: Gymnosperms: naked seeds, roots and leaves

learn.hook: The tallest trees on Earth, the redwoods, are gymnosperms. So is the pine whose resin makes turpentine, and the cycad in your local park.
points: Gymnosperms (gymnos = naked, sperma = seeds) have ovules not enclosed by an ovary wall, before or after fertilisation.
They include medium to tall trees and shrubs. Sequoia, the giant redwood, is one of the tallest tree species.
Roots are generally tap roots. Pinus has mycorrhizal roots (fungal association); Cycas has small coralloid roots associated with N₂-fixing cyanobacteria.
Stems may be unbranched (Cycas) or branched (Pinus, Cedrus). Leaves may be simple or compound; Cycas has pinnate leaves that last a few years.

Conifer needle-like leaves reduce surface area, and a thick cuticle and sunken stomata reduce water loss, helping them survive extremes of temperature, humidity and wind. Economic uses include timber, and products such as resin and turpentine from pines.

example.q: How do needle leaves help a Himalayan pine survive cold, dry winds?
steps: Needles have a small surface area, so less water is lost.

example.answer: Small area, thick cuticle and sunken stomata reduce water loss.

topics.title: Reproduction in gymnosperms

learn.hook: In spring, pine forests release clouds of yellow pollen. The wind carries it to female cones, and no water is needed at all.
points: Gymnosperms are heterosporous: haploid microspores and megaspores form in sporangia on sporophylls arranged spirally in strobili (cones).
Male strobili carry microsporophylls with microsporangia. Microspores develop into a highly reduced male gametophyte, the pollen grain, inside the microsporangium.

Female strobili carry megasporophylls with ovules. The ovule is the nucellus (megasporangium) protected by envelopes (integuments). A megaspore mother cell in the nucellus divides by meiosis into four megaspores; one forms the multicellular female gametophyte with two or more archegonia.

In Pinus, male and female cones are on the same tree; in Cycas, male cones and megasporophylls are on different trees. Male and female gametophytes are not free-living; they stay within sporangia on the sporophyte.

Pollen is carried by air to the ovule opening. A pollen tube carries male gametes to the archegonia. After fertilisation the zygote forms the embryo and the ovule becomes a seed, which is not covered.

example.q: Trace the path from microspore to seed in Pinus.
steps: Microspore develops into a pollen grain in the microsporangium.
Air carries pollen to an ovule on the female cone.

Fertilisation forms a zygote, which becomes the embryo.
The ovule develops into a naked seed.
example.answer: Microspore → pollen → pollination by air → pollen tube → fertilisation → embryo → naked seed.

topics.title: Comparing plant groups: from algae to gymnosperms

learn.hook: Imagine plants climbing a ladder out of the water: algae in the sea, mosses at the shore, ferns with pipes, pines with seeds, and flowering plants at the top.
points: Increasing complexity: algae → bryophytes → pteridophytes → gymnosperms → angiosperms. Angiosperms have ovules inside an ovary and seeds inside fruits.
Dominant phase: haploid gametophyte in bryophytes; diploid sporophyte in pteridophytes and gymnosperms.
Vascular tissue is absent in algae and bryophytes, present in pteridophytes and gymnosperms. Seeds appear first in gymnosperms (naked); angiosperm seeds are enclosed in fruits.
Water is needed for fertilisation in bryophytes and pteridophytes; gymnosperms use pollen tubes.

Ploidy check: moss protonema, leafy gametophyte, gemma cell, fern prothallus, spores and gametes are haploid (n); zygotes and sporophytes are diploid (2n). Algae are classified mainly by pigments, stored food, cell wall and flagella.

topics.title: Basis of classification: levels of organisation, gut and circulation

learn.hook: A sponge and a cheetah are both animals, yet one is a loose bag of cells and the other a high-speed machine. How do we compare them fairly?
points: Animals differ hugely in structure, but share fundamental features (arrangement of cells, body symmetry, coelom, digestive, circulatory and reproductive patterns) that are used for classification.

Levels of organisation: cellular level in sponges (loose cell aggregates); tissue level in coelenterates; organ level in Platyhelminthes; organ-system level in annelids, arthropods, molluscs, echinoderms and chordates.
Incomplete digestive system: a single opening serves as both mouth and anus (e.g. Platyhelminthes). Complete digestive system: two openings, mouth and anus.

Open circulatory system: blood is pumped out of the heart and cells and tissues are directly bathed in it (e.g. arthropods, molluscs). Closed circulatory system: blood flows through a series of vessels of varying diameters (e.g. annelids, chordates).

example.q: A flatworm takes food in and throws undigested waste out through the same opening. What type of digestive system is this?
steps: Only one opening to the gut.
One opening working as both mouth and anus means an incomplete digestive system.
example.answer: Incomplete digestive system.

topics.title: Symmetry and germ layers

learn.hook: Cut a starfish like a pizza and every slice looks alike. Cut yourself (only in imagination!) and only one cut gives two mirror halves.
points: Asymmetrical: no plane divides the body into equal halves (most sponges).
Radial symmetry: any plane through the central axis gives two identical halves (coelenterates, ctenophores, adult echinoderms).
Bilateral symmetry: only one plane divides the body into identical left and right halves (annelids, arthropods and others).
Diploblastic animals have two germ layers, external ectoderm and internal endoderm, with an undifferentiated mesoglea in between (coelenterates).
Triploblastic animals have a third germ layer, mesoderm, between ectoderm and endoderm (Platyhelminthes to chordates).

example.q: A Hydra has ectoderm and endoderm with a jelly-like layer in between. Classify its germ-layer organisation and symmetry.

topics.title: Coelom, segmentation and notochord

learn.hook: A body cavity is like a padded room inside you where organs can move and grow. Not every animal has one, and some have a 'fake' one.
points: Coelom: a body cavity lined by mesoderm. Coelomates: annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates.
Pseudocoelom: the cavity is not lined by mesoderm; mesoderm is present as scattered pouches between ectoderm and endoderm (Aschelminthes). Acoelomates have no body cavity (Platyhelminthes).
Metameric segmentation (metamerism): the body is divided externally and internally into segments with serial repetition of some organs, as in the earthworm.

Notochord: a mesodermally derived rod-like structure formed on the dorsal side during embryonic development. Animals with it are chordates; those without are non-chordates (Porifera to Echinodermata).

Broad flowchart: cellular level (Porifera) → tissue level, diploblastic, radial (Coelenterata, Ctenophora) → triploblastic acoelomate (Platyhelminthes), pseudocoelomate (Aschelminthes), coelomate (annelids onwards) → notochord (Chordata).

Pseudocoelomates are Aschelminthes.
example.answer: Aschelminthes (roundworms).

topics.title: Porifera, Coelenterata and Ctenophora

learn.hook: Swimmers in the Andaman Sea learn to respect jellyfish tentacles. Each one is loaded with thousands of tiny harpoons.
points: Porifera (sponges): mostly marine, asymmetrical, cellular level. A water canal system: water enters through ostia into the spongocoel and leaves by the osculum; it helps in food gathering, gas exchange and waste removal. Choanocytes (collar cells) line the spongocoel and canals. Digestion is intracellular. Skeleton of spicules or spongin fibres. Hermaphrodite; asexual reproduction by fragmentation; fertilisation internal; development indirect. Sycon, Spongilla (freshwater), Euspongia (bath sponge).

Coelenterata (Cnidaria): aquatic, mostly marine, radial, diploblastic, tissue level. Cnidoblasts (cnidocytes) with nematocysts on tentacles are used for anchorage, defence and prey capture. Gastrovascular cavity with a single opening, the mouth on the hypostome; digestion extracellular and intracellular. Corals have a calcium carbonate skeleton.

Two body forms: polyp (sessile, cylindrical; Hydra, Adamsia) and medusa (umbrella-shaped, free-swimming; Aurelia). In Obelia, polyps produce medusae asexually and medusae form polyps sexually: metagenesis (alternation of generation). Examples: Physalia (Portuguese man-of-war), Adamsia (sea anemone), Pennatula (sea-pen), Gorgonia (sea-fan), Meandrina (brain coral).

Ctenophora (sea walnuts or comb jellies): exclusively marine, radial, diploblastic, tissue level. Eight external rows of ciliated comb plates help locomotion. Bioluminescence is well marked. Sexes not separate; only sexual reproduction; external fertilisation; indirect development. Pleurobrachia, Ctenoplana.

topics.title: Flatworms, roundworms and annelids

learn.hook: Deworming tablets are given to crores of Indian children on National Deworming Day. The targets are flatworms and roundworms.
points: Platyhelminthes (flatworms): dorsoventrally flattened, mostly endoparasites; bilateral, triploblastic, acoelomate, organ level. Hooks and suckers in parasites; some absorb nutrients through the body surface. Flame cells help osmoregulation and excretion. Sexes not separate; fertilisation internal; many larval stages. Planaria has high regeneration capacity. Taenia (tapeworm), Fasciola (liver fluke).

Aschelminthes (roundworms): circular in cross-section; free-living or parasitic; organ-system level; bilateral, triploblastic, pseudocoelomate. Complete alimentary canal with a muscular pharynx; an excretory tube opens by an excretory pore. Dioecious, with females often longer than males (sexual dimorphism). Fertilisation internal; development direct or indirect. Ascaris (roundworm), Wuchereria (filarial worm), Ancylostoma (hookworm).

Annelida: aquatic or terrestrial; organ-system level; bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate, metamerically segmented. Longitudinal and circular muscles help locomotion; Nereis has parapodia for swimming.

Annelids have a closed circulatory system and nephridia for osmoregulation and excretion; the nervous system has paired ganglia joined to a double ventral nerve cord. Nereis is dioecious; earthworms and leeches are monoecious. Pheretima (earthworm), Hirudinaria (blood-sucking leech).

example.answer: Aschelminthes, e.g. Ascaris.

topics.title: Arthropoda and Mollusca

learn.hook: More than two out of every three named species on Earth are arthropods. Honeybees, silkworms, mosquitoes and crabs all wear armour.
points: Arthropoda: the largest phylum (over two-thirds of named species). Organ-system level; bilateral, triploblastic, segmented, coelomate. Chitinous exoskeleton; body of head, thorax and abdomen; jointed appendages (arthros = joint, poda = appendages).

Arthropods breathe by gills, book gills, book lungs or tracheae; circulation is open; excretion by Malpighian tubules; senses include antennae, compound and simple eyes and statocysts. Mostly dioecious, fertilisation usually internal, mostly oviparous.

Arthropod examples: Apis (honeybee), Bombyx (silkworm), Laccifer (lac insect) are useful; Anopheles, Culex and Aedes (mosquitoes) are vectors; Locusta (locust) is a gregarious pest; Limulus (king crab) is a living fossil.

Mollusca: the second largest phylum; organ-system level; bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate. Unsegmented soft body with a calcareous shell, distinct head, muscular foot and visceral hump. The mantle covers the hump; feather-like gills in the mantle cavity do respiration and excretion. Head has sensory tentacles; the mouth has a rasping, file-like radula.

Molluscs are usually dioecious and oviparous with indirect development. Pila (apple snail), Pinctada (pearl oyster), Sepia (cuttlefish), Loligo (squid), Octopus (devil fish), Aplysia (sea-hare), Dentalium (tusk shell), Chaetopleura (chiton).

topics.title: Echinodermata and Hemichordata

learn.hook: A starfish walks on hundreds of tiny water-filled feet and has no excretory system at all. Strange, but true.
points: Echinodermata (spiny-skinned): endoskeleton of calcareous ossicles; all marine; organ-system level; triploblastic, coelomate. Adults are radially symmetrical, larvae bilaterally symmetrical.

Complete gut with mouth on the lower (ventral) side and anus on the upper (dorsal) side. The water vascular system, their most distinctive feature, helps locomotion, capture and transport of food, and respiration. There is no excretory system. Sexes separate; fertilisation usually external; development indirect with a free-swimming larva.
Examples: Asterias (starfish), Echinus (sea urchin), Antedon (sea lily), Cucumaria (sea cucumber), Ophiura (brittle star).

Hemichordata: small group of worm-like marine animals, once a sub-phylum of Chordata, now a separate non-chordate phylum. Body of proboscis, collar and trunk. A rudimentary stomochord in the collar is similar to a notochord. Open circulation; respiration by gills; excretion by a proboscis gland; sexes separate; external fertilisation; indirect development. Balanoglossus, Saccoglossus.

Signature features to remember: water canal system (Porifera), cnidoblasts (Coelenterata), comb plates (Ctenophora), flame cells (Platyhelminthes), parapodia (Nereis), Malpighian tubules (insects), radula (Mollusca), water vascular system (Echinodermata).

example.q: Why are Balanoglossus and its relatives no longer placed in Chordata?
steps: They have only a stomochord in the collar, a rudimentary structure similar to a notochord, not a true notochord.
So they are placed in a separate phylum, Hemichordata, under non-chordates.
example.answer: They lack a true notochord; the stomochord is only notochord-like.

topics.title: Phylum Chordata: key features and subphyla

learn.hook: A tiny sea squirt larva has a notochord in its tail, then loses it as an adult. Yet both it and you are chordates.
points: Fundamental chordate features: notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits and a post-anal tail. Chordates are bilateral, triploblastic, coelomate, at organ-system level, with a closed circulatory system.

Chordates vs non-chordates: notochord present vs absent; nerve cord dorsal, hollow, single vs ventral, solid, double; pharynx with gill slits vs no gill slits; heart ventral vs dorsal (if present); post-anal tail present vs absent.

Subphyla: Urochordata (Tunicata), notochord only in the larval tail (Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum); Cephalochordata, notochord from head to tail throughout life (Branchiostoma, also called Amphioxus or lancelet); Vertebrata.

Vertebrates have a notochord only in the embryo; it is replaced by a cartilaginous or bony vertebral column. They have a ventral muscular heart (2, 3 or 4 chambers), kidneys and paired appendages (fins or limbs). All vertebrates are chordates, but not all chordates are vertebrates.

Vertebrata: Agnatha (no jaws; class Cyclostomata) and Gnathostomata (jaws; superclass Pisces with fins: Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes; superclass Tetrapoda with limbs: Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia).

example.answer: It keeps a notochord all its life and has no vertebral column.

learn.reallife: The soft jelly-like core of each disc in your spine is a remnant of your embryonic notochord, which is why spine surgeons treating slipped discs care about it.

topics.title: Cyclostomes and fishes

learn.hook: Sharks must keep swimming or they sink, while a rohu in a Bengal pond can hover still. The secret is an air bladder.
points: Cyclostomata: jawless ectoparasites on fishes; elongated body with 6–15 pairs of gill slits; sucking circular mouth without jaws; no scales or paired fins; cartilaginous cranium and vertebral column; closed circulation. Marine, but migrate to fresh water to spawn, and die within a few days; larvae return to the ocean. Petromyzon (lamprey), Myxine (hagfish).

Chondrichthyes: marine, streamlined, cartilaginous endoskeleton; ventral mouth; notochord persists throughout life; gill slits separate, no operculum; tough skin with minute placoid scales; teeth are modified placoid scales directed backwards. No air bladder, so they swim constantly to avoid sinking. Two-chambered heart; cold-blooded.

Chondrichthyes contd.: some have electric organs (Torpedo) or a poison sting (Trygon); males have claspers on pelvic fins; internal fertilisation; many viviparous. Scoliodon (dogfish), Pristis (sawfish), Carcharodon (great white shark), Trygon (stingray).

Osteichthyes: marine and freshwater, bony endoskeleton; mouth mostly terminal; four pairs of gills covered by an operculum on each side; cycloid or ctenoid scales; air bladder regulates buoyancy; two-chambered heart; cold-blooded; fertilisation usually external; mostly oviparous, development direct.
Osteichthyes examples: Exocoetus (flying fish), Hippocampus (sea horse), Labeo (rohu), Catla (katla), Clarias (magur), Betta (fighting fish), Pterophyllum (angel fish).

example.q: A fish has a ventral mouth, placoid scales, no operculum and claspers on its pelvic fins. Classify it and say why it must keep swimming.
steps: Ventral mouth, placoid scales and no operculum indicate cartilaginous fish.
Claspers are in males of Chondrichthyes.
They lack an air bladder, so they would sink if they stopped.
example.answer: Chondrichthyes; no air bladder.

topics.title: Amphibians and reptiles

learn.hook: A frog breathes through its skin, and a crocodile has a four-chambered heart like ours. Tetrapods start getting interesting.
points: Amphibia: live in water and on land; most have two pairs of limbs; body of head and trunk; moist skin without scales; eyelids; a tympanum represents the ear.

Amphibians: the gut, urinary and reproductive tracts open into a common cloaca; respiration by gills, lungs and skin; three-chambered heart (two auricles, one ventricle); cold-blooded; sexes separate; external fertilisation; oviparous; development indirect. Bufo (toad), Rana (frog), Hyla (tree frog), Salamandra (salamander), Ichthyophis (limbless amphibian).
Reptilia (Latin repere, to creep): mostly terrestrial; dry, cornified skin with epidermal scales or scutes; no external ear openings, a tympanum represents the ear; limbs, when present, two pairs.

Reptiles: heart usually three-chambered but four-chambered in crocodiles; poikilotherms; snakes and lizards shed scales as skin cast; internal fertilisation; oviparous; development direct. Chelone (turtle), Testudo (tortoise), Chameleon (tree lizard), Calotes (garden lizard), Crocodilus (crocodile), Alligator, Hemidactylus (wall lizard), and poisonous snakes Naja (cobra), Bangarus (krait), Vipera (viper).

example.q: Compare fertilisation and development in a frog and a garden lizard.
steps: Frog: external fertilisation, eggs hatch into tadpoles, so development is indirect.
Garden lizard: internal fertilisation; young hatch looking like adults, so development is direct.
example.answer: Frog: external fertilisation, indirect development. Lizard: internal fertilisation, direct development.

topics.title: Birds and mammals

learn.hook: A peacock's bones are hollow like bamboo, and a platypus lays eggs yet feeds its young milk. Nature loves exceptions.
points: Aves: feathers; most fly (flightless: ostrich); beak; forelimbs modified into wings; hind limbs scaly, adapted for walking, swimming or perching. Dry skin with only an oil gland at the base of the tail.

Birds: fully ossified endoskeleton with hollow, air-filled (pneumatic) long bones; crop and gizzard in the gut; completely four-chambered heart; warm-blooded (homoiothermous); lungs with air sacs; internal fertilisation; oviparous; direct development. Corvus (crow), Columba (pigeon), Psittacula (parrot), Struthio (ostrich), Pavo (peacock), Aptenodytes (penguin), Neophron (vulture).

Mammalia: mammary glands (milk-producing) are the most unique feature. Two pairs of limbs adapted for walking, running, climbing, burrowing, swimming or flying. Hair on the skin; external ears (pinnae); different types of teeth; four-chambered heart; homoiothermous; lungs.

Mammals: sexes separate, internal fertilisation; viviparous with few exceptions; development direct. Oviparous: Ornithorhynchus (platypus). Viviparous: Macropus (kangaroo), Pteropus (flying fox), Camelus, Macaca (monkey), Rattus, Canis, Felis, Elephas, Equus, Delphinus (dolphin), Balaenoptera (blue whale), Panthera tigris, Panthera leo.

topics.title: Salient features of the phyla: putting it together

learn.hook: Board exams love a 'which phylum is this?' question. Master the summary table and you can crack any of them.
points: Porifera: cellular level, asymmetrical, canal system. Coelenterata and Ctenophora: tissue level, radial, diploblastic.
Platyhelminthes: organ level, bilateral, triploblastic, acoelomate, incomplete gut. Aschelminthes: pseudocoelomate, complete gut. Annelida: coelomate, segmented, closed circulation.

Arthropoda: segmented, jointed appendages, open circulation. Mollusca: unsegmented, open circulation. Echinodermata: adult radial, coelomate, water vascular system, complete gut. Hemichordata: open circulation. Chordata: notochord, closed circulation.
Direct development: young resemble adults (e.g. reptiles, birds, mammals, bony fish). Indirect development: a larval stage different from the adult (e.g. sponges, echinoderms, amphibians).
Open circulation in arthropods, molluscs and hemichordates; closed in annelids and chordates.

topics.title: Morphology and root systems

learn.hook: Pull out a mustard seedling and a wheat seedling from a Punjab field. One has a single deep anchor; the other has a bushy beard of roots.
points: Morphology is the study of the external form and features of organisms. A flowering plant has a root, stem, leaves, flowers and fruits.
Tap root system: in most dicots the radicle elongates into a primary root that bears secondary and tertiary lateral roots, e.g. mustard.
Fibrous root system: in monocots the primary root is short-lived and is replaced by many roots arising from the base of the stem, e.g. wheat.
Adventitious roots arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle, e.g. grass, Monstera and the banyan tree.
Functions of roots: absorption of water and minerals, anchorage, storage of reserve food, and synthesis of plant growth regulators.

example.q: A banyan's hanging roots grow down from its branches. Classify these roots and explain.
steps: Tap and fibrous roots develop from the radicle or stem base of a seedling.
These roots arise from branches, a part other than the radicle.
example.answer: They are adventitious roots.

learn.reallife: The banyan, India's national tree, spreads using adventitious roots that become pillar-like; the Great Banyan in Howrah's botanical garden covers several acres.

topics.title: Regions of the root, and the stem

learn.hook: A root tip pushes through hard soil every day without getting hurt. It wears a helmet, just like a cricketer facing a fast bowler.
points: The root apex is covered by a thimble-like root cap that protects it as it pushes through soil.
Region of meristematic activity, a few millimetres above the root cap: small, thin-walled cells with dense protoplasm that divide repeatedly.

Region of elongation: cells elongate and enlarge rapidly, making the root grow in length. Region of maturation: cells differentiate; some epidermal cells form fine root hairs that absorb water and minerals.

The stem is the ascending part of the axis that develops from the plumule. It bears nodes (where leaves arise), internodes (between nodes), and terminal or axillary buds. It is green when young, often woody and dark brown later.
Stem functions: spreading out branches with leaves, flowers and fruits; conducting water, minerals and photosynthates; and in some plants storage, support, protection and vegetative propagation.

example.q: List the regions of a root from the tip upwards.
steps: Tip is covered by the root cap.
Next is the region of meristematic activity.
Then the region of elongation.
Then the region of maturation, which bears root hairs.
example.answer: Root cap → meristematic region → elongation region → maturation region

learn.reallife: Sugarcane growers in Uttar Pradesh plant stem cuttings with nodes to raise new plants, using the stem's power of vegetative propagation.

topics.title: The leaf: parts and venation

learn.hook: Watch a peepal leaf flutter in the slightest breeze. Its long, flexible petiole is cooling the leaf, a design trick worth learning.
points: A leaf is a lateral, generally flattened structure borne on the stem at a node, with a bud in its axil. Leaves arise from the shoot apical meristem in acropetal order.

A typical leaf has a leaf base, petiole and lamina. The leaf base may bear two small leaf-like stipules. In monocots the leaf base forms a sheath around the stem; in some legumes it is swollen into a pulvinus.
The petiole holds the blade to the light. Long, thin, flexible petioles let blades flutter, cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air to its surface.
The lamina is the green expanded part with veins and veinlets; the prominent middle vein is the midrib. Veins give rigidity and carry water, minerals and food.
Venation: reticulate (veinlets form a network), generally in dicots; parallel (veins run parallel), generally in monocots.

example.q: A leaf has parallel veins and a sheathing leaf base. What group does the plant probably belong to?
steps: Parallel venation is typical of monocots.
A sheathing leaf base is also a monocot feature.
example.answer: A monocot.

learn.reallife: Banana and maize leaves show parallel venation, while the mango and peepal leaves used in Indian festive decorations show reticulate venation.

topics.title: Simple and compound leaves, and phyllotaxy

learn.hook: Is a neem 'leaf' one leaf or many? The answer depends on where you find a bud.
points: Simple leaf: the lamina is entire, or its incisions do not reach the midrib.
Compound leaf: incisions reach the midrib, breaking the lamina into leaflets. A bud is present in the axil of the petiole, but never in the axil of a leaflet.

Pinnately compound: leaflets on a common axis, the rachis (which represents the midrib), e.g. neem. Palmately compound: leaflets attached at a common point at the tip of the petiole, e.g. silk cotton.
Phyllotaxy is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem.
Alternate: one leaf per node (china rose, mustard, sunflower). Opposite: a pair of leaves per node, facing each other (Calotropis, guava). Whorled: more than two leaves per node (Alstonia).

example.q: How can you tell a leaflet of neem from a simple leaf?
steps: A simple leaf has a bud in its axil.
In a compound leaf, the bud is only in the axil of the petiole, not of each leaflet.
So a leaflet has no axillary bud.
example.answer: A leaflet has no bud in its axil; a simple leaf does.
