topics.title: Inflorescence: racemose and cymose

learn.hook: On a mustard spike in a Rajasthan field, the youngest buds are at the top. On some other plants, the oldest flower sits at the tip. The axis decides.
points: A flower is a modified shoot: the shoot apical meristem becomes a floral meristem, internodes do not elongate, the axis condenses, and floral appendages form at successive nodes instead of leaves.
When the shoot tip itself becomes a flower, the flower is solitary. The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is the inflorescence.
Racemose: the main axis continues to grow, and flowers are borne laterally in acropetal succession (older flowers at the base, younger towards the tip).
Cymose: the main axis ends in a flower, so its growth is limited; flowers are borne in basipetal order (older at the tip, younger below).
Quick test: if the apex keeps growing, it is racemose; if the apex has become a flower, it is cymose.

example.q: On an inflorescence, the topmost flower opened first and the lower ones later. Which type is it?
steps: The terminal flower is the oldest, so the axis ended in a flower.

topics.title: The flower: whorls, sex and symmetry

learn.hook: Cut a datura flower in any direction through the centre and you get two equal halves. Try that with a pea flower and only one cut works.
points: The flower is the reproductive unit of angiosperms. Its four whorls sit on the swollen end of the pedicel, the thalamus (receptacle): calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
Calyx and corolla are accessory organs; androecium and gynoecium are reproductive organs. When calyx and corolla are not distinct, as in lily, they are called perianth.
Bisexual flower: has both androecium and gynoecium. Unisexual flower: has only stamens or only carpels.

Symmetry: actinomorphic (radial) if any radial plane through the centre gives two equal halves (mustard, datura, chilli); zygomorphic (bilateral) if only one vertical plane does (pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia); asymmetric if none does (canna).

Trimerous, tetramerous and pentamerous flowers have floral parts in multiples of 3, 4 and 5. Flowers with bracts (reduced leaves at the base of the pedicel) are bracteate; those without are ebracteate.

example.q: A flower has 5 sepals, 5 petals, 5 stamens and can be cut into two equal halves along any radial plane. Describe it.
steps: Parts in multiples of five: pentamerous.
Equal halves in any radial plane: actinomorphic.
example.answer: Pentamerous and actinomorphic.

learn.reallife: Chilli flowers in Andhra Pradesh's Guntur district, India's chilli capital, are small, white and actinomorphic.

games.title: Term to meaning
pairs: Reduced leaf at the base of the pedicel

quiz.q: The swollen end of the pedicel on which floral whorls are borne is the:
quiz.explain: The thalamus (receptacle) carries all four whorls.
steps: The floral whorls sit on the swollen end of the pedicel.
This is the thalamus (receptacle).
Answer: Thalamus

quiz.q: A flower that can be divided into two similar halves only in one vertical plane is:
quiz.explain: Pea and gulmohur flowers are zygomorphic.
steps: If only one vertical plane gives similar halves, the flower is zygomorphic.
Examples: pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia.
Actinomorphic has many such planes.
Answer: Zygomorphic

quiz.q: Canna has which type of flower symmetry?
quiz.explain: No vertical plane divides a canna flower into similar halves.
steps: Canna cannot be cut into similar halves by any vertical plane.
So it is asymmetric.
Answer: Asymmetric

quiz.q: When calyx and corolla cannot be told apart, as in lily, they are called:
quiz.explain: The undifferentiated outer whorls form the perianth.
steps: In lily, calyx and corolla are not distinct.
Together they are called perianth.
Answer: Perianth

quiz.q: Which are the reproductive whorls of a flower?
quiz.explain: Stamens and carpels are reproductive; sepals and petals are accessory.
steps: Calyx and corolla are accessory whorls.
Androecium (stamens) and gynoecium (carpels) are reproductive.
Answer: Androecium and gynoecium
quiz.mistake: Mixes up accessory and reproductive whorls

quiz.q: A flower with floral parts in multiples of four is:
quiz.explain: Tetra- means four.
steps: Trimerous = multiples of 3; tetramerous = 4; pentamerous = 5.
Multiples of four = tetramerous.
Answer: Tetramerous

quiz.q: A flower lacking bracts is described as:
quiz.explain: Ebracteate means without bracts.
steps: Bracts are reduced leaves at the base of the pedicel.
A flower without bracts is ebracteate.
Answer: Ebracteate
quiz.mistake: Confuses bracts with sex of the flower

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A unisexual flower has only stamens or only carpels. Reason (R): In a unisexual flower, the calyx and corolla are always absent.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is the definition of unisexual. R is false: unisexual flowers can have sepals and petals.
steps: A: a unisexual flower has only stamens or only carpels. True.
R: its calyx and corolla are always absent. False: unisexual flowers can have them.
So A is true, R is false.
Answer: A is true, but R is false
quiz.mistake: Thinks unisexual flowers lack all accessory whorls

teach.ask: Gappu holds a datura flower and a pea flower. Explain the parts of a flower and the types of symmetry!

teach.nudge: Good! What are the four whorls, and how do the symmetry types differ?

revise.summary: A flower has four whorls on the thalamus: calyx and corolla (accessory) and androecium and gynoecium (reproductive). Flowers may be bisexual or unisexual; actinomorphic, zygomorphic or asymmetric; trimerous, tetramerous or pentamerous; bracteate or ebracteate.

Actinomorphic, zygomorphic and asymmetric with examples
remember: Thalamus = swollen end of pedicel
Perianth: undifferentiated calyx and corolla (lily)

Don't call a pea flower actinomorphic

topics.title: Position of ovary, calyx and corolla aestivation

learn.hook: Look at a guava fruit: the dried flower parts sit on its top. That tells you the ovary was 'inferior', sunk inside the thalamus.
points: Hypogynous: gynoecium highest, other parts below it; ovary superior (mustard, china rose, brinjal). Perigynous: gynoecium in the centre, other parts on the rim of the thalamus at about the same level; ovary half-inferior (plum, rose, peach). Epigynous: thalamus grows up and fuses with the ovary, other parts arise above it; ovary inferior (guava, cucumber, ray florets of sunflower).
Calyx: outermost whorl of sepals, usually green and leaf-like, protecting the bud. Gamosepalous (sepals united) or polysepalous (free).
Corolla: petals, usually brightly coloured to attract insects for pollination; gamopetalous or polypetalous. Shapes include tubular, bell-shaped, funnel-shaped and wheel-shaped.

Aestivation is the arrangement of sepals or petals in the bud relative to others in the same whorl. Valvate: margins just touch, no overlap (Calotropis). Twisted: each margin overlaps the next in one direction (china rose, lady's finger, cotton). Imbricate: margins overlap in no particular direction (Cassia, gulmohur).
Vexillary (papilionaceous) in pea and bean: the largest petal (standard) overlaps two lateral wings, which overlap the two smallest anterior petals (keel).

example.q: In a pea flower, which petal is outermost in the bud and which is innermost?
steps: Vexillary aestivation has five petals.
The large standard overlaps the two wings.
The wings overlap the two keel petals.
example.answer: Standard is outermost; keel is innermost.

learn.reallife: Cotton and bhindi (lady's finger), both major crops in Gujarat and Maharashtra, show twisted aestivation in their petals.

quiz.q: In which flower is the ovary inferior?
quiz.explain: Guava is epigynous with an inferior ovary.
steps: An inferior ovary is found in epigynous flowers.
Guava is epigynous.
Mustard, china rose and brinjal are hypogynous (superior ovary).
Answer: Guava

quiz.q: Perigynous flowers have an ovary that is:
quiz.explain: Other parts are on the thalamus rim at about the ovary's level.
steps: In perigynous flowers other parts are on the rim of the thalamus at about the ovary's level.
So the ovary is half-inferior.
Answer: Half-inferior

quiz.q: Twisted aestivation is found in:
quiz.explain: Each petal overlaps the next in one direction.
steps: Twisted: each margin overlaps the next in one direction.
Seen in china rose, lady's finger and cotton.
Calotropis is valvate; Cassia imbricate; pea vexillary.
Answer: China rose, lady's finger and cotton
options: China rose, lady's finger and cotton

quiz.q: In valvate aestivation, the sepals or petals:
quiz.explain: Valvate means edge-to-edge contact, as in Calotropis.
steps: In valvate aestivation the margins just touch.
They do not overlap, as in Calotropis.
Answer: Just touch at the margins without overlapping

quiz.explain: Standard is largest, wings are lateral, keel is smallest and anterior.
steps: Vexillary: standard (largest), two wings, two keel petals.
The two smallest anterior petals are the keel.
Answer: Keel

quiz.q: A calyx with united sepals is:
quiz.explain: Gamo- means united.
steps: Gamo- means united; poly- means free.
United sepals = gamosepalous.
Answer: Gamosepalous

quiz.q: Brinjal flowers are:
quiz.explain: Brinjal has a superior ovary.
steps: Brinjal has a superior ovary with other parts below it.
A superior ovary means a hypogynous flower.
Answer: Hypogynous

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Petals are usually brightly coloured. Reason (R): Bright petals attract insects for pollination.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; attracting pollinators is the reason for bright colours.

R: bright petals attract insects for pollination. True.

Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

revise.summary: By ovary position, flowers are hypogynous (superior ovary), perigynous (half-inferior) or epigynous (inferior). Sepals and petals may be free or united, and their arrangement in bud (aestivation) is valvate, twisted, imbricate or vexillary.

Vexillary: standard → wings → keel

topics.title: Androecium: stamens and their unions

learn.hook: In a hibiscus flower, the stamens form a single tube around the style. In a pea, nine join and one stays apart. Stamens love teamwork in different ways.
points: The androecium is made of stamens, the male reproductive organs. Each stamen has a stalk (filament) and an anther.
An anther is usually bilobed, and each lobe has two chambers, the pollen sacs, where pollen grains form. A sterile stamen is a staminode.
Epipetalous stamens are attached to petals (brinjal). Epiphyllous stamens are attached to the perianth (lily).
Stamens may be free (polyandrous) or united: monoadelphous (one bundle, china rose), diadelphous (two bundles, pea), polyadelphous (more than two bundles, citrus).
Filament length may vary within a flower, as in Salvia and mustard.

example.q: How many pollen sacs does a typical stamen have?
steps: A typical anther is bilobed: 2 lobes.
Each lobe has 2 chambers (pollen sacs).
Total = 2 × 2 = 4.
example.answer: 4 pollen sacs

learn.reallife: Lemon and orange orchards of Nagpur grow citrus flowers with polyadelphous stamens in several bundles.

Each anther lobe has two pollen sacs.

Lily stamens are on the perianth.
Answer: Epiphyllous

quiz.explain: Two lobes, each with two pollen sacs: 2 × 2 = 4.

Pollen sacs per lobe = 2
Answer: 4

quiz.explain: All stamens of china rose are united in one bundle around the style.

One bundle = monoadelphous.
Answer: Monoadelphous

quiz.q: Citrus has stamens that are:
quiz.explain: Citrus stamens form more than two bundles.

More than two bundles = polyadelphous.
Answer: Polyadelphous

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Brinjal has epipetalous stamens. Reason (R): In brinjal, stamens are fused with the gynoecium.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

R: brinjal stamens are fused with the gynoecium. False: they are attached to petals.

revise.summary: The androecium is made of stamens, each a filament and a usually bilobed anther with four pollen sacs. Stamens may be epipetalous or epiphyllous, free or united into one, two or many bundles; a sterile stamen is a staminode.

Monoadelphous, diadelphous and polyadelphous with examples

topics.title: Gynoecium and placentation

learn.hook: Slice a tomato across and you see seeds attached to a central axis in separate chambers. Slice a pea pod and they sit along one edge. That's placentation.
points: The gynoecium is the female reproductive part, made of one or more carpels. Each carpel has a stigma (receptive surface for pollen), style (connects stigma to ovary) and ovary (enlarged base).
Ovules are attached to a flattened, cushion-like placenta in the ovary. After fertilisation ovules become seeds and the ovary becomes the fruit.
Apocarpous: carpels free (lotus, rose). Syncarpous: carpels fused (mustard, tomato).

Placentation types: marginal (ridge along the ventral suture, two rows of ovules; pea), axile (central axis in a multilocular ovary; china rose, tomato, lemon), parietal (ovules on the inner wall; one-chambered ovary made two-chambered by a false septum; mustard, Argemone).
Free central: ovules on a central axis with no septa (Dianthus, Primrose). Basal: placenta at the base with a single ovule (sunflower, marigold).

example.q: A lemon cut crosswise shows several chambers with seeds attached at the centre. Name the placentation.
steps: Multilocular ovary.
Ovules attached to a central axis.
This is axile placentation.
example.answer: Axile placentation.

learn.reallife: Marigold flowers, used in lakhs of garlands during Diwali, have basal placentation with a single ovule.

quiz.q: Placentation in pea is:
quiz.explain: Ovules lie in two rows on a ridge along the ventral suture.
steps: In pea, ovules lie in two rows on a ridge along the ventral suture.
That is marginal placentation.
Answer: Marginal

quiz.q: Axile placentation is found in:
quiz.explain: Ovules are on a central axis in a multilocular ovary.
steps: Axile: ovules on a central axis in a multilocular ovary.
Examples: china rose, tomato, lemon.
Answer: Tomato and lemon

quiz.q: In which placentation does a false septum make a one-chambered ovary two-chambered?
quiz.explain: Mustard and Argemone show parietal placentation with a false septum.
steps: In parietal placentation ovules are on the inner wall.
A false septum makes the one-chambered ovary two-chambered (mustard, Argemone).
Answer: Parietal

quiz.q: Free central placentation is seen in:
quiz.explain: Ovules are on a central axis without septa.
steps: Free central: ovules on a central axis with no septa.
Examples: Dianthus and Primrose.
Answer: Dianthus and Primrose

quiz.q: A gynoecium with free carpels is called:
quiz.explain: Lotus and rose have free carpels.
steps: Free carpels = apocarpous (lotus, rose).
Fused carpels = syncarpous.
Answer: Apocarpous

quiz.q: The receptive surface for pollen grains is the:
quiz.explain: Pollen lands on the stigma.
steps: Each carpel has stigma, style and ovary.
The stigma is the receptive surface for pollen.
Answer: Stigma

quiz.q: In sunflower and marigold, placentation is:
quiz.explain: The placenta is at the base with a single ovule.
steps: In sunflower and marigold the placenta is at the base.
It bears a single ovule: basal placentation.
Answer: Basal

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A ripened ovary forms the fruit. Reason (R): After fertilisation, ovules develop into seeds.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true statements about events after fertilisation, but seed formation from ovules does not explain how the ovary becomes the fruit.
steps: A: ripened ovary forms the fruit. True.
R: ovules develop into seeds. True.
Seed formation does not explain fruit formation, so R is not the explanation.
Answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Links two parallel facts as cause and effect

teach.praise: Tweet! Stigma, style, ovary, and seeds placed in five different ways. Tomato science!

revise.summary: The gynoecium is made of carpels, each with stigma, style and ovary; it may be apocarpous or syncarpous. Ovules sit on placentae in marginal, axile, parietal, free central or basal placentation. After fertilisation ovules form seeds and the ovary forms the fruit.

remember: Marginal: pea; axile: china rose, tomato, lemon
Parietal: mustard, Argemone (false septum)
Free central: Dianthus, Primrose; basal: sunflower, marigold
traps: Don't confuse parietal (on wall) with axile (central axis with septa)
Don't call free central placentation axile; it has no septa

topics.title: Fruit and the parts of a seed

learn.hook: In a mango, you eat the middle layer and throw away the hard inner one. In a coconut, the middle layer becomes coir ropes.
points: A fruit is a mature or ripened ovary that develops after fertilisation; it is a characteristic feature of flowering plants. A fruit formed without fertilisation is parthenocarpic.
A fruit has a wall (pericarp) and seeds. A thick, fleshy pericarp is differentiated into an outer epicarp, middle mesocarp and inner endocarp.
Mango and coconut fruits are drupes: they develop from monocarpellary superior ovaries and are one-seeded.
In mango, the epicarp is thin, the mesocarp is fleshy and edible, and the endocarp is stony and hard. In coconut, the mesocarp is fibrous.
A seed develops from a fertilised ovule. It has a seed coat and an embryo; the embryo has a radicle, an embryonal axis and one (wheat, maize) or two (gram, pea) cotyledons.

example.q: Which layer of a mango do we eat, and which forms the hard 'guthli' shell?
steps: Mango is a drupe with epicarp, mesocarp and endocarp.
The fleshy edible part is the mesocarp.
The stony layer around the seed is the endocarp.
example.answer: We eat the mesocarp; the hard shell is the endocarp.

learn.reallife: Kerala's coir industry turns the fibrous mesocarp of coconut into ropes and mats; seedless banana and grapes are parthenocarpic varieties sold in Indian markets.

games.title: Fruit and seed facts
items: A fruit is a ripened ovary.
One-seeded, from a monocarpellary superior ovary.
The mesocarp of coconut is fleshy and edible.
The ovary forms the fruit; ovules form seeds.
Maize is a monocot with one cotyledon.

quiz.q: A fruit that develops without fertilisation is called:
quiz.explain: Parthenocarpy means fruit formation without fertilisation.
steps: A fruit formed without fertilisation is parthenocarpic.
Answer: Parthenocarpic
quiz.mistake: Confuses a fruit type with its mode of formation

topics.title: Structure of dicot and monocot seeds

learn.hook: Soak a gram seed overnight and it splits into two fat halves. A maize grain refuses to split. Their insides are built differently.
points: Dicot seed: the seed coat has an outer testa and inner tegmen. The hilum is the scar where the seed was attached to the fruit; the micropyle is a small pore above the hilum.
The dicot embryo has an embryonal axis with a radicle and plumule at its ends, and two cotyledons that are often fleshy and full of food.
Endospermic seeds keep the endosperm (formed by double fertilisation) as food-storing tissue, e.g. castor. Non-endospermic seeds have no endosperm in the mature seed, e.g. bean, gram, pea.

Monocot seeds are generally endospermic (orchids are non-endospermic). In maize, the seed coat is membranous and fused with the fruit wall; the bulky endosperm is separated from the embryo by a proteinous aleurone layer.

The maize embryo lies in a groove at one end of the endosperm. It has one large, shield-shaped cotyledon, the scutellum, and a short axis with plumule and radicle enclosed in sheaths, the coleoptile and coleorhiza respectively.

example.q: Name the sheaths that cover the plumule and the radicle in a maize embryo.
steps: The plumule is the future shoot; its sheath is the coleoptile.
The radicle is the future root; its sheath is the coleorhiza.
example.answer: Coleoptile covers the plumule; coleorhiza covers the radicle.

learn.reallife: India's maize belt in Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh grows corn whose grains are endospermic; soaked chana (gram) sprouts show two cotyledons and no endosperm.

topics.title: Semi-technical description, floral formula and floral diagram

learn.hook: A floral formula is like a cricket scorecard: a single line tells you everything about a flower if you know the symbols.
points: A semi-technical description uses brief, scientific language in a set sequence: habit, then vegetative characters (root, stem, leaves), then floral characters (inflorescence and flower parts), followed by the floral diagram and floral formula.
Symbols: Br bracteate, K calyx, C corolla, P perianth, A androecium, G gynoecium; ♂ male, ♀ female, ⚥ bisexual; ⊕ actinomorphic, % zygomorphic.
A line below G (G̲) shows a superior ovary; a line above G (Ḡ) shows an inferior ovary. Numbers give the count of parts.

Fusion (cohesion) of members of a whorl is shown by putting the number in brackets, e.g. C(5) means five united petals. Adhesion between whorls is shown by a line drawn above the symbols of those whorls, e.g. joining C and A for epipetalous stamens.

Floral diagram: a dot at the top shows the position of the mother axis. Calyx (outermost), corolla, androecium and gynoecium (centre) are drawn as successive whorls, showing number, aestivation, cohesion, adhesion and placentation. The NCERT example is mustard (family Brassicaceae).

example.q: Decode: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2), with a line joining C and A, and G(2) underlined.
steps: ⊕ actinomorphic, ⚥ bisexual.
K(5): five united sepals; C(5): five united petals.
A5 joined to C by a line: five epipetalous stamens.
G(2) underlined: bicarpellary, syncarpous, superior ovary.
example.answer: An actinomorphic bisexual flower with 5 united sepals, 5 united petals, 5 epipetalous stamens and a bicarpellary syncarpous superior ovary.

learn.reallife: Botanists at the Botanical Survey of India write floral formulae in field notebooks to record new plants quickly, much like a scorer's shorthand at a Ranji Trophy match.

topics.title: Family Solanaceae: the potato family

learn.hook: Your aloo paratha, tomato chutney, baingan bharta and green chilli all come from one plant family. Meet Solanaceae.
points: Solanaceae (potato family) is a large family spread across tropics, subtropics and temperate zones. Plants are mostly herbs and shrubs, rarely small trees.

Stem: herbaceous, rarely woody; erect, cylindrical, branched, solid or hollow, hairy or glabrous; underground stem in potato (Solanum tuberosum). Leaves: alternate, simple, rarely pinnately compound, exstipulate, reticulate venation.

Floral characters: inflorescence solitary, axillary or cymose (as in Solanum); flowers bisexual and actinomorphic. Calyx: five united sepals, persistent, valvate. Corolla: five united petals, valvate. Androecium: five epipetalous stamens.

Gynoecium: bicarpellary, syncarpous; ovary superior, bilocular, placenta swollen with many ovules; axile placentation. Fruit: berry or capsule. Seeds: many, endospermous. Floral formula: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2), with C and A joined (epipetalous) and G underlined (superior).
Uses: food (tomato, brinjal, potato), spice (chilli), medicine (belladonna, ashwagandha), fumigatory (tobacco), ornamental (petunia).

example.q: A brinjal flower has 5 united persistent sepals, 5 united petals, 5 stamens attached to petals, and a 2-carpelled fused superior ovary. Write its floral formula.
steps: Actinomorphic and bisexual: ⊕ ⚥.
Sepals united: K(5). Petals united: C(5).
Stamens epipetalous: A5 joined to C(5) by a line.
Two fused carpels, superior: G(2) underlined.
example.answer: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G(2) (C and A joined by a line, G underlined)

learn.reallife: India is among the world's largest producers of potato, tomato and brinjal, and ashwagandha is a major medicinal crop grown in Madhya Pradesh's Mandsaur and Neemuch districts.

topics.title: Anatomy, tissues and the three tissue systems

learn.hook: Slice a bhindi or a sugarcane and look closely: inside are neat layers and bundles, like cables in an underground metro tunnel.
points: Anatomy is the study of internal structure. Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and monocots and dicots differ in their internal structure.
Meristematic tissues divide (apical, intercalary, lateral). Permanent tissues are simple (one cell type: parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) or complex (many cell types: xylem and phloem).

Parenchyma: living, thin-walled, with spaces, for storage and photosynthesis. Collenchyma: living, thickened at corners, gives mechanical support to young stems. Sclerenchyma: dead, lignified fibres and sclereids for strength.
Xylem conducts water and minerals (tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, xylem parenchyma). Phloem transports food (sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres).
Based on location, tissues form three systems: epidermal tissue system, ground (fundamental) tissue system and vascular (conducting) tissue system.

example.q: Classify xylem and collenchyma as simple or complex tissues.
steps: Collenchyma is made of one type of cell: simple.

example.answer: Collenchyma is simple; xylem is complex.

topics.title: Epidermal tissue system: epidermis, stomata and hairs

learn.hook: A single mango leaf has thousands of tiny 'mouths' that open and close all day. Each is guarded by two kidney-bean cells.
points: The epidermis is the outermost layer: elongated, compactly arranged cells forming a continuous, usually single layer of parenchyma with little cytoplasm and a large vacuole.
A waxy cuticle often covers the epidermis to prevent water loss; it is absent in roots.

Stomata in the leaf epidermis regulate transpiration and gas exchange. Each stoma has two guard cells around a pore: bean-shaped in dicots, dumb-bell shaped in grasses. Their outer walls (away from the pore) are thin and inner walls (towards the pore) are highly thickened; guard cells have chloroplasts.
Subsidiary cells are specialised epidermal cells near the guard cells. The stomatal aperture, guard cells and subsidiary cells together form the stomatal apparatus.

Root hairs are unicellular elongations of epidermal cells that absorb water and minerals. Trichomes on the shoot are usually multicellular, branched or unbranched, soft or stiff, sometimes secretory, and help prevent water loss.

example.q: Name the parts of the stomatal apparatus.
steps: The pore itself: stomatal aperture.
Two cells enclosing the pore: guard cells.
Specialised epidermal cells around them: subsidiary cells.
example.answer: Stomatal aperture + guard cells + subsidiary cells

topics.title: Ground tissue and vascular bundles

learn.hook: Why can a neem trunk grow thicker every year but a coconut trunk can't? The answer is a thin strip of cambium in the vascular bundles.
points: Ground tissue system: all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles, made of parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma. Parenchyma is found in the cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays of primary stems and roots. In leaves, ground tissue is the chloroplast-rich mesophyll.
The vascular tissue system has xylem and phloem, which together form vascular bundles.
Open vascular bundles have cambium between phloem and xylem and can form secondary tissues (dicot stems). Closed vascular bundles lack cambium and form no secondary tissues (monocots).

Radial bundles: xylem and phloem alternate on different radii (roots). Conjoint bundles: xylem and phloem lie on the same radius (stems and leaves), usually with phloem on the outer side (collateral).
Exarch xylem: protoxylem towards the periphery, metaxylem towards the centre (roots). Endarch xylem: protoxylem towards the centre (pith), metaxylem towards the periphery (stems).

example.q: A section shows xylem and phloem on the same radius with cambium between them and protoxylem towards the pith. Describe the bundle.
steps: Same radius: conjoint.
Cambium present: open.
Protoxylem towards centre: endarch.
example.answer: Conjoint, open, endarch: typical of a dicot stem.

learn.reallife: Coconut palms of Kerala have closed bundles and no true secondary growth, so their trunks stay nearly the same width; neem and teak keep thickening.

topics.title: Anatomy of dicot and monocot roots

learn.hook: Inside a sunflower root sits a ring of cells with waxy belts, the Casparian strips, acting like a security checkpoint for water.
points: Dicot root (sunflower): outermost epiblema, many cells forming unicellular root hairs; cortex of several layers of thin-walled parenchyma with intercellular spaces.
Endodermis is the innermost cortical layer: one layer of barrel-shaped cells without intercellular spaces; their tangential and radial walls have water-impermeable, waxy suberin as Casparian strips.
Pericycle: a few layers of thick-walled parenchyma next to the endodermis; lateral roots and the vascular cambium (during secondary growth) arise here.

Dicot root has 2 to 4 xylem and phloem patches, parenchymatous conjunctive tissue between them, and a small or inconspicuous pith. Everything inside the endodermis (pericycle, vascular bundles, pith) is the stele.
Monocot root: same basic layers but usually more than six xylem bundles (polyarch), a large well-developed pith, and no secondary growth.

example.q: A root T.S. shows 12 xylem patches and a large pith. Is it dicot or monocot? Will it show secondary growth?
steps: More than six xylem bundles is polyarch, typical of monocot roots.
A large pith also fits monocot root.
Monocot roots do not undergo secondary growth.
example.answer: Monocot root; no secondary growth.

learn.reallife: Maize roots in Bihar's fields are polyarch monocot roots, while sunflower roots in Karnataka are the classic dicot example.

topics.title: Anatomy of dicot and monocot stems

learn.hook: Cut a sunflower stem and the bundles form a neat ring. Cut a maize stalk and they are sprinkled everywhere like masala on chaat.
points: Dicot stem: epidermis with a thin cuticle, may bear trichomes and a few stomata. The cortex has three zones: hypodermis (a few layers of collenchyma for mechanical strength), parenchymatous cortex with intercellular spaces, and endodermis rich in starch grains (starch sheath).
Pericycle lies inside the endodermis and above the phloem as semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma. Radially placed parenchyma cells between bundles form medullary rays.

Many vascular bundles are arranged in a ring, characteristic of dicot stems. Each bundle is conjoint, open, with endarch protoxylem. A large central pith of rounded parenchyma cells with large spaces.
Monocot stem: sclerenchymatous hypodermis; many scattered vascular bundles, each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath; large, conspicuous parenchymatous ground tissue.
Monocot bundles are conjoint and closed; peripheral ones are smaller than central ones; phloem parenchyma is absent; water-containing cavities are present within the bundles.

example.q: A stem T.S. shows scattered bundles, each with a bundle sheath and a water-containing cavity. Identify it.
steps: Scattered bundles: monocot stem.
Bundle sheath of sclerenchyma and water cavities confirm a monocot stem.
example.answer: Monocot stem.

learn.reallife: Sugarcane and maize stalks, key crops in Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka, are monocot stems with scattered bundles.

Monocot peripheral bundles smaller than central ones

Don't call monocot stem bundles open

topics.title: Dorsiventral and isobilateral leaves

learn.hook: In a hot afternoon in Rajasthan, wheat and grass leaves roll into tubes. Special 'hinge' cells are saving water.
points: Dorsiventral (dicot) leaf: epidermis on the upper (adaxial) and lower (abaxial) surfaces with a conspicuous cuticle. The abaxial epidermis generally has more stomata; the adaxial may even lack them.

Mesophyll is parenchyma with chloroplasts, for photosynthesis. Palisade parenchyma (adaxial) has elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel. Spongy parenchyma (below it) has oval or round, loosely arranged cells with large spaces and air cavities.
Vascular bundles in veins and midrib vary in size with reticulate venation and are surrounded by thick-walled bundle sheath cells.
Isobilateral (monocot) leaf: stomata on both surfaces, and mesophyll not differentiated into palisade and spongy layers.

In grasses, some adaxial epidermal cells along veins become large, empty, colourless bulliform cells. When turgid, the leaf stays open; when flaccid under water stress, the leaf curls inwards to reduce water loss. Parallel venation shows as bundles of nearly similar size.

example.q: Why do maize leaves roll up on a very hot, dry day?
steps: Water stress makes bulliform cells lose water and become flaccid.
Flaccid bulliform cells make the leaf curl inwards.
Curling reduces the exposed surface and water loss.
example.answer: Bulliform cells become flaccid and the leaf rolls to cut water loss.

learn.reallife: During heat waves in north India, farmers notice maize and sugarcane leaves rolling at noon, a sign of bulliform cells at work and of water stress in the crop.

topics.title: Comparing dicot and monocot anatomy and identifying sections

learn.hook: In the practical exam, the examiner hands you an unlabelled slide. Two minutes, one question: root or stem, dicot or monocot?
points: Root or stem? Roots have radial bundles with exarch xylem, an epiblema with root hairs and no cuticle. Stems have conjoint bundles with endarch xylem and a cuticle-covered epidermis.
Dicot root: 2 to 4 xylem patches, small pith, secondary growth possible. Monocot root: more than six xylem bundles (polyarch), large pith, no secondary growth.

Dicot stem: collenchymatous hypodermis, bundles in a ring, open, starch sheath, medullary rays, distinct pith. Monocot stem: sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered closed bundles with bundle sheath and water cavities, no distinct pith.
Dicot leaf: dorsiventral, palisade and spongy mesophyll, more stomata on the lower side. Monocot leaf: isobilateral, stomata on both sides, undifferentiated mesophyll, bulliform cells.

In T.S. diagrams, label: epidermis or epiblema, cortex, endodermis, pericycle, xylem (protoxylem and metaxylem), phloem, cambium where present, pith; for leaves: cuticle, epidermis, palisade, spongy cells, stomata, bundle sheath, xylem and phloem.

example.q: A T.S. shows radial bundles, exarch xylem with 4 patches, and a small pith. Identify it.
steps: Radial bundles and exarch xylem: root.
Only 4 xylem patches and small pith: dicot.
example.answer: Dicot root.

topics.title: Tissues, organs and organ systems

learn.hook: A cricket team works because the bowler, keeper and batters each do one job well. Your body runs on the same idea: division of labour.
points: In multicellular animals, similar cells with their intercellular material form tissues that perform a common function.
Animals have four basic tissue types: epithelial (covering and lining), connective (linking and supporting), muscular (movement) and neural (control and coordination).

Tissues are organised in specific proportions and patterns to form organs such as the stomach, lungs, heart and kidney. Organs working together form organ systems, such as the digestive and respiratory systems.
Division of labour among cells, tissues, organs and organ systems helps the whole body survive. The complexity of organs and organ systems shows a discernible evolutionary trend.
Morphology studies the externally visible form and features; in animals, anatomy refers to the study of the morphology of internal organs.

topics.title: The frog: habits and external features

learn.hook: When the monsoon arrives, frogs suddenly croak everywhere. Where were they all summer? Sleeping underground.
points: The common Indian frog is Rana tigrina (class Amphibia, phylum Chordata). Frogs are poikilotherms: their body temperature changes with the surroundings. They change colour to hide from enemies (camouflage); this protective colouration is called mimicry.
In peak summer and winter, frogs shelter in deep burrows: summer sleep is aestivation and winter sleep is hibernation.

Skin is smooth, slippery with mucus, and always moist. The dorsal side is olive green with dark irregular spots; the ventral side is uniformly pale yellow. A frog never drinks water; it absorbs water through its skin.

Body is divided into head and trunk; there is no neck or tail. A pair of nostrils lies above the mouth; bulging eyes are covered by a nictitating membrane that protects them in water; a membranous tympanum (ear) on each side receives sound.

Forelimbs end in four digits; hind limbs are larger and more muscular and end in five webbed digits for swimming. Males have vocal sacs and a copulatory pad on the first digit of each forelimb, absent in females (sexual dimorphism).

steps: Look for sound-producing vocal sacs: present only in males.

example.answer: Males have vocal sacs and copulatory pads on the forelimbs.

topics.title: Frog digestive and respiratory systems

learn.hook: A frog can breathe through its skin while sitting at the bottom of a pond. Humans cannot: we depend entirely on our lungs.
points: The body cavity holds the digestive, circulatory, respiratory, nervous, excretory and reproductive systems.
Digestive system: the alimentary canal is short because frogs are carnivores. Mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → intestine → rectum → cloaca. Food is caught by a bilobed tongue.

Stomach walls secrete HCl and gastric juices; partly digested food (chyme) passes to the duodenum, which receives bile (from liver via gall bladder) and pancreatic juice through a common bile duct. Bile emulsifies fat; pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins. Villi and microvilli in the intestine absorb digested food.

Respiration in water: through the skin by diffusion (cutaneous respiration). On land: buccal cavity, skin and lungs (pulmonary respiration through elongated pink sac-like lungs in the thorax). During aestivation and hibernation, gas exchange is through the skin.
Adaptations to amphibious life: moist skin for breathing, webbed hind feet for swimming, nictitating membrane for eyes, lungs for air, and the ability to aestivate or hibernate.

topics.title: Frog circulatory and excretory systems

learn.hook: A frog's heart has three chambers, but its red blood cells keep their nuclei, unlike ours. Small differences, big stories.
points: Circulation is closed, with a well-developed lymphatic system (lymph, lymph channels, lymph nodes). The heart is in the upper body cavity, covered by the pericardium, with three chambers: two atria and one ventricle.
The sinus venosus, a triangular structure, joins the right atrium and receives blood through the venae cavae. The ventricle opens into the sac-like conus arteriosus on the ventral side.
Arteries carry blood from the heart; veins bring it back. Special venous connections: hepatic portal system (between intestine and liver) and renal portal system (between lower body and kidney).
Blood has plasma and cells: RBCs (erythrocytes) that are nucleated and have haemoglobin, WBCs (leucocytes) and platelets. Lymph lacks some proteins and RBCs.

Excretory system: a pair of compact, dark red, bean-like kidneys made of uriniferous tubules (nephrons), ureters, cloaca and a thin-walled urinary bladder. In males the ureters act as urinogenital ducts; in females ureters and oviducts open separately into the cloaca. Frogs excrete urea, so they are ureotelic.

topics.title: Frog control, coordination and sense organs

learn.hook: A frog's brain is tiny, but it still has three parts and ten pairs of cranial nerves, enough to snap a fly mid-air.
points: Control and coordination use both the neural system and endocrine glands. Endocrine glands of the frog: pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, pineal body, pancreatic islets, adrenals and gonads.
Nervous system: central (brain and spinal cord), peripheral (cranial and spinal nerves) and autonomic (sympathetic and parasympathetic). Ten pairs of cranial nerves arise from the brain.

The brain, in a bony brain box (cranium), has fore-brain (olfactory lobes, paired cerebral hemispheres, unpaired diencephalon), mid-brain (pair of optic lobes) and hind-brain (cerebellum and medulla oblongata).
The medulla oblongata passes out through the foramen magnum and continues as the spinal cord inside the vertebral column.

Sense organs: touch (sensory papillae), taste (taste buds), smell (nasal epithelium), vision (eyes) and hearing (tympanum with internal ears). Eyes and internal ears are well organised; the others are cellular aggregations around nerve endings. Frog eyes are simple; the ear is for hearing and balance; there is no external ear.

learn.hook: One female frog can lay up to 3000 eggs at a time. From each, a tadpole may swim out and transform into a frog.
points: Male organs: a pair of yellowish, ovoid testes attached to the upper part of the kidneys by a double fold of peritoneum (mesorchium). 10 to 12 vasa efferentia enter the kidneys and open into Bidder's canal, which joins the urinogenital duct opening into the cloaca.
The cloaca is a small median chamber that passes faecal matter, urine and sperms to the exterior.
Female organs: a pair of ovaries near the kidneys with no functional connection to them; a pair of oviducts opens separately into the cloaca. A mature female lays 2500 to 3000 ova at a time.
Fertilisation is external, in water. Development includes a larval stage, the tadpole, which undergoes metamorphosis into the adult.
Usefulness: frogs eat insects and protect crops; they keep ecological balance as an important link in food chains and food webs; in some countries frog legs are eaten.

topics.title: What is a cell? The cell theory

learn.hook: Every living thing, from the bacteria in your dahi to a blue whale, is made of cells. It took three scientists and two centuries to say this clearly.
points: The cell is the fundamental structural and functional unit of all living organisms. Unicellular organisms are a single cell that lives independently; multicellular organisms have many cells.
Anton von Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell. Robert Brown later discovered the nucleus.

Matthias Schleiden (1838, botanist) showed that all plants are made of different kinds of cells forming tissues. Theodor Schwann (1839, zoologist) studied animal cells, reported the thin outer layer now called the plasma membrane, and concluded that the cell wall is unique to plant cells. Together they formulated the cell theory.
Their theory did not explain how new cells form. Rudolf Virchow (1855) explained that cells divide and new cells arise from pre-existing cells: Omnis cellula-e cellula.
Modern cell theory: (i) all living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells; (ii) all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

example.q: What did Virchow add to the cell theory of Schleiden and Schwann?
steps: Schleiden and Schwann said organisms are made of cells and cell products.
They could not explain where new cells come from.
Virchow showed new cells arise from pre-existing cells by division.
example.answer: That all cells arise from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula-e cellula).

learn.reallife: Every pathology lab in India, from AIIMS to a district hospital, diagnoses disease by examining cells, a direct use of the cell theory.

topics.title: An overview of the cell: size, shape and parts

learn.hook: The smallest known cell is about 0.3 micrometre long; the largest single cell is an ostrich egg. That is a size range of about five lakh times.
points: Cytoplasm, a semi-fluid matrix, fills the cell and is the main arena of cellular activities. Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus with chromosomes carrying DNA; prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus.
Eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles: ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes, mitochondria, microbodies and vacuoles. Prokaryotic cells lack these.

Ribosomes are non-membrane-bound organelles found in all cells: in the cytoplasm, on rough ER, and inside chloroplasts and mitochondria. Animal cells also have a non-membrane-bound centrosome that helps in cell division.
Size: Mycoplasma about 0.3 µm long; bacteria 3 to 5 µm; human red blood cells about 7.0 µm in diameter; the ostrich egg is the largest isolated single cell; nerve cells are among the longest cells.
Shape varies with function: disc-like, polygonal, columnar, cuboid, thread-like or irregular.

topics.title: Prokaryotic cells: DNA, plasmids and the cell envelope

learn.hook: Antibiotic resistance, one of India's biggest health worries, often travels on tiny rings of extra DNA in bacteria called plasmids.
points: Prokaryotic cells include bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma and PPLO (pleuro-pneumonia-like organisms). They are generally smaller and multiply faster than eukaryotic cells. Shapes: bacillus, coccus, vibrio, spirillum.
All prokaryotes except mycoplasma have a cell wall around the cell membrane. The genetic material is naked, not enclosed by a nuclear membrane: a single circular genomic DNA in the nucleoid.
Many bacteria also have small circular DNA outside the genomic DNA, called plasmids, which give special traits such as resistance to antibiotics.

Cell envelope: a tightly bound three-layered structure: outer glycocalyx, then cell wall, then plasma membrane, working together as one protective unit. The glycocalyx may be a loose slime layer or a thick, tough capsule. The cell wall gives shape and prevents bursting or collapsing; the plasma membrane is semi-permeable.
Based on their cell envelopes and response to Gram's staining, bacteria are Gram-positive (take up the stain) or Gram-negative (do not).

steps: Outermost is the glycocalyx (slime layer or capsule).

example.answer: Glycocalyx → cell wall → plasma membrane

topics.title: Mesosomes, flagella, pili, ribosomes and inclusions

learn.hook: A bacterial flagellum spins like a ship's propeller. It has a 'motor' (basal body), a 'joint' (hook) and a long 'blade' (filament).
points: Mesosomes are infoldings of the plasma membrane (vesicles, tubules, lamellae). They help in cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution to daughter cells, respiration, secretion, and increase membrane surface area and enzyme content. Cyanobacteria have pigment-containing chromatophores.
Motile bacteria have thin filamentous flagella extending from the cell wall. A bacterial flagellum has three parts: filament (longest, outside), hook and basal body.
Pili (elongated tubular structures of a special protein) and fimbriae (small bristle-like fibres) do not help in motility. Fimbriae help some bacteria attach to rocks in streams and to host tissues.
Prokaryotic ribosomes are associated with the plasma membrane, about 15 nm by 20 nm, made of 50S and 30S subunits forming 70S ribosomes. Several ribosomes on one mRNA form a polyribosome (polysome).

Inclusion bodies store reserve material free in the cytoplasm without membranes: phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules and glycogen granules. Gas vacuoles occur in blue-green, purple and green photosynthetic bacteria.

Together they form the 70S ribosome. (S values are not simply added; 50S + 30S gives 70S.)
example.answer: 50S and 30S subunits; 70S ribosome.

topics.title: Eukaryotic cells: plant cell versus animal cell

learn.hook: An onion peel cell and a cheek cell are both eukaryotic, yet one has a wall and a big vacuole, and the other has centrioles. Spot the difference!
points: Eukaryotes include all protists, plants, animals and fungi. Their cytoplasm is extensively compartmentalised by membrane-bound organelles; they have an organised nucleus with a nuclear envelope, complex locomotory and cytoskeletal structures, and genetic material organised into chromosomes.
Plant cells have a cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole, which are absent in animal cells.
Animal cells have centrioles, which are absent in almost all plant cells.
Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic: no nuclear membrane vs true nucleus; no membrane-bound organelles vs many; 70S vs 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes; circular naked DNA vs linear DNA in chromosomes with proteins.

Key labels in diagrams: plant cell (cell wall, plasma membrane, chloroplast, large vacuole, nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi, ER); animal cell (plasma membrane, centrioles, lysosome, nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi, ER).

example.q: A cell has a nuclear envelope, mitochondria, a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole, but no centrioles. What is it?
steps: Nuclear envelope and mitochondria: eukaryotic.

example.answer: A eukaryotic plant cell.

topics.title: The cell membrane: structure and transport

learn.hook: Your RBC membrane is about half protein and half fat, and the proteins drift around like boats on a lake. That's the fluid mosaic model.
points: The membrane is mainly lipids and proteins. Phospholipids form a bilayer with polar heads facing outwards and hydrophobic tails inwards; cholesterol is also present, along with carbohydrates.
The protein-lipid ratio varies; the human RBC membrane has about 52% protein and 40% lipids. Peripheral proteins lie on the surface; integral proteins are partly or totally buried in the membrane.

Fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972): the quasi-fluid lipid lets proteins move laterally. This fluidity is important for cell growth, intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division.

Passive transport needs no energy: simple diffusion of neutral solutes from higher to lower concentration; osmosis is diffusion of water. Polar molecules need carrier proteins to cross the non-polar bilayer.
Active transport moves ions or molecules against the concentration gradient (low to high) using ATP, e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.

example.q: In a human RBC membrane, protein is 52% and lipid 40%. What percentage is left for other components such as carbohydrates?
steps: Total = 100%.
Protein + lipid = 52 + 40 = 92%.
Remaining = 100 - 92 = 8%.

learn.reallife: ORS (oral rehydration solution), promoted in India for diarrhoea, works because glucose and sodium are carried into gut cells together by membrane transport proteins, pulling water in by osmosis.

topics.title: The cell wall

learn.hook: Your cotton T-shirt is made of almost pure plant cell wall material: cellulose. Cell walls literally clothe India.
points: The cell wall is a non-living rigid outer covering of the plasma membrane in fungi and plants. It gives shape, protects from mechanical damage and infection, helps cell-to-cell interaction and blocks undesirable macromolecules.
Algal cell walls contain cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals such as calcium carbonate. In other plants, the wall has cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins.
The primary wall of a young plant cell can grow; this capacity diminishes as the cell matures, and a secondary wall is laid on the inner side (towards the membrane).
The middle lamella, mainly calcium pectate, glues neighbouring cells together.
Plasmodesmata traverse the cell wall and middle lamella and connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells.

example.answer: Membrane → secondary wall → primary wall → middle lamella → primary wall → secondary wall → membrane

topics.title: Endomembrane system: ER and Golgi apparatus

learn.hook: Insulin made in your pancreas is built on the rough ER, polished in the Golgi and shipped out in vesicles, like a factory with a packing department.
points: The endomembrane system includes the ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles, whose functions are coordinated. Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not part of it.

The ER is a network of tubules dividing the cell into luminal (inside ER) and extra-luminal (cytoplasm) compartments. Rough ER (RER) has ribosomes, is common in cells making and secreting proteins, and is continuous with the outer nuclear membrane.
Smooth ER (SER) lacks ribosomes and is the major site of lipid synthesis; in animal cells, steroidal hormones are made in the SER.
Golgi apparatus (Camillo Golgi, 1898): stacks of flat disc-shaped cisternae (0.5 to 1.0 µm across) near the nucleus, with a convex cis (forming) face and a concave trans (maturing) face.

Vesicles from the ER fuse with the cis face and move to the trans face. The Golgi packages materials for targets inside the cell or for secretion, modifies proteins, and is an important site for forming glycoproteins and glycolipids.

example.q: Trace a secretory protein from synthesis to release.
steps: Ribosomes on the RER make the protein.

It is modified in the cisternae and moves to the trans face.
It is packaged into vesicles and secreted.
example.answer: RER → vesicle → cis Golgi → trans Golgi → secretory vesicle → outside

topics.title: Lysosomes, vacuoles and microbodies

learn.hook: Amoeba lives in fresh water that keeps flooding in. It survives by pumping water out with a contractile vacuole, like bailing a leaking boat.
points: Lysosomes are membrane-bound vesicles formed by packaging in the Golgi. They are rich in hydrolytic enzymes (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) that are optimally active at acidic pH and can digest carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

A vacuole is a membrane-bound space containing water, sap, excretory products and materials not useful to the cell. Its single membrane is the tonoplast. In plant cells, vacuoles can occupy up to 90% of cell volume.
In plants the tonoplast moves ions and other materials into the vacuole against their concentration gradients, so their concentration in the vacuole is much higher than in the cytoplasm.
In Amoeba, the contractile vacuole is important for osmoregulation and excretion. In many protists, food vacuoles form by engulfing food particles.
Microbodies are many minute membrane-bound vesicles containing various enzymes, found in both plant and animal cells.

They work best at acidic pH, which is maintained inside the lysosome, not in the cytoplasm.

topics.title: Mitochondria and plastids

learn.hook: Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry their own DNA and ribosomes, almost like tiny tenants with their own furniture inside your cells.
points: Mitochondria: usually sausage-shaped or cylindrical, about 0.2 to 1.0 µm wide (average 0.5 µm) and 1.0 to 4.1 µm long; number depends on activity. Double membrane: the outer is a continuous boundary; the inner folds into cristae that increase surface area, enclosing the matrix.

Mitochondria are sites of aerobic respiration and make ATP, so they are the 'power houses' of the cell. The matrix has a single circular DNA, a few RNAs, 70S ribosomes and components for protein synthesis. Mitochondria divide by fission.

Plastids occur in all plant cells and in euglenoids. Chloroplasts have chlorophyll and carotenoids for photosynthesis. Chromoplasts have fat-soluble carotenoids (carotene, xanthophylls) giving yellow, orange or red colours. Leucoplasts are colourless storage plastids: amyloplasts (starch, e.g. potato), elaioplasts (oils and fats), aleuroplasts (proteins).

Chloroplasts are found mostly in leaf mesophyll; they are lens-shaped, oval, spherical, discoid or ribbon-like, 5 to 10 µm long and 2 to 4 µm wide. Numbers range from 1 per cell in Chlamydomonas to 20 to 40 per mesophyll cell.

Chloroplast: double membrane (inner less permeable); stroma inside; flattened sacs called thylakoids stacked as grana; stroma lamellae connect grana; thylakoids enclose a lumen and carry chlorophyll. The stroma has enzymes for making carbohydrates and proteins, double-stranded circular DNA and 70S ribosomes.

example.answer: Amyloplasts in potato; chromoplasts in tomato.

topics.title: Ribosomes, cytoskeleton, cilia, flagella and centrioles

learn.hook: Cilia lining your windpipe beat like oars hundreds of times a minute to sweep out dust from Delhi's winter smog.
points: Ribosomes were first observed by George Palade (1953). They are made of RNA and proteins, not surrounded by a membrane. Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S (60S + 40S); prokaryotic are 70S (50S + 30S). S (Svedberg unit) is the sedimentation coefficient, an indirect measure of density and size.
The cytoskeleton is a network of protein filaments (microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments) for mechanical support, motility and maintaining cell shape.

Cilia are small and work like oars to move the cell or surrounding fluid; flagella are longer and move the cell. Their core, the axoneme, has nine doublets of peripheral microtubules and a central pair: the 9+2 array. A central sheath joins each peripheral doublet by a radial spoke (nine spokes); doublets are joined by linkers. Both arise from basal bodies. Bacterial flagella are structurally different.

The centrosome usually has two cylindrical centrioles lying perpendicular to each other, surrounded by amorphous pericentriolar material. Each centriole has a cartwheel organisation of nine evenly spaced peripheral triplet fibrils of tubulin; the central proteinaceous hub is joined to the triplets by radial spokes.
Centrioles form the basal bodies of cilia and flagella, and the spindle fibres that make the spindle apparatus during cell division in animal cells.

example.q: How many microtubules are there in the axoneme of a cilium with the 9+2 arrangement?
steps: Nine peripheral doublets = 9 × 2 = 18 microtubules.
Central pair = 2 microtubules.
example.answer: 20 microtubules

topics.title: The nucleus and chromosomes

learn.hook: Each of your cells packs about two metres of DNA into a nucleus a few micrometres wide. That's like stuffing about 20 km of thread into a tennis ball.
points: The nucleus was first described by Robert Brown (1831); Flemming named its stainable material chromatin. The interphase nucleus has chromatin, a nuclear matrix (nucleoplasm) and one or more nucleoli.

The nuclear envelope has two parallel membranes with a perinuclear space (10 to 50 nm). The outer membrane is continuous with the ER and bears ribosomes. Nuclear pores let RNA and proteins move both ways. Mature mammalian RBCs and sieve tube cells lack a nucleus.

The nucleolus is a spherical, non-membrane-bound body, the site of active rRNA synthesis; it is larger and more numerous in cells actively making proteins. Chromatin has DNA, basic histone proteins, non-histone proteins and RNA. A human cell has about 2 m of DNA in 46 (23 pairs) chromosomes.

Each chromosome has a primary constriction, the centromere, with disc-shaped kinetochores on its sides. By centromere position: metacentric (middle, equal arms), sub-metacentric (slightly away from middle, one shorter and one longer arm), acrocentric (close to the end, one very short and one very long arm), telocentric (terminal).
Some chromosomes have a non-staining secondary constriction at a constant location, giving a small fragment called a satellite.

example.q: A chromosome has arms of 2 µm and 8 µm. Where is the centromere and how would you classify it?
steps: The arms are very unequal: one very short, one very long.
So the centromere is close to one end.
This is an acrocentric chromosome.
example.answer: Acrocentric (centromere near one end).

learn.reallife: Karyotyping labs at AIIMS and other genetic centres look at centromere position and satellites to identify each human chromosome and diagnose disorders.

topics.title: How do we analyse the chemicals in living tissue?

learn.hook: Carbon is a tiny 0.03% of the Earth's crust, but about 18.5% of your body. Life is a carbon-hungry chemist.
points: Grind a living tissue in trichloroacetic acid (Cl₃CCOOH) with a mortar and pestle to get a slurry. Strain it through cheesecloth or cotton to get two fractions: the filtrate (acid-soluble pool) and the retentate (acid-insoluble fraction).
Analytical techniques applied to separated compounds give their molecular formula and probable structure. All carbon compounds obtained from living tissues are called biomolecules.

Ash analysis: weigh the tissue (wet weight), dry it to remove water (dry weight), then burn it completely. Carbon compounds are oxidised to gases (CO₂, water vapour) and removed; the remaining ash contains inorganic elements such as calcium and magnesium.
Inorganic compounds such as sulphate and phosphate are also seen in the acid-soluble fraction.

Living matter is far richer in carbon (18.5% vs 0.03%), hydrogen (0.5% vs 0.14%), oxygen (65.0% vs 46.6%) and nitrogen (3.3% vs very little) than the Earth's crust, but much poorer in silicon (negligible vs 27.7%).

example.q: Order the steps of ash analysis.
steps: Weigh the fresh tissue: wet weight.
Dry it to evaporate water: dry weight.
Burn it completely: carbon compounds leave as CO₂ and water vapour.
Weigh and analyse the remaining ash for inorganic elements.
example.answer: Wet weight → dry weight → burning → ash with inorganic elements

learn.reallife: Food testing labs under FSSAI measure ash content in spices and flours to check for adulteration with sand or chalk.

topics.title: Amino acids, sugars and nucleotides: the small building blocks

learn.hook: Only 20 kinds of amino acids build every protein in your body, from hair keratin to the enzymes in your saliva.
points: Amino acids have an amino group and a carboxyl group on the same carbon, the α-carbon; they are substituted methanes with four groups: hydrogen, carboxyl, amino and a variable R group. Twenty types occur in proteins.

R group: hydrogen in glycine, methyl in alanine, hydroxymethyl in serine. Amino acids may be acidic (glutamic acid), basic (lysine) or neutral (valine); aromatic ones are tyrosine, phenylalanine and tryptophan.
The –NH₂ and –COOH groups ionise, so the structure of an amino acid changes with pH; at a particular pH it exists as a zwitterion carrying both a positive and a negative charge.
Simple sugars (monosaccharides) such as glucose and ribose are carbohydrate units.

Nitrogen bases: adenine, guanine, cytosine, uracil, thymine. Base + sugar = nucleoside (adenosine, guanosine, thymidine, uridine, cytidine). Base + sugar + phosphate = nucleotide (adenylic, guanylic, thymidylic, uridylic, cytidylic acids).

example.q: Adenine is joined to a sugar, and a phosphate is then esterified to the sugar. Name the compound at each stage.
steps: Adenine + sugar = nucleoside: adenosine.
Adding a phosphate gives a nucleotide: adenylic acid.
example.answer: Adenosine (nucleoside), then adenylic acid (nucleotide).

topics.title: Lipids: fatty acids, glycerides and phospholipids

learn.hook: Why does coconut oil turn solid on a cold Delhi winter morning, but gingelly (til) oil stays liquid? Melting points tell the story.
points: Lipids are generally water-insoluble. A fatty acid has a carboxyl group attached to an R group, which may be methyl, ethyl or a chain of –CH₂ groups (1 to 19 carbons).
Palmitic acid has 16 carbons and arachidonic acid has 20 carbons, including the carboxyl carbon. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bond; unsaturated ones have one or more.

Glycerol is trihydroxy propane. Fatty acids esterified with glycerol give monoglycerides, diglycerides and triglycerides. These are called fats or oils by melting point; oils (e.g. gingelly oil) have lower melting points and stay liquid in winter.
Phospholipids contain phosphorus and a phosphorylated organic compound; they are found in cell membranes, e.g. lecithin. Neural tissues have more complex lipids.
Lipids are small (below 800 Da) and are not true macromolecules. They appear in the acid-insoluble fraction because grinding breaks membranes into water-insoluble vesicles.

example.q: How many fatty acid molecules are esterified to one glycerol in a triglyceride?

topics.title: Primary and secondary metabolites

learn.hook: The yellow of haldi, the bitterness of neem and the latex of rubber trees in Kerala are all 'extra' chemicals that plants did not need just to stay alive.
points: Primary metabolites, such as amino acids and sugars, have identifiable functions and known roles in normal physiological processes.
Secondary metabolites are found in plants, fungi and microbes. We do not yet understand the role of all of them in their hosts, but many are useful to humans and some have ecological importance.
Pigments: carotenoids, anthocyanins. Alkaloids: morphine, codeine. Terpenoids: monoterpenes, diterpenes. Essential oils: lemon grass oil.
Toxins: abrin, ricin. Lectins: concanavalin A. Drugs: vinblastine, curcumin. Polymeric substances: rubber, gums, cellulose.
Human uses include rubber, drugs, spices, scents and pigments.

topics.title: Biomacromolecules and the composition of a cell

learn.hook: If you dried out a typical cell, most of what's left would be protein. But first, you'd have to remove a lot of water.
points: The acid-soluble pool contains molecules with molecular weights from about 18 to around 800 daltons (Da).

The acid-insoluble fraction contains four types of organic compounds: proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides and lipids. Except lipids, they have molecular weights of ten thousand daltons and above.
Biomolecules are micromolecules (molecular weight below 1000 Da) or macromolecules (biomacromolecules). Proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides are true macromolecules.
Average composition of cells: water 70 to 90%, proteins 10 to 15%, nucleic acids 5 to 7%, carbohydrates 3%, lipids 2%, ions 1%.
So water is the most abundant chemical in living organisms, followed by proteins.

example.q: Which is the second most abundant component of a cell after water?
steps: Water is 70 to 90%.

example.answer: Proteins

topics.title: Proteins: heteropolymers with many jobs

learn.hook: The most abundant protein on the whole planet is not in animals at all. It sits in every green leaf, fixing CO₂.
points: Proteins are polypeptides: linear chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
With 20 types of amino acids, a protein is a heteropolymer, not a homopolymer (which repeats a single type of monomer).
Essential amino acids must come from the diet; non-essential amino acids can be made by the body.

Functions: collagen (intercellular ground substance), trypsin (enzyme), insulin (hormone), antibody (fights infectious agents), receptor (sensory reception: smell, taste, hormone), GLUT-4 (glucose transport into cells). Some proteins transport nutrients across membranes.
Collagen is the most abundant protein in the animal world; RuBisCO (ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase) is the most abundant protein in the whole biosphere.

example.q: Why is a protein called a heteropolymer while cellulose is a homopolymer?
steps: A protein is built from up to 20 different amino acids.
Cellulose is built from only one monomer, glucose.
example.answer: Protein has many kinds of monomers; cellulose has only glucose.

topics.title: Polysaccharides

learn.hook: Drop iodine on a slice of potato and it turns blue-black. Drop it on cotton wool and nothing happens. Both are chains of glucose. Why the difference?
points: Polysaccharides are long chains of sugars (monosaccharides) as building blocks.
Cellulose is a homopolymer of glucose. Starch (plant energy store) and glycogen (animal store) are other variants; inulin is a polymer of fructose.
In a chain such as glycogen, the right end is the reducing end and the left end the non-reducing end; glycogen is branched.
Starch forms helical secondary structures that can hold I₂ molecules, giving a blue colour. Cellulose has no complex helices, cannot hold iodine and gives no colour.

Plant cell walls are made of cellulose; paper and cotton fibre are cellulosic. Complex polysaccharides with amino sugars and modified sugars (e.g. glucosamine, N-acetyl galactosamine) include chitin in arthropod exoskeletons.

example.q: Why does iodine solution turn blue with starch but not with cellulose?
steps: Starch forms helices that can hold iodine molecules; starch-I₂ is blue.
Cellulose lacks complex helices and cannot hold iodine.
example.answer: Only starch's helices trap iodine to form a blue complex.

learn.reallife: School and FSSAI-style kitchen tests use iodine to detect starch added as an adulterant to milk or paneer: a blue colour gives it away.

topics.title: Nucleic acids

learn.hook: Your entire genetic instruction book is written with just four letters, A, T, G and C, strung on a sugar-phosphate thread.
points: Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are polynucleotides. With polysaccharides and polypeptides, they form the true macromolecular fraction of tissues.
A nucleotide has three chemically distinct parts: a heterocyclic nitrogen base, a monosaccharide (pentose sugar) and phosphoric acid (phosphate).
Bases: adenine, guanine, cytosine, uracil, thymine. Adenine and guanine are substituted purines; cytosine, uracil and thymine are substituted pyrimidines.
The sugar is ribose in RNA and 2'-deoxyribose in DNA.
Thymine occurs in DNA and uracil in RNA; adenine, guanine and cytosine occur in both.

example.answer: Adenine and guanine.

topics.title: Structure of proteins: four levels

learn.hook: A protein is like a phone charger cable: first a sequence of wires, then twisted, then coiled into a ball, and sometimes several bundled together.
points: Primary structure: the sequence of amino acids, i.e. the positional information. The first amino acid is the N-terminal amino acid; the last is the C-terminal amino acid.
Secondary structure: the chain is not a rigid rod; some portions fold into a helix (only right-handed helices occur in proteins), and other regions fold into other forms.
Tertiary structure: the long chain folds upon itself like a hollow woollen ball, giving a 3-D shape. It is absolutely necessary for many biological activities of proteins.
Quaternary structure: the arrangement of two or more folded polypeptides (subunits) with respect to each other.
Adult human haemoglobin has 4 subunits: two α and two β.

example.q: Which structural level is shown by haemoglobin but not by a single-chain protein?
steps: A single chain can have primary, secondary and tertiary structure.
Haemoglobin has four subunits (2 α + 2 β) arranged together.
Arrangement of subunits is quaternary structure.
example.answer: Quaternary structure.

learn.reallife: Thalassaemia, common in parts of India, is linked to defects in the α or β chains of haemoglobin, a protein with quaternary structure.

topics.title: Enzymes and the speed of chemical reactions

learn.hook: Without an enzyme, about 200 molecules of carbonic acid form in an hour. With carbonic anhydrase, about 600,000 form every second.
points: Almost all enzymes are proteins; some nucleic acids act as enzymes, called ribozymes. In the tertiary structure, a crevice or pocket called the active site holds the substrate.

Inorganic catalysts work well at high temperature and pressure, but enzymes are damaged at high temperatures (say above 40°C). Enzymes from thermophilic organisms in hot vents and sulphur springs stay stable even at 80 to 90°C.
A physical change alters shape or state without breaking bonds (ice melting). A chemical reaction breaks and forms bonds, e.g. Ba(OH)₂ + H₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2H₂O, or hydrolysis of starch to glucose.
Rate of reaction = amount of product formed per unit time. As a rule of thumb, the rate doubles or halves for every 10°C change. Carbonic anhydrase speeds CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ about 10 million times.

A metabolic pathway is a series of enzyme-catalysed steps. Glucose becomes pyruvic acid through ten enzyme-catalysed reactions; in skeletal muscle under anaerobic conditions lactic acid forms, and in yeast during fermentation ethanol forms.

example.q: A reaction at 25°C gives 100 units of product per minute. Using the 10°C rule of thumb, estimate the rate at 35°C.
steps: A 10°C rise roughly doubles the rate.
100 × 2 = 200 units per minute.
example.answer: About 200 units per minute

learn.reallife: Enzymes from heat-loving microbes are used in PCR machines in Indian diagnostic labs, which cycle up to about 95°C to test for infections.

topics.title: How enzymes work: ES complex, activation energy and the catalytic cycle

learn.hook: Rolling a heavy boulder over a hill takes a big push even if the other side is downhill. Enzymes dig a tunnel through that hill.
points: The substrate (S) binds the enzyme's active site to form a short-lived enzyme-substrate complex (ES), which is essential for catalysis: E + S ⇌ ES → EP → E + P.
The substrate is converted to product through an unstable, high-energy transition state.

If the product is at a lower energy level than the substrate, the reaction is exothermic and needs no heating; if higher, it is endothermic. Either way, the substrate must pass through the transition state.
Activation energy is the difference in energy between the substrate and the transition state. Enzymes lower this energy barrier, making S → P easier.

Catalytic cycle: (i) substrate binds the active site; (ii) binding induces the enzyme to change shape and fit more tightly (induced fit); (iii) the active site breaks bonds of the substrate and an enzyme-product complex forms; (iv) products are released, and the free enzyme is ready for another substrate.

example.q: In an energy diagram, the substrate is at 40 units, the transition state without enzyme at 100 units and with enzyme at 70 units. Find the activation energy with and without the enzyme.
steps: Without enzyme: 100 - 40 = 60 units.
With enzyme: 70 - 40 = 30 units.
The enzyme halves the barrier here.
example.answer: Without enzyme 60 units; with enzyme 30 units.

topics.title: Factors affecting enzyme activity and inhibition

learn.hook: Why do we keep curd in the fridge and boil milk to stop it spoiling? Temperature controls enzymes.
points: Enzymes work in a narrow range of temperature and pH. Each has an optimum temperature and optimum pH where activity is highest; activity falls above and below the optimum.
Low temperature keeps an enzyme temporarily inactive; high temperature destroys activity because the protein is denatured by heat.
As substrate concentration rises, the reaction velocity first rises and then reaches a maximum, Vmax, which is not exceeded by adding more substrate, because all enzyme molecules are saturated.

A chemical that binds an enzyme and shuts off its activity is an inhibitor. A competitive inhibitor closely resembles the substrate and competes for the substrate-binding site, so the substrate cannot bind.
Example: malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase because it resembles succinate. Competitive inhibitors are often used to control bacterial pathogens.

steps: Velocity stops rising at 100 units.

example.answer: Vmax = 100 units; the enzyme is saturated.

topics.title: Classification of enzymes and co-factors

learn.hook: Some enzymes can't work alone. They need a 'sidekick' such as zinc, haem or a vitamin-derived NAD.
points: Six classes: oxidoreductases/dehydrogenases (oxidation-reduction between two substrates), transferases (transfer of a group other than hydrogen, S–G + S' → S + S'–G), hydrolases (hydrolysis of ester, ether, peptide, glycosidic, C–C, C–halide or P–N bonds).

Lyases remove groups from substrates by mechanisms other than hydrolysis, leaving double bonds. Isomerases interconvert optical, geometric or positional isomers. Ligases link two compounds, joining C–O, C–S, C–N, P–O bonds and so on.
Many enzymes need non-protein co-factors to be active; the protein part is the apoenzyme. Removing the co-factor destroys catalytic activity.

Prosthetic groups are organic and tightly bound, e.g. haem in peroxidase and catalase (which break down H₂O₂ into water and oxygen). Co-enzymes are organic but bind only transiently and serve many enzymes; many contain vitamins, e.g. NAD and NADP contain niacin.
Metal ions form coordination bonds with the active site and substrate, e.g. zinc for carboxypeptidase.

topics.title: The cell cycle and its two phases

learn.hook: A human cell in culture takes about 24 hours to divide, but spends only about one hour actually dividing. What is it doing the other 23?
points: The cell cycle is the sequence of events by which a cell duplicates its genome, synthesises other constituents and finally divides into two daughter cells. Cell growth is continuous, but DNA synthesis occurs in only one specific stage.
Human cells in culture divide about once every 24 hours; yeast can complete a cycle in only about 90 minutes. Duration varies between organisms and cell types.
Two basic phases: interphase (between two M phases) and M phase (mitosis phase, when actual division occurs). In a 24-hour human cycle, M phase lasts only about an hour.
M phase starts with nuclear division (karyokinesis, separation of daughter chromosomes) and usually ends with division of cytoplasm (cytokinesis).
Interphase, often called the resting phase, takes more than 95% of the cycle. It is not idle: the cell grows and replicates DNA in an orderly way. It has three sub-phases: G1, S and G2.

example.q: In a 24-hour human cell cycle with M phase lasting 1 hour, what percentage of the cycle is interphase?

topics.title: G1, S, G2 and G0: inside interphase

learn.hook: Heart muscle cells mostly stop dividing in adults. They park in a special 'waiting room' of the cell cycle called G0.
points: G1 (Gap 1): between mitosis and the start of DNA replication. The cell is metabolically active and grows but does not replicate its DNA.

S phase (synthesis): DNA replicates and the DNA content doubles from 2C to 4C, but the chromosome number stays the same (2n stays 2n). In animal cells, DNA replication begins in the nucleus and the centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm.
G2 (Gap 2): proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis, and cell growth continues.
Quiescent stage (G0): cells that stop dividing (e.g. heart cells) exit G1 into G0. They remain metabolically active but do not proliferate unless needed.
In animals, mitosis occurs only in diploid somatic cells. Plants can show mitosis in both haploid and diploid cells.

topics.title: Mitosis: prophase and metaphase

learn.hook: Cytogenetics labs make karyotypes from cells stopped at metaphase, because chromosomes are then at their most compact and clearest.
points: M phase is also called equational division because parent and daughter cells have the same number of chromosomes. Mitosis is described in four stages of karyokinesis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase), though it is a continuous process.

Prophase: chromatin condenses into compact mitotic chromosomes, each with two chromatids joined at the centromere. The centrosome (duplicated in S phase) moves to opposite poles; each radiates microtubules called asters; asters and spindle fibres form the mitotic apparatus.
At the end of prophase, the Golgi complex, ER, nucleolus and nuclear envelope are no longer visible.

Metaphase begins with complete disintegration of the nuclear envelope. Chromosomes are fully condensed, so morphology is best studied now. Each has two sister chromatids held at the centromere, with disc-shaped kinetochores where spindle fibres attach.
Chromosomes align at the equator; each chromatid's kinetochore is connected to spindle fibres from one pole and its sister's to the opposite pole. The plane of alignment is the metaphase plate.
