topics.title: Mitosis: anaphase, telophase and cytokinesis

learn.hook: Tender coconut water is liquid endosperm with many free nuclei and no cell walls between them. The nuclei divided, but the cytoplasm never did.
points: Anaphase: each chromosome at the metaphase plate splits simultaneously; centromeres split and the two daughter chromatids (now chromosomes) move to opposite poles, centromere leading and arms trailing.
Telophase: chromosomes at the poles decondense and lose their individuality; a nuclear envelope forms around each cluster, giving two daughter nuclei; the nucleolus, Golgi complex and ER reform.
Cytokinesis in animal cells: a furrow appears in the plasma membrane, deepens and joins at the centre, dividing the cytoplasm.

Cytokinesis in plant cells: wall formation starts at the centre and grows outward to meet the lateral walls. It begins with a cell plate, which becomes the middle lamella between the walls of the two cells. Organelles such as mitochondria and plastids are distributed to the daughters.
If karyokinesis is not followed by cytokinesis, a multinucleate condition called a syncytium forms, e.g. the liquid endosperm of coconut.

example.answer: Their rigid cell wall prevents furrowing, so a cell plate forms from the centre.

topics.title: Meiosis and the early stages of prophase I

learn.hook: Why are you not an exact copy of your elder sibling? Part of the answer is a gene swap that happens in pachytene.
points: Meiosis is a reductional division that halves the chromosome number to form haploid cells. It produces the haploid phase in sexually reproducing organisms; fertilisation restores the diploid phase. It occurs during gametogenesis in plants and animals.

Key features: two sequential cycles of nuclear and cell division (meiosis I and II) but only one cycle of DNA replication; pairing of homologous chromosomes and recombination between non-sister chromatids; four haploid cells at the end of meiosis II.
Prophase I is longer and more complex than mitotic prophase and has five sub-stages: leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene, diakinesis.

Leptotene: chromosomes become gradually visible and keep compacting. Zygotene: homologous chromosomes start pairing (synapsis), with formation of a synaptonemal complex; a pair of synapsed homologues is a bivalent or tetrad.

Pachytene (longer than the first two stages): the four chromatids of each bivalent become distinct as tetrads. Recombination nodules appear, where crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes. Crossing over is enzyme-mediated (recombinase) and leads to recombination.

example.answer: 23 bivalents

learn.reallife: Recombination during pachytene is one reason children of the same parents look different; plant breeders at ICAR rely on it to combine useful traits in new crop varieties.

topics.title: Diplotene to telophase I

learn.hook: In human females, oocytes pause in diplotene before birth and may stay paused for over a decade until puberty. Patience at the cellular level!
points: Diplotene: the synaptonemal complex dissolves and recombined homologues tend to separate except at crossover sites, which appear as X-shaped chiasmata. In oocytes of some vertebrates, diplotene can last for months or years (this arrested stage is often called dictyotene).

Diakinesis: terminalisation of chiasmata; chromosomes are fully condensed and the meiotic spindle assembles. By the end, the nucleolus disappears and the nuclear envelope breaks down. It is the transition to metaphase.
Metaphase I: bivalents align on the equatorial plate; microtubules from opposite poles attach to the pair of homologous chromosomes.
Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes separate, while sister chromatids remain together at their centromeres.

Telophase I: the nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear, cytokinesis follows, giving a dyad of cells. Interkinesis, the stage between the two meiotic divisions, is generally short and has no DNA replication.

example.q: A cell with 2n = 8 completes meiosis I. How many chromosomes, and how many chromatids per chromosome, does each daughter cell have?
steps: Anaphase I separates homologues, so each cell gets one of each pair: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 chromosomes.
Sister chromatids are still joined, so each chromosome has 2 chromatids.
example.answer: 4 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids

learn.reallife: In human females, oocytes arrested in diplotene before birth resume meiosis only at puberty, a fact gynaecologists use to explain the age-related risk of chromosomal errors.

topics.title: Meiosis II and the significance of meiosis

learn.hook: If gametes were not haploid, chromosome number would double every generation. Meiosis keeps the count steady, generation after generation.
points: Meiosis II starts right after cytokinesis of meiosis I, usually before chromosomes have fully elongated, and resembles normal mitosis. Prophase II: nuclear membrane disappears by its end and chromosomes compact again.

Metaphase II: chromosomes align at the equator; microtubules from opposite poles attach to the kinetochores of sister chromatids. Anaphase II: the centromere of each chromosome splits and sister chromatids move to opposite poles.
Telophase II: the two groups of chromosomes are enclosed by nuclear envelopes; cytokinesis follows, giving a tetrad of four haploid daughter cells.
Meiosis I is reductional (homologues separate, halving chromosome number); meiosis II is equational (sister chromatids separate, number stays the same as at the start of meiosis II).

Significance: meiosis conserves the chromosome number of each species across generations in sexually reproducing organisms, although it halves the number in gametes. It increases genetic variability (crossing over and independent assortment of chromosomes), which is very important for evolution.

example.q: Why is meiosis II called equational even though it is part of meiosis?
steps: At the start of meiosis II each cell is already haploid (n), each chromosome with two chromatids.
In anaphase II, sister chromatids separate.
Each daughter cell still has n chromosomes, the same as the cell entering meiosis II.
example.answer: Because chromosome number does not change during meiosis II; only sister chromatids separate.

learn.reallife: Variation produced by meiosis is the raw material that let farmers and ICAR scientists select drought-tolerant and disease-resistant crop varieties.

topics.title: Mitosis versus meiosis: comparing and identifying

learn.hook: Exam favourite: 'Identify the stage from the diagram.' Learn the clues once and you'll never confuse anaphase I with anaphase II again.
points: Mitosis: one division, two diploid daughter cells, identical to parent; no pairing or crossing over; occurs in somatic cells for growth and repair.
Meiosis: two divisions, four haploid cells, genetically different; synapsis and crossing over in prophase I; occurs in gamete-forming cells.
Metaphase of mitosis and metaphase II: single chromosomes (two chromatids each) at the equator. Metaphase I: bivalents (paired homologues) at the equator.
Anaphase of mitosis and anaphase II: centromeres split, sister chromatids move apart. Anaphase I: centromeres do not split; homologous chromosomes move apart.
DNA tracking for a 2n cell: G1 2C → after S 4C → after mitosis 2C each; in meiosis, 4C → after meiosis I 2C (n chromosomes) → after meiosis II 1C (n chromosomes).

example.q: A diagram shows chromosomes moving to poles with each chromosome still made of two chromatids, and the homologues separating. Name the stage.
steps: Chromosomes moving to poles means anaphase.
Each still has two chromatids, so centromeres have not split.
Homologues separating means meiosis I.
example.answer: Anaphase I

topics.title: Photosynthesis: why it matters and simple experiments

learn.hook: Every grain of rice, every roti and every breath of oxygen you take traces back to a green leaf trapping sunlight.
points: Photosynthesis is a physico-chemical process by which green plants use light energy to synthesise organic compounds.
It is the primary source of all food on Earth and is responsible for the release of oxygen into the atmosphere.
Variegated leaf experiment: a leaf with green and non-green patches, kept in light and tested for starch, shows starch only in green parts, so chlorophyll is needed.
Half-covered leaf experiment: a leaf partly covered with black paper and kept in light shows starch only in the exposed part, so light is needed.
KOH half-leaf experiment: part of a leaf is enclosed in a tube with KOH-soaked cotton (KOH absorbs CO₂); only the part exposed to air tests positive for starch, so CO₂ is needed.

example.q: In the KOH half-leaf experiment, why does the enclosed half give a negative starch test?
steps: KOH absorbs CO₂ from the air in the tube.
Without CO₂, that part cannot photosynthesise.
No photosynthesis means no starch.
example.answer: KOH removes CO₂, so no photosynthesis and no starch.

learn.reallife: In school labs, the starch test uses iodine solution, and boiling the leaf in alcohol must be done in a water bath, never over a direct flame, because alcohol catches fire easily.

topics.title: Early experiments: from Priestley to van Niel

learn.hook: A candle, a mouse, a mint plant and a glass jar: Joseph Priestley's 1770s experiments launched our understanding of photosynthesis.
points: Joseph Priestley (1770s): a candle in a closed bell jar went out and a mouse suffocated; with a mint plant inside, the candle kept burning and the mouse lived. He hypothesised that plants restore to the air what breathing animals and burning candles remove. He discovered oxygen in 1774.

Jan Ingenhousz: sunlight is essential for the plant to purify the air; an aquatic plant formed bubbles (later shown to be oxygen) around its green parts in bright sunlight, not in the dark. So only green parts release oxygen.
Julius von Sachs (1854): glucose is made in the green parts of plants and is usually stored as starch; chlorophyll is located in special bodies later called chloroplasts.

T.W. Engelmann: split light with a prism and lit the green alga Cladophora placed in a suspension of aerobic bacteria. Bacteria gathered mainly in blue and red light, giving the first action spectrum of photosynthesis.

Cornelius van Niel, studying purple and green bacteria: photosynthesis is a light-dependent reaction where hydrogen from an oxidisable compound reduces CO₂ (2H₂A + CO₂ → 2A + CH₂O + H₂O). With H₂S, sulphur bacteria give sulphur, not O₂, so in green plants O₂ comes from water. Correct equation: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 6O₂ (in light).

example.q: Using the equation 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 6O₂, how many oxygen atoms in the O₂ released come from water?
steps: 6O₂ contains 12 oxygen atoms.
van Niel showed all released O₂ comes from water.
12 H₂O supply exactly 12 oxygen atoms.
example.answer: All 12 oxygen atoms come from water.

learn.reallife: Engelmann's bacteria trick is similar to how scientists now use oxygen sensors to measure photosynthesis of crops in ICAR field trials.

topics.title: Where photosynthesis takes place

learn.hook: The 'dark reaction' doesn't happen in the dark. That's one of the most misunderstood names in biology.
points: Photosynthesis occurs mainly in green leaves, but also in other green parts. Mesophyll cells have many chloroplasts.
Chloroplasts usually align along the walls of mesophyll cells so they receive optimum incident light.
Inside the chloroplast there is a division of labour. The membrane system (grana and stroma lamellae) traps light energy and makes ATP and NADPH: the light reactions (photochemical reactions).

In the stroma, enzymatic reactions synthesise sugar, which forms starch. These are not directly light-driven but depend on ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, so by convention they are called dark reactions (carbon reactions).
The term 'dark reaction' does not mean they occur in darkness or that they do not depend on light.

example.q: Why does sugar synthesis in the stroma stop soon after the light is switched off?
steps: Sugar synthesis needs ATP and NADPH.
These are made only by the light reactions in the thylakoid membranes.
Once light stops, ATP and NADPH run out, and the carbon reactions stop.
example.answer: Because the dark reactions depend on ATP and NADPH from the light reactions.

learn.reallife: Paddy farmers in Punjab know rice plants grow best in full sun; shaded rice gives poorer yield because the light reactions slow down.

topics.title: Photosynthetic pigments and spectra

learn.hook: Leaves look green because chlorophyll reflects green light. The colours it actually uses are blue and red.
points: Paper chromatography of leaf pigments separates four pigments: chlorophyll a (bright or blue-green), chlorophyll b (yellow-green), xanthophylls (yellow) and carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange).
Pigments absorb light at specific wavelengths. A graph of absorption at different wavelengths is the absorption spectrum; chlorophyll a absorbs most in the blue and red regions.

A graph of the rate of photosynthesis at different wavelengths is the action spectrum. It correlates closely with the absorption spectrum: most photosynthesis occurs in blue and red light, though some occurs at other wavelengths.
Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment of photosynthesis.

Accessory pigments (chlorophyll b, xanthophylls, carotenoids) absorb light and transfer energy to chlorophyll a. They widen the range of wavelengths used and protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.

example.q: A student runs a chromatogram of spinach pigments. Name the four bands and their colours.
steps: Chlorophyll a: bright or blue-green.
Chlorophyll b: yellow-green.

example.answer: Chlorophyll a (blue-green), chlorophyll b (yellow-green), xanthophylls (yellow), carotenoids (yellow-orange).

topics.title: Light reaction: photosystems, Z scheme and splitting of water

learn.hook: Photosystem II comes first in the chain but was discovered second. Its name is a history lesson, not a sequence.
points: The light reactions (photochemical phase) include light absorption, water splitting, oxygen release and formation of ATP and NADPH.

Pigments form light harvesting complexes (LHC) in Photosystem I (PS I) and Photosystem II (PS II), named in the order of discovery, not function. Each LHC has hundreds of pigment molecules bound to proteins forming the antennae; a single chlorophyll a molecule is the reaction centre.
The PS I reaction centre absorbs maximally at 700 nm (P700); the PS II reaction centre at 680 nm (P680).

Z scheme: PS II absorbs 680 nm light, electrons are excited and accepted by an acceptor, then pass downhill through an electron transport chain (cytochromes) to PS I. PS I electrons, excited by 700 nm light, go to another acceptor and then downhill to NADP⁺, reducing it to NADPH + H⁺.
Water splitting, associated with PS II on the inner side of the thylakoid membrane, replaces the electrons lost by PS II: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻. Protons and O₂ are released into the thylakoid lumen.

example.q: How many molecules of water must be split to release 3 molecules of O₂?
steps: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻: 2 water molecules give 1 O₂.
For 3 O₂: 3 × 2 = 6 water molecules.
example.answer: 6 molecules of water

learn.reallife: The oxygen in the air over India's forests, from the Sundarbans to the Western Ghats, is released by this water-splitting reaction.

topics.title: Photophosphorylation and the chemiosmotic hypothesis

learn.hook: ATP synthase is a real molecular turbine: protons rush through it like water through a dam at Bhakra-Nangal, and that flow makes ATP.
points: Photophosphorylation is the synthesis of ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate in the presence of light.
Non-cyclic photophosphorylation: PS II and PS I work in series, connected by the electron transport chain; both ATP and NADPH + H⁺ are made.

Cyclic photophosphorylation: only PS I works; electrons cycle back to PS I through the electron transport chain. It occurs in stroma lamellae, which lack PS II and NADP reductase. Only ATP is made, not NADPH. It also occurs when only light beyond 680 nm is available.

Chemiosmotic hypothesis: ATP synthesis is linked to a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane. Protons build up in the lumen because (a) water is split on the inner side, (b) a carrier moves protons from the stroma into the lumen as electrons are transported, and (c) NADP reductase on the stroma side removes protons from the stroma. The lumen pH falls.

ATP synthase has two parts: F₀ (CF₀), a transmembrane channel for facilitated diffusion of protons, and F₁ (CF₁), protruding into the stroma. Protons flowing back through F₀ cause a conformational change in F₁ that makes ATP. Chemiosmosis needs a membrane, a proton pump, a proton gradient and ATP synthase.

example.q: Give two differences between cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
steps: Cyclic: only PS I; non-cyclic: PS II and PS I.
Cyclic makes only ATP; non-cyclic makes ATP and NADPH.
Cyclic occurs in stroma lamellae; non-cyclic in grana.
example.answer: Cyclic uses only PS I and makes only ATP (stroma lamellae); non-cyclic uses both photosystems and makes ATP and NADPH (grana).

topics.title: The Calvin cycle (C3 pathway)

learn.hook: Melvin Calvin fed radioactive ¹⁴CO₂ to algae and traced where the carbon went. The first stop was a 3-carbon acid, and a Nobel Prize followed.
points: ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, with CO₂, are used in the biosynthetic phase to make sugars. O₂ diffuses out. Synthesis continues briefly after light stops, then halts.

Melvin Calvin used radioactive ¹⁴C in algal photosynthesis and found the first CO₂ fixation product is a 3-carbon acid, 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA): the C3 pathway. In some plants the first product is oxaloacetic acid (OAA), a 4-carbon acid: the C4 pathway.
In C3 plants the primary CO₂ acceptor is ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP), a 5-carbon ketose sugar.

The Calvin cycle occurs in all photosynthetic plants and has three stages: carboxylation (RuBisCO fixes CO₂ with RuBP to give two molecules of 3-PGA), reduction (2 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO₂ fixed, leading to carbohydrate), and regeneration of RuBP (1 ATP per CO₂).
So each CO₂ needs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH. One glucose needs 6 CO₂ and 6 turns: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. The extra ATP need may be met by cyclic photophosphorylation.

example.q: How much ATP and NADPH are needed to make 2 molecules of glucose by the Calvin cycle?
steps: One glucose: 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
Two glucose: 2 × 18 = 36 ATP and 2 × 12 = 24 NADPH.
example.answer: 36 ATP and 24 NADPH

topics.title: The C4 pathway (Hatch and Slack pathway)

learn.hook: Maize, sorghum and sugarcane thrive in hot Indian summers with super yields. Their leaves have a 'wreath' of special cells that act like CO₂ pumps.
points: C4 plants are adapted to dry tropical regions (e.g. maize, sorghum). Their first CO₂ fixation product is the 4-carbon OAA, but they still use the Calvin cycle as the main biosynthetic pathway. They tolerate higher temperatures, respond to high light, lack photorespiration and have greater biomass productivity.
Kranz anatomy ('Kranz' = wreath): large bundle sheath cells around vascular bundles, with many chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gas exchange and no intercellular spaces.

In mesophyll cells, the primary CO₂ acceptor is the 3-carbon phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP), fixed by PEP carboxylase (PEPcase) to OAA. OAA forms other 4-carbon acids such as malic acid or aspartic acid, which move to the bundle sheath cells.

In bundle sheath cells, the C4 acids are broken down to release CO₂ and a 3-carbon molecule. The CO₂ enters the Calvin cycle; the 3-carbon molecule returns to the mesophyll and is converted back to PEP, completing the cycle.
Mesophyll cells lack RuBisCO; bundle sheath cells are rich in RuBisCO but lack PEPcase.

example.q: Trace one carbon from atmospheric CO₂ to sugar in a maize leaf.
steps: In mesophyll, PEPcase fixes CO₂ with PEP to form OAA.
OAA becomes malate or aspartate and moves to the bundle sheath.
There it is decarboxylated, releasing CO₂.
RuBisCO fixes this CO₂ in the Calvin cycle to make sugar.
example.answer: Mesophyll (PEP → OAA → malate) → bundle sheath (CO₂ released) → Calvin cycle

topics.title: Photorespiration and C3 versus C4

learn.hook: The world's most abundant enzyme sometimes grabs the wrong gas. When RuBisCO binds O₂ instead of CO₂, the plant wastes energy.
points: RuBisCO, the most abundant enzyme in the world, has an active site that can bind both CO₂ and O₂. It has a much greater affinity for CO₂, but the relative concentrations of O₂ and CO₂ decide which binds.
In C3 plants some O₂ binds RuBisCO, reducing CO₂ fixation. RuBP then combines with O₂ to form one molecule of PGA and one of phosphoglycolate: photorespiration.
Photorespiration makes no sugar, no ATP and no NADPH; instead CO₂ is released and ATP is used. So it is a wasteful process.

C4 plants do not show photorespiration: breaking down C4 acids in bundle sheath cells raises the CO₂ concentration around RuBisCO, so it acts as a carboxylase and its oxygenase activity is minimised. This is one reason C4 plants have higher productivity and tolerate higher temperatures.

C3 vs C4: primary acceptor RuBP (5C) vs PEP (3C); first product PGA (3C) vs OAA (4C); fixing enzyme RuBisCO vs PEPcase (then RuBisCO); Kranz anatomy absent vs present; photorespiration present vs negligible; Calvin cycle in mesophyll vs bundle sheath.

example.answer: Because it uses energy and releases CO₂ without making sugar, ATP or NADPH.

topics.title: Factors affecting photosynthesis

learn.hook: Greenhouse tomato growers pump extra CO₂ into their glasshouses. Why would anyone add a 'pollutant' to plants on purpose?
points: Internal (plant) factors: number, size, age and orientation of leaves, mesophyll cells and chloroplasts, internal CO₂ and amount of chlorophyll. External factors: light, CO₂, temperature and water.

Blackman's law of limiting factors (1905): if a chemical process is affected by more than one factor, its rate is determined by the factor nearest to its minimal value. E.g. a leaf with optimal light and CO₂ may not photosynthesise if the temperature is very low.

Light: rate rises linearly with light at low intensities, then levels off; light saturation occurs at about 10% of full sunlight, so light is rarely limiting except in shade. Excess light breaks down chlorophyll and reduces photosynthesis.

CO₂: the major limiting factor (only about 0.03 to 0.04% in air). Up to about 0.05% it increases fixation; higher levels can be damaging over long periods. C4 plants saturate at about 360 µL L⁻¹; C3 plants respond up to beyond 450 µL L⁻¹, so present CO₂ levels limit C3 plants. Greenhouse tomatoes and bell peppers grown in CO₂-enriched air give higher yields.

Temperature: dark reactions are enzymatic and temperature-controlled; light reactions are much less affected. C4 plants have higher temperature optima than C3; tropical plants have higher optima than temperate ones. Water acts indirectly: water stress closes stomata (less CO₂) and makes leaves wilt (less surface area and activity).

example.q: A C3 plant under bright light shows no increase in photosynthesis when light is doubled, but a large increase when CO₂ is raised. What is the limiting factor?
steps: Increasing light has no effect, so light is not limiting.
Increasing CO₂ raises the rate, so CO₂ is nearest its minimum.
By Blackman's law, CO₂ is the limiting factor.
example.answer: CO₂ concentration.

topics.title: Respiration, respiratory substrates and do plants breathe?

learn.hook: A banyan tree can be hundreds of years old and enormous, yet it has no lungs. How does every cell in it get oxygen?
points: Cellular respiration is the breaking of C–C bonds of complex compounds by oxidation within cells, releasing energy. The compounds oxidised are respiratory substrates: usually carbohydrates, but also proteins, fats and even organic acids in some plants.
Energy is not released in one step but in a series of slow, enzyme-controlled steps, and trapped as ATP, the energy currency of the cell.
Plants have no specialised respiratory organs; gas exchange occurs through stomata and lenticels.

Why plants manage without lungs: each part handles its own gas exchange; plants respire at far lower rates than animals; during photosynthesis O₂ is released inside the cells; living cells are close to the surface (in stems they lie in thin layers beneath the bark, with lenticels; interior cells are dead); loosely packed parenchyma gives a network of air spaces.

Complete combustion of glucose: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (mostly heat). Cells instead oxidise glucose step by step. Some organisms are facultative or obligate anaerobes, and all organisms keep the machinery to partly oxidise glucose without O₂ (glycolysis), reflecting anaerobic ancestors.

steps: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O.

example.answer: 1 molecule of O₂ per CO₂

topics.title: Glycolysis: the steps

learn.hook: Every organism on Earth, from bacteria to blue whales, runs glycolysis in its cytoplasm. It's the oldest energy app.
points: Glycolysis (Greek glycos = sugar, lysis = splitting) is the EMP pathway, worked out by Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and J. Parnas. It occurs in the cytoplasm of all living organisms; in anaerobes it is the only respiratory process. It has ten enzyme-controlled reactions.
Glucose is phosphorylated to glucose-6-phosphate by hexokinase (ATP used). This isomerises to fructose-6-phosphate, which is phosphorylated to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (second ATP used).
Fructose-1,6-bisphosphate splits into dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and 3-phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL).
PGAL is oxidised (two redox equivalents to NAD⁺, forming NADH + H⁺) and, with inorganic phosphate, becomes 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (BPGA).
ATP is made directly (substrate-level phosphorylation) when BPGA becomes 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA) and when phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP) becomes pyruvic acid.

steps: Glucose → glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase).

topics.title: Glycolysis: net yield and the fate of pyruvate

learn.hook: Glycolysis spends 2 ATP and makes 4. Like a shopkeeper's ledger, the net profit is what counts.
points: In plants, glucose comes from sucrose (the end product of photosynthesis) or from storage carbohydrates. Invertase converts sucrose into glucose and fructose, which both enter glycolysis.
ATP used: 2 (hexokinase step and fructose-6-P step). ATP made: 4 (two at BPGA → PGA and two at PEP → pyruvate, since each glucose gives two 3-carbon molecules). Net gain: 2 ATP.
Per glucose, glycolysis also gives 2 NADH + H⁺ and 2 molecules of pyruvic acid.
Pyruvic acid is the key product of glycolysis. Its fate depends on the cell's need.

Three fates: lactic acid fermentation, alcoholic fermentation (both anaerobic, in many prokaryotes and unicellular eukaryotes), and aerobic respiration (Krebs cycle, needs O₂) for complete oxidation to CO₂ and H₂O.

steps: ATP used: 2.

example.answer: Net 2 ATP

topics.title: Fermentation

learn.hook: Idli batter rises overnight and your legs ache after a long run. Both are fermentation stories.
points: Alcoholic fermentation (e.g. yeast): incomplete oxidation of glucose under anaerobic conditions; pyruvic acid is converted to CO₂ and ethanol by pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase.

Lactic acid fermentation: some bacteria convert pyruvic acid to lactic acid. In animal cells such as muscles during exercise, when O₂ is inadequate, pyruvic acid is reduced to lactic acid by lactate dehydrogenase.
In both, NADH + H⁺ is reoxidised to NAD⁺, so glycolysis can continue.
Fermentation releases less than 7% of the energy in glucose, and not all of it is trapped as ATP. The net gain is only the 2 ATP of glycolysis.
The products are hazardous: acid or alcohol. Yeasts poison themselves to death when alcohol reaches about 13%.

learn.hook: Hans Krebs worked out a cycle that turns one pyruvate into three CO₂ molecules and a stash of energy carriers. It runs nonstop in your mitochondria.
points: Aerobic respiration needs complete oxidation of pyruvate in mitochondria: stepwise removal of hydrogen leaving three CO₂ (in the matrix), and passing the electrons to O₂ with ATP synthesis (on the inner membrane).

Link reaction: in the matrix, pyruvate undergoes oxidative decarboxylation by pyruvic dehydrogenase (needing NAD⁺, coenzyme A and Mg²⁺): pyruvic acid + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH + H⁺. Two NADH form per glucose.
Krebs cycle (TCA cycle): acetyl group condenses with oxaloacetic acid (OAA) and water to form citric acid, catalysed by citrate synthase, releasing CoA. Citrate isomerises to isocitrate.

Two successive decarboxylations give α-ketoglutaric acid and then succinyl CoA. Succinyl CoA → succinic acid makes one GTP (substrate-level phosphorylation), which gives ATP. The remaining steps regenerate OAA.
Per pyruvate in the cycle: 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 ATP (via GTP). Including the link reaction: pyruvic acid + 4NAD⁺ + FAD⁺ + 2H₂O + ADP + Pi → 3CO₂ + 4NADH + 4H⁺ + FADH₂ + ATP.

example.q: How many NADH and FADH₂ are produced from one glucose in the link reaction plus Krebs cycle?
steps: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvate.
Per pyruvate: 1 NADH (link) + 3 NADH (cycle) = 4 NADH, and 1 FADH₂.
For 2 pyruvate: 8 NADH and 2 FADH₂.
example.answer: 8 NADH and 2 FADH₂ (plus 2 ATP)

learn.reallife: Endurance athletes, like marathoners at the Mumbai Marathon, depend heavily on aerobic respiration through the Krebs cycle in their muscle mitochondria.

topics.title: Electron transport system and oxidative phosphorylation

learn.hook: Cyanide is deadly because it blocks the last step of the electron transport chain. Without that step, oxygen can't do its job.
points: The electron transport system (ETS) is on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Electrons from NADH are oxidised by NADH dehydrogenase (complex I) and passed to ubiquinone.

FADH₂ (from succinate oxidation) passes its reducing equivalents to ubiquinone via complex II. Reduced ubiquinone (ubiquinol) passes electrons to cytochrome c via the cytochrome bc₁ complex (complex III).

Cytochrome c is a small mobile protein on the outer surface of the inner membrane carrying electrons from complex III to complex IV. Complex IV is cytochrome c oxidase, with cytochromes a and a₃ and two copper centres.
Oxygen is the final hydrogen (electron) acceptor, forming water. Its role is only at the terminal stage, but it drives the whole process by removing hydrogen from the system.

Electron flow is coupled to ATP synthase (complex V: F₁ headpiece makes ATP; F₀ is the proton channel). Energy of oxidation-reduction builds a proton gradient (oxidative phosphorylation). 2H⁺ pass through F₀ from the intermembrane space to the matrix per ATP. One NADH gives 3 ATP; one FADH₂ gives 2 ATP.

example.q: How many ATP are produced by oxidising 4 NADH and 1 FADH₂ in the ETS?
steps: NADH: 4 × 3 = 12 ATP.
FADH₂: 1 × 2 = 2 ATP.
Total = 12 + 2 = 14 ATP.
example.answer: 14 ATP

topics.title: The respiratory balance sheet: fermentation vs aerobic respiration

learn.hook: Aerobic respiration can yield up to 38 ATP per glucose; fermentation only 2. That's like comparing a full salary to pocket money.
points: Balance sheet assumptions: a sequential, orderly pathway (glycolysis → TCA → ETS); NADH from glycolysis enters mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation; no intermediates are withdrawn to make other compounds; only glucose is respired. These are not fully valid in real cells, where pathways run simultaneously.
Under these assumptions there is a net gain of 38 ATP per glucose in aerobic respiration.
Count: glycolysis 2 ATP + 2 NADH; link reaction 2 NADH; Krebs 2 ATP + 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂. NADH total 10 × 3 = 30 ATP; FADH₂ 2 × 2 = 4 ATP; direct ATP 4. Total 38.
Fermentation vs aerobic: partial vs complete breakdown of glucose; net 2 ATP vs many more; NADH oxidised slowly vs vigorously.

Glycolysis vs Krebs: cytoplasm vs mitochondrial matrix; anaerobic vs needs O₂ (via ETS); glucose → 2 pyruvate vs acetyl CoA → CO₂. Respiration differs from combustion: it is stepwise, enzyme-controlled and traps energy as ATP rather than releasing it all as heat.

example.q: Use the balance sheet to verify 38 ATP per glucose.
steps: Direct ATP: 2 (glycolysis) + 2 (Krebs) = 4.
FADH₂: 2, giving 2 × 2 = 4.
example.answer: 38 ATP

topics.title: The amphibolic pathway

learn.hook: The respiratory pathway is not a one-way street to the dump yard. It's a busy junction where raw materials are also picked up to build new molecules.
points: Glucose is the favoured substrate, but others can be respired.
Fats are first broken into glycerol and fatty acids. Fatty acids are degraded to acetyl CoA and enter the pathway; glycerol enters after conversion to PGAL.
Proteins are degraded by proteases; amino acids (after deamination) enter at various points: within the Krebs cycle, or as pyruvate or acetyl CoA.
The same intermediates are withdrawn when the organism needs to make fatty acids or proteins (e.g. acetyl CoA is withdrawn to make fatty acids).
Since the respiratory pathway is involved in both catabolism (breakdown) and anabolism (synthesis), it is better called an amphibolic pathway than a catabolic one.

example.q: Where do glycerol and fatty acids from a fat enter the respiratory pathway?
steps: Glycerol is converted to PGAL, an intermediate of glycolysis.
Fatty acids are degraded to acetyl CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle.
example.answer: Glycerol enters as PGAL; fatty acids as acetyl CoA.

learn.reallife: Groundnut and mustard seeds, rich in oil, germinate by respiring stored fats through acetyl CoA, the same molecule they later use to build new fatty acids.

topics.title: Respiratory quotient (RQ)

learn.hook: By measuring just two gases, CO₂ out and O₂ in, you can guess whether a seed is burning starch, oil or protein.
points: Respiratory quotient (RQ) = volume of CO₂ evolved ÷ volume of O₂ consumed in respiration. It depends on the respiratory substrate.
Carbohydrates (completely oxidised): equal volumes of CO₂ and O₂, so RQ = 1. For glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O gives RQ = 6/6 = 1.
Fats: RQ is less than 1. Tripalmitin: 2(C₅₁H₉₈O₆) + 145O₂ → 102CO₂ + 98H₂O; RQ = 102/145 ≈ 0.7.
Proteins: RQ is about 0.9.
In living organisms, substrates are usually a mixture; pure proteins or fats are never used alone.

example.q: Calculate the RQ for malic acid: C₄H₆O₅ + 3O₂ → 4CO₂ + 3H₂O.
steps: CO₂ evolved = 4; O₂ consumed = 3.
example.answer: RQ ≈ 1.33 (more than 1)

topics.title: Growth and development: an open-ended story

learn.hook: A neem tree can keep growing for centuries, but you stop growing taller by your early twenties. Plants have a superpower: meristems that never retire.
points: Development is the sum of growth and differentiation, from the zygote to senescence. A seed germinates under favourable conditions and develops into a seedling and a mature plant.
Development is controlled by intrinsic factors (genetic, and intracellular chemicals such as plant growth regulators) and extrinsic factors (light, temperature, water, oxygen, nutrition).

Growth is an irreversible, permanent increase in size of an organ, its parts or even a single cell. It is generally accompanied by metabolic processes (anabolic and catabolic) that use energy. Example: expansion of a leaf.

Plant growth is generally indeterminate: plants retain the capacity for unlimited growth throughout life because of meristems, whose cells divide and self-perpetuate. New cells are always being added: the open form of growth.

Root and shoot apical meristems cause primary growth (elongation along the axis). In dicots and gymnosperms, lateral meristems, the vascular cambium and cork cambium, appear later and cause secondary growth (increase in girth).

example.q: Classify the growth caused by (a) the shoot apical meristem and (b) the vascular cambium.
steps: Apical meristems increase length along the axis: primary growth.
Vascular cambium is a lateral meristem that increases girth: secondary growth.
example.answer: (a) Primary growth; (b) secondary growth.

learn.reallife: Teak trees in Madhya Pradesh and Kerala thicken year after year because their vascular cambium keeps adding wood, which is why mature teak is valuable timber.

topics.title: Measuring growth and the phases of growth

learn.hook: A single maize root tip can make more than 17,500 new cells every hour. A watermelon cell can swell up to 3,50,000 times. Both are growth, measured differently.
points: At the cellular level, growth is mainly an increase in protoplasm. Since this is hard to measure, we measure quantities proportional to it: fresh weight, dry weight, length, area, volume and cell number.
One maize root apical meristem can give more than 17,500 new cells per hour (growth as cell number). Watermelon cells may increase in size up to 3,50,000 times (growth as cell size).
Pollen tube growth is measured as length; growth of a dorsiventral leaf as increase in surface area.
Meristematic phase: constantly dividing cells at root and shoot apices, rich in protoplasm with large nuclei; thin, primary cellulose walls with abundant plasmodesmata.

Elongation phase (just behind the meristem): increased vacuolation, cell enlargement and new wall deposition. Maturation phase (further from the apex): cells reach maximal size in wall thickening and protoplasmic modifications.

example.q: A maize root apical meristem makes 17,500 cells per hour. How many cells does it make in 4 hours?

example.answer: 70,000 cells

topics.title: Growth rates: arithmetic and geometric

learn.hook: A cricket score growing 6 runs every over is arithmetic. A WhatsApp forward doubling every hour is geometric. Plant growth can follow either pattern.
points: Growth rate is the increase in growth per unit time.

Arithmetic growth: after mitosis, only one daughter cell keeps dividing; the other differentiates. A root elongating at a constant rate gives a linear curve: Lt = L₀ + rt (Lt = length at time t, L₀ = length at time zero, r = growth rate).

Geometric growth: both daughter cells keep dividing. Growth is slow at first (lag phase), then rapid and exponential (log phase), then slows as nutrients become limited (stationary phase), giving a sigmoid (S) curve, typical of organisms in natural environments.

Exponential growth: W₁ = W₀eʳᵗ, where W₁ is final size, W₀ initial size, r the relative growth rate (efficiency index), t time and e the base of natural logarithms. Final size depends on initial size.

Absolute growth rate: total growth per unit time. Relative growth rate: growth per unit time per unit initial size. Example: leaf A grows from 5 to 10 cm² and leaf B from 50 to 55 cm²: same absolute growth (5 cm²), but A has a relative rate of 100% and B only 10%.

example.q: A root is 4 cm long and grows arithmetically at 0.5 cm per day. Find its length after 6 days.
steps: Use Lt = L₀ + rt.
L₀ = 4 cm, r = 0.5 cm/day, t = 6 days.
example.answer: 7 cm

topics.title: Conditions for growth; differentiation, dedifferentiation and redifferentiation

learn.hook: A xylem cell sacrifices its own living contents to become a water pipe. Some mature cells can even 'turn back the clock' and divide again.
points: Conditions for growth: water (cell enlargement needs it; turgidity aids extension growth; it is the medium for enzymes), oxygen (releases metabolic energy), nutrients (macro and micro elements for protoplasm and energy), an optimum temperature range, and environmental signals such as light and gravity.

Differentiation: cells from apical meristems and cambium mature to perform specific functions, with changes in walls and protoplasm. E.g. tracheary elements lose their protoplasm and develop strong, elastic lignocellulosic secondary walls to carry water under tension.
Dedifferentiation: living differentiated cells that had lost the capacity to divide regain it, e.g. formation of interfascicular cambium and cork cambium from parenchyma.
Redifferentiation: cells produced by dedifferentiated tissues lose the capacity to divide again and mature to perform specific functions (e.g. secondary xylem, secondary phloem, cork).

Differentiation in plants is open: cells from the same meristem mature differently depending on location, e.g. cells pushed away from the root apical meristem become root-cap cells, while those pushed to the periphery become epidermis.

example.q: Classify each: (a) parenchyma forming interfascicular cambium; (b) cambium-derived cells maturing into secondary xylem; (c) meristem cells becoming tracheids.
steps: (a) A mature cell regaining division: dedifferentiation.
(b) Products of dedifferentiated tissue maturing: redifferentiation.
(c) Meristem cells maturing into specialised cells: differentiation.
example.answer: (a) Dedifferentiation, (b) redifferentiation, (c) differentiation

topics.title: Development and plasticity

learn.hook: A coriander seedling's first leaves are broad and round, but later leaves are feathery. Same plant, different leaf designs.
points: Development includes all changes an organism goes through in its life cycle, from germination of the seed to senescence.
The sequence involves cell division, growth, differentiation and maturation of cells leading to mature tissues and organs, and finally senescence.
Plasticity is the ability of plants to follow different developmental pathways in response to the environment or phase of life, forming different kinds of structures.
Heterophylly due to life phase: juvenile and mature leaves differ in shape in cotton, coriander and larkspur. Heterophylly due to environment: buttercup forms different leaves in air and in water.

Development (growth plus differentiation) is controlled by intrinsic factors (genes, PGRs) and extrinsic factors (environment). (Photoperiodism, vernalisation and seed dormancy are not part of this rationalised chapter.)

example.answer: Environmental heterophylly, an example of plasticity.

topics.title: Plant growth regulators: nature and discovery

learn.hook: One discovery began with 'foolish' rice seedlings in Japan that grew absurdly tall. Another began with ripe oranges that made stored bananas ripen faster.
points: PGRs are small, simple molecules of diverse chemistry: indole compounds (indole-3-acetic acid, IAA), adenine derivatives (N⁶-furfurylamino purine, kinetin), carotenoid derivatives (abscisic acid, ABA), terpenes (gibberellic acid, GA₃) and gases (ethylene, C₂H₄).

Growth promoters (cell division, enlargement, pattern formation, tropic growth, flowering, fruiting, seed formation): auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins. Growth inhibitors (responses to wounds and stress, dormancy, abscission): abscisic acid. Ethylene can fit either group but is largely an inhibitor.

Auxin: Charles and Francis Darwin saw canary grass coleoptiles bend towards unilateral light (phototropism) and found the tip was the site of a transmittable influence. F.W. Went isolated auxin from oat coleoptile tips.

Gibberellin: E. Kurosawa found that sterile filtrates of the fungus Gibberella fujikuroi, which causes 'bakanae' (foolish seedling) disease of rice, produced the symptoms in uninfected rice seedlings; the active substance was gibberellic acid. Cytokinin: Skoog and co-workers found tobacco callus grew only with extra supplements; Skoog and Miller crystallised kinetin. Kinetin came from autoclaved herring sperm DNA; zeatin was later isolated from corn kernels and coconut milk.

ABA: in the mid-1960s, inhibitor-B, abscission II and dormin were found to be chemically identical and named abscisic acid. Ethylene: Cousins confirmed that ripened oranges release a volatile substance that hastened ripening of stored unripe bananas; it was identified as ethylene.

Ethylene: gas.
example.answer: Indole, adenine derivative, carotenoid derivative, terpene, gas.

topics.title: Auxins: physiological effects

learn.hook: Tea gardens in Assam and Darjeeling are pruned regularly so the bushes grow sideways into flat 'plucking tables'. The trick works by removing the auxin source.
points: Auxins (Greek auxein, to grow) were first isolated from human urine. Natural auxins: IAA and IBA (indole butyric acid). Synthetic: NAA (naphthalene acetic acid) and 2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid). They are produced at growing apices of stems and roots and migrate to regions of action.

Uses: initiate rooting in stem cuttings (plant propagation); promote flowering, e.g. in pineapple; prevent fruit and leaf drop at early stages but promote abscission of older mature leaves and fruits.
Apical dominance: the growing apical bud inhibits growth of lateral (axillary) buds. Decapitation (removing the shoot tip) lets lateral buds grow; used in tea plantations and hedge-making.
Auxins induce parthenocarpy, e.g. in tomatoes.
Auxins are used as herbicides: 2,4-D kills dicot weeds but does not affect mature monocots, so it is used for weed-free lawns. Auxin also controls xylem differentiation and helps in cell division.

example.q: Why does 2,4-D sprayed on a lawn kill broad-leaved weeds but not the grass?
steps: 2,4-D is a synthetic auxin used as a herbicide.
It kills dicotyledonous weeds.
It does not affect mature monocots such as lawn grasses.
example.answer: It is selective: it kills dicot weeds but spares mature monocot grass.

topics.title: Gibberellins and cytokinins

learn.hook: Spraying sugarcane with gibberellins can add as much as 20 tonnes per acre to the yield. Sweet results from a hormone.
points: More than 100 gibberellins (GA₁, GA₂, GA₃ ...) are reported from fungi and higher plants; GA₃ (gibberellic acid) was among the first discovered and is the most studied. All GAs are acidic.

Gibberellin uses: increase axis length (longer grape stalks); elongate and improve shape of fruits like apple; delay senescence so fruits stay on the tree longer; speed up malting in brewing; increase sugarcane stem length and yield (up to 20 tonnes per acre); hasten maturity and early seed production in juvenile conifers; promote bolting (internode elongation just before flowering) in beet, cabbage and other rosette plants.
Cytokinins promote cytokinesis. Kinetin, a modified adenine (purine), does not occur naturally in plants; zeatin is a natural cytokinin from corn kernels and coconut milk.
Natural cytokinins are made where rapid cell division occurs: root apices, developing shoot buds, young fruits.

Cytokinin effects: production of new leaves and chloroplasts, lateral shoot growth, adventitious shoot formation; overcoming apical dominance; promoting nutrient mobilisation, which delays leaf senescence.

example.q: A farmer wants cabbage to bolt for seed production and wants a stored leaf to stay green longer. Which PGR suits each?
steps: Bolting (internode elongation before flowering) is promoted by gibberellins.
Delay of leaf senescence through nutrient mobilisation is a cytokinin effect.
example.answer: Gibberellins for bolting; cytokinins to delay leaf senescence.

learn.reallife: Sugarcane growers in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra may use gibberellins to lengthen stems, and table-grape farmers in Nashik use GA₃ to lengthen bunches and enlarge berries.

topics.title: Ethylene and abscisic acid

learn.hook: One gas ripens mangoes and pineapples in Indian markets; another hormone tells plants to shut their stomata when drought hits. Meet ethylene and ABA.
points: Ethylene is a simple gaseous PGR made in large amounts by senescing tissues and ripening fruits. In dicot seedlings it causes horizontal growth, swelling of the axis and apical hook formation (the triple response).

Ethylene promotes senescence and abscission of leaves and flowers; is highly effective in fruit ripening, raising the respiration rate (respiratory climacteric); breaks seed and bud dormancy (germination of peanut, sprouting of potato tubers); promotes rapid internode and petiole elongation in deep-water rice; promotes root growth and root hairs; initiates flowering and synchronises fruit-set in pineapple; induces flowering in mango.

Ethephon is the most widely used source of ethylene; in water it is absorbed and releases ethylene slowly. It hastens ripening in tomatoes and apples, accelerates abscission (thinning of cotton, cherry, walnut) and promotes female flowers in cucumber.
Abscisic acid (ABA) regulates abscission and dormancy; it is a general inhibitor of growth and metabolism, and inhibits seed germination.

ABA stimulates stomatal closure and increases tolerance to stresses, so it is the stress hormone. It is important in seed development, maturation and dormancy, helping seeds withstand desiccation. In most situations ABA is an antagonist of GAs.

steps: Ethephon releases ethylene slowly inside the plant.

example.answer: To increase female flowers and hence the yield.

topics.title: Interaction of PGRs and practical applications

learn.hook: Plant hormones rarely act alone. Like players in a cricket team, they combine, compete or cover for each other.
points: Every phase of growth, differentiation and development is influenced by one PGR or another. Their roles may be complementary or antagonistic, individualistic or synergistic.
Many events involve interaction of more than one PGR: dormancy in seeds and buds, abscission, senescence and apical dominance.
Apical dominance: auxin from the apex maintains it, while cytokinins help overcome it. Dormancy: ABA maintains it, while GAs and ethylene can break it.
PGRs are only one kind of intrinsic control; along with genomic control and extrinsic factors they regulate growth and development.

Practical choices: rooting of cuttings (auxin, IBA/NAA); weed control in lawns (2,4-D); seedless tomato (auxin); longer grape stalks, malting, sugarcane yield, bolting (GAs); fruit ripening, female flowers in cucumber, flowering in pineapple and mango (ethylene/ethephon); stomatal closure under drought (ABA); delay leaf senescence (cytokinin).

topics.title: Breathing and respiratory organs across animals

learn.hook: A sponge breathes through its whole body, an insect through a network of air tubes, a fish through gills and you through lungs. Same goal, different plumbing.
points: Breathing is the exchange of O₂ from the atmosphere with CO₂ produced by the cells. It is different from cellular respiration, which is the use of O₂ in cells to break down food.
Lower invertebrates (sponges, coelenterates, flatworms) exchange gases by simple diffusion over the whole body surface.
Earthworms use their moist cuticle; insects have a network of tracheal tubes carrying air within the body.
Gills (branchial respiration) are used by most aquatic arthropods and molluscs and by fishes. Lungs (pulmonary respiration) are used by terrestrial forms: reptiles, birds and mammals.
Amphibians such as frogs can also respire through their moist skin (cutaneous respiration).

steps: (a) Insects use tracheal tubes.

(d) Frogs under water use moist skin (cutaneous).

topics.title: The human respiratory system

learn.hook: Your lungs have hundreds of millions of tiny alveoli. Spread out, their surface area would be about the size of a badminton court.
points: Path of air: external nostrils (above the upper lip) → nasal passage → nasal chamber → pharynx (common passage for food and air) → larynx → trachea → primary bronchi → secondary and tertiary bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles → alveoli.

The larynx is a cartilaginous box for sound production (sound box). During swallowing the glottis is covered by a thin elastic cartilaginous flap, the epiglottis, preventing food from entering the larynx.

The trachea extends to the mid-thoracic cavity and divides at the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra into right and left primary bronchi. The trachea, bronchi and initial bronchioles are supported by incomplete cartilaginous rings.

Alveoli are very thin, irregular-walled, vascularised bag-like structures where gas exchange occurs. The lungs are covered by a double-layered pleura with pleural fluid between, which reduces friction.

Conducting part (nostrils to terminal bronchioles) transports, filters, humidifies and warms air; exchange (respiratory) part (alveoli and their ducts) is the site of diffusion. The lungs lie in an air-tight thoracic chamber formed by the vertebral column (dorsal), sternum (ventral), ribs (lateral) and dome-shaped diaphragm (below). Steps of respiration: pulmonary ventilation, alveolar diffusion, transport of gases by blood, diffusion between blood and tissues, and cellular respiration.

steps: Nostrils → nasal chamber → pharynx → larynx.
Larynx → trachea → primary bronchi → secondary and tertiary bronchi.
Bronchioles → terminal bronchioles → alveoli (gas exchange).
example.answer: Nostrils → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli

topics.title: Mechanism of breathing

learn.hook: Your lungs have no muscles of their own. A dome-shaped muscle below them and small muscles between your ribs do all the pumping.
points: Breathing has two stages: inspiration (air drawn in) and expiration (alveolar air released). Air moves because of a pressure gradient between the lungs and the atmosphere.
Inspiration occurs when intra-pulmonary pressure is less than atmospheric pressure (negative pressure); expiration when it is higher.

Inspiration: the diaphragm contracts, increasing thoracic volume in the antero-posterior axis; the external intercostal muscles contract, lifting the ribs and sternum and increasing volume in the dorso-ventral axis. Pulmonary volume rises, pressure falls, and air rushes in.

Expiration: the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax, thoracic and pulmonary volume decrease, intra-pulmonary pressure rises slightly above atmospheric, and air is expelled. Additional abdominal muscles can increase the strength of inspiration and expiration.
A healthy human breathes 12 to 16 times per minute. A spirometer measures volumes of air in breathing and helps clinical assessment of lung function.

example.q: What happens to intra-pulmonary pressure when the diaphragm contracts, and why?
steps: Diaphragm contraction increases thoracic volume.

example.answer: It falls below atmospheric pressure, causing inspiration.

topics.title: Respiratory volumes and capacities

learn.hook: Athletes and wind-instrument players often have large vital capacities. A spirometer can tell how much air you can move in one big breath.
points: Tidal volume (TV): air inspired or expired in normal breathing, about 500 mL. So a healthy person breathes about 6000 to 8000 mL per minute (minute ventilation = TV × breaths per minute).

Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV): extra air inspired by forcible inspiration, 2500 to 3000 mL. Expiratory reserve volume (ERV): extra air expired by forcible expiration, 1000 to 1100 mL. Residual volume (RV): air left after forcible expiration, 1100 to 1200 mL.
Inspiratory capacity (IC) = TV + IRV. Expiratory capacity (EC) = TV + ERV. Functional residual capacity (FRC) = ERV + RV.

Vital capacity (VC) = ERV + TV + IRV: the maximum air a person can breathe in after forced expiration (or out after forced inspiration). It indicates the strength of the lungs and respiratory muscles.
Total lung capacity (TLC) = VC + RV = RV + ERV + TV + IRV: total air in the lungs at the end of forced inspiration.

example.q: TV = 500 mL, IRV = 2500 mL, ERV = 1000 mL, RV = 1200 mL. Find VC and TLC.
example.answer: VC = 4000 mL; TLC = 5200 mL

topics.title: Exchange of gases at the alveoli and tissues

learn.hook: Oxygen moves into your blood without any pump. It simply slides 'downhill' from high to low partial pressure.
points: Alveoli are the primary sites of gas exchange; exchange also occurs between blood and tissues. O₂ and CO₂ move by simple diffusion along pressure (concentration) gradients. Solubility and membrane thickness also matter.

Partial pressure is the pressure contributed by one gas in a mixture (pO₂, pCO₂). In mm Hg: atmosphere O₂ 159, CO₂ 0.3; alveoli O₂ 104, CO₂ 40; deoxygenated blood O₂ 40, CO₂ 45; oxygenated blood O₂ 95, CO₂ 40; tissues O₂ 40, CO₂ 45.
So O₂ diffuses from alveoli (104) to deoxygenated blood (40), and from oxygenated blood (95) to tissues (40). CO₂ diffuses from tissues (45) to blood and from deoxygenated blood (45) to alveoli (40).
CO₂ is 20 to 25 times more soluble than O₂, so more CO₂ diffuses per unit difference in partial pressure.

The diffusion membrane has three layers: thin squamous epithelium of alveoli, endothelium of alveolar capillaries, and basement substance between them. Its total thickness is much less than a millimetre.

example.q: Using the table, find the pO₂ gradient between alveoli and deoxygenated blood.
steps: Alveolar pO₂ = 104 mm Hg.
Deoxygenated blood pO₂ = 40 mm Hg.
Gradient = 104 - 40 = 64 mm Hg.
example.answer: 64 mm Hg

topics.title: Transport of oxygen

learn.hook: Haemoglobin is a smart carrier: it grabs oxygen in the lungs and lets it go in hard-working muscles, exactly where it's needed.
points: About 97% of O₂ is carried by RBCs (bound to haemoglobin); about 3% is dissolved in plasma.
Haemoglobin is a red, iron-containing pigment in RBCs. O₂ binds reversibly to form oxyhaemoglobin; each haemoglobin molecule can carry at most four O₂ molecules.
Binding depends mainly on pO₂; pCO₂, hydrogen ion concentration and temperature also affect it.

The oxygen dissociation curve (percentage saturation of haemoglobin vs pO₂) is sigmoid. In alveoli, high pO₂, low pCO₂, low H⁺ and lower temperature favour oxyhaemoglobin formation; in tissues, low pO₂, high pCO₂, high H⁺ and higher temperature favour dissociation.
Every 100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL of O₂ to the tissues under normal conditions.

example.q: If cardiac output is 5000 mL of blood per minute, how much O₂ (mL) reaches the tissues per minute?
steps: Each 100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL O₂.
5000 mL blood = 50 × 100 mL.
O₂ delivered = 50 × 5 = 250 mL per minute.
example.answer: About 250 mL O₂ per minute

topics.title: Transport of carbon dioxide

learn.hook: Most of the CO₂ you breathe out travelled from your cells disguised as bicarbonate ions, thanks to one super-fast enzyme.
points: CO₂ transport: about 20 to 25% by RBCs as carbamino-haemoglobin, about 70% as bicarbonate, and about 7% dissolved in plasma.
Carbamino-haemoglobin formation depends on pCO₂, and pO₂ also affects it. In tissues (high pCO₂, low pO₂) more CO₂ binds; in alveoli (low pCO₂, high pO₂) CO₂ is released.
RBCs have a very high concentration of carbonic anhydrase (small amounts in plasma). It catalyses both directions: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺.

At tissues, high pCO₂ drives formation of HCO₃⁻ and H⁺; at alveoli, low pCO₂ reverses the reaction, releasing CO₂ and H₂O. So CO₂ is trapped as bicarbonate in tissues and released as CO₂ in the lungs.
Every 100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers about 4 mL of CO₂ to the alveoli.

example.q: Why does carbonic anhydrase make CO₂ in the tissues but release CO₂ in the lungs?
steps: The enzyme speeds the reaction in both directions.
In tissues, pCO₂ is high, so CO₂ + H₂O → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺.
In alveoli, pCO₂ is low, so HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O, and CO₂ is breathed out.
example.answer: The direction is set by pCO₂: high in tissues (forms bicarbonate), low in alveoli (releases CO₂).

learn.reallife: Blood gas tests in Indian ICUs measure bicarbonate levels to check how well a patient's body is handling CO₂.

topics.title: Regulation of respiration

learn.hook: Hold your breath and the urge to breathe grows stronger. Surprisingly, it's rising CO₂, not falling O₂, that sounds the alarm.
points: Humans can moderate their respiratory rhythm to suit the body's demands; this is done by the neural system.
The respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla region of the brain is mainly responsible for regulation.
The pneumotaxic centre in the pons can moderate the rhythm centre; its signals can reduce the duration of inspiration and so alter the respiratory rate.

A chemosensitive area next to the rhythm centre is highly sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺; a rise activates it, and it signals the rhythm centre to adjust breathing and eliminate them. Receptors in the aortic arch and carotid artery also detect changes in CO₂ and H⁺.
The role of oxygen in regulating respiratory rhythm is quite insignificant.

example.q: During a 400 m race, CO₂ and H⁺ rise in the blood. Trace how breathing speeds up.
steps: The chemosensitive area (and aortic and carotid receptors) detect higher CO₂ and H⁺.
They signal the respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla.
The rhythm centre increases the rate and depth of breathing to remove CO₂.
example.answer: Chemoreceptors detect CO₂/H⁺ → rhythm centre in medulla → faster, deeper breathing.

topics.title: Disorders of the respiratory system

learn.hook: Stone-crushing workers in parts of Rajasthan breathe dust all day. Without masks, their lungs slowly scar.
points: Asthma: difficulty in breathing causing wheezing, due to inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles.
Emphysema: a chronic disorder in which alveolar walls are damaged, so the respiratory surface decreases. Cigarette smoking is one of the major causes.

Occupational respiratory disorders: in industries involving grinding or stone-breaking, so much dust is produced that the body's defences cannot cope. Long exposure causes inflammation leading to fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous tissue) and serious lung damage.
Workers in such industries should wear protective masks.

topics.title: Body fluids, blood and plasma

learn.hook: When you donate blood at a camp, the bag looks red, but more than half of it is a straw-coloured liquid called plasma.
points: All cells need a supply of nutrients and O₂ and removal of wastes, so organisms have circulating fluids. Simple organisms such as sponges and coelenterates circulate water from their surroundings through body cavities. Blood and lymph are the most common body fluids in higher animals.
Blood is a special connective tissue made of a fluid matrix (plasma) and formed elements.

Plasma is a straw-coloured, viscous fluid forming nearly 55% of blood. It is 90 to 92% water; proteins make up 6 to 8%. It also has minerals (Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, HCO₃⁻, Cl⁻) and glucose, amino acids and lipids in transit.
Main plasma proteins: fibrinogen (clotting), globulins (defence mechanisms) and albumins (osmotic balance). Clotting factors are present in inactive form.
Serum is plasma without the clotting factors.

example.q: A blood sample is 5 L. About how much of it is plasma?
steps: Plasma is nearly 55% of blood.
example.answer: About 2.75 L

topics.title: Formed elements: RBCs, WBCs and platelets

learn.hook: During dengue season in India, doctors anxiously watch one number on the blood report: the platelet count.
points: Formed elements (RBCs, WBCs and platelets) make up nearly 45% of blood. RBCs are the most abundant: 5 to 5.5 million per mm³ in a healthy adult man. They are formed in red bone marrow in adults, lack a nucleus in most mammals and are biconcave.

RBCs contain haemoglobin, a red, iron-containing protein; a healthy person has 12 to 16 g of haemoglobin per 100 mL of blood. RBCs live about 120 days and are destroyed in the spleen (graveyard of RBCs).

WBCs (leucocytes) are colourless, nucleated, short-lived, 6000 to 8000 per mm³. Granulocytes: neutrophils (60 to 65%, most abundant, phagocytic), eosinophils (2 to 3%, resist infections, allergic reactions), basophils (0.5 to 1%, least, secrete histamine, serotonin, heparin; inflammation).
Agranulocytes: lymphocytes (20 to 25%, B and T types, immune responses) and monocytes (6 to 8%, phagocytic).

Platelets (thrombocytes) are cell fragments from megakaryocytes in bone marrow, 1,50,000 to 3,50,000 per mm³. They release substances involved in clotting; a fall in their number causes clotting disorders and excessive blood loss.

topics.title: Blood groups: ABO, Rh and erythroblastosis foetalis

learn.hook: In an emergency, an O-negative donor's blood can save almost anyone. But mixing the wrong groups can be fatal. Blood groups decide.
points: ABO grouping is based on two surface antigens (A and B) on RBCs and two natural antibodies (anti-A, anti-B) in plasma.

Group A: antigen A, anti-B; can receive A, O. Group B: antigen B, anti-A; can receive B, O. Group AB: antigens A and B, no antibodies; can receive AB, A, B, O. Group O: no antigens, anti-A and anti-B; can receive only O.
Group O individuals are universal donors; group AB individuals are universal recipients.

The Rh antigen (similar to one in Rhesus monkeys) is present on RBCs of nearly 80% of humans (Rh+ve); those without it are Rh-ve. An Rh-ve person exposed to Rh+ve blood forms antibodies, so Rh should also be matched before transfusion.

Erythroblastosis foetalis: an Rh-ve mother with an Rh+ve foetus may be exposed to foetal blood during the first delivery and make anti-Rh antibodies. In later pregnancies these can leak into the Rh+ve foetus and destroy its RBCs, causing severe anaemia and jaundice or even death. It is prevented by giving the mother anti-Rh antibodies immediately after the first delivery.

topics.title: Coagulation of blood and lymph

learn.hook: Scrape your elbow in a game of kabaddi and within minutes a dark scab forms. That's a cascade of enzymes building a net of fibrin threads.
points: Coagulation (clotting) in response to injury prevents excessive blood loss. A clot (coagulum) is mainly a network of fibrin threads in which dead and damaged formed elements are trapped.

Fibrin is formed from inactive fibrinogen by the enzyme thrombin; thrombin is formed from inactive prothrombin by the enzyme complex thrombokinase, produced by a cascade of linked enzyme reactions involving plasma factors.
Injury stimulates platelets to release factors that activate coagulation; factors released by injured tissues can also start it. Calcium ions play a very important role.

As blood passes through tissue capillaries, water and small soluble substances move into spaces between cells, leaving larger proteins and most formed elements in the vessels. This interstitial (tissue) fluid has the same mineral distribution as plasma and is the medium of exchange between blood and cells.

The lymphatic system collects this fluid and drains it into major veins; the fluid inside it is lymph: colourless, containing lymphocytes for immunity, carrying nutrients and hormones, and absorbing fats through lacteals in intestinal villi. Unlike blood, lymph lacks RBCs and has fewer proteins.

example.q: Write the clotting cascade in order from injury to clot.
steps: Injury: platelets and tissues release factors.
A cascade forms thrombokinase.
Thrombokinase converts prothrombin to thrombin (Ca²⁺ needed).
Thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, whose threads trap cells to form a clot.
example.answer: Injury → thrombokinase → prothrombin to thrombin → fibrinogen to fibrin → clot

topics.title: Circulatory pathways and evolution of the vertebrate heart

learn.hook: A fish heart sends blood on one loop; your heart runs two separate loops at once. Evolution kept adding chambers.
points: Open circulatory system (arthropods, molluscs): blood pumped by the heart passes through large vessels into open spaces or body cavities called sinuses.
Closed circulatory system (annelids, chordates): blood always circulates through a closed network of vessels; flow can be regulated more precisely, so it is more advantageous.
Fishes: 2-chambered heart (one atrium, one ventricle); the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the gills, oxygenated blood goes to the body and returns: single circulation.

Amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles): 3-chambered heart (two atria, one ventricle). The left atrium gets oxygenated blood and the right atrium deoxygenated blood, but they mix in the single ventricle: incomplete double circulation.
Crocodiles, birds and mammals: 4-chambered heart (two atria, two ventricles); oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept separate: double circulation.

topics.title: The human heart: structure, valves and nodal tissue

learn.hook: Your heart has its own built-in electrician, the SA node, which fires about 72 times a minute without any instruction from the brain.
points: The human circulatory (blood vascular) system has a muscular chambered heart, a closed network of branching blood vessels, and blood.

The heart is mesodermal, lies in the thoracic cavity between the lungs, slightly tilted to the left, about the size of a clenched fist. It is protected by a double-walled pericardium with pericardial fluid. It has two small upper atria and two larger lower ventricles; ventricle walls are much thicker than atrial walls.

A thin inter-atrial septum separates the atria; a thick inter-ventricular septum separates the ventricles; a thick fibrous atrio-ventricular septum separates atrium and ventricle of each side, with openings between them.

Valves: tricuspid valve (three cusps) between right atrium and right ventricle; bicuspid (mitral) valve between left atrium and left ventricle; semilunar valves at the openings of the pulmonary artery and aorta. Valves allow one-way flow and prevent backflow.

Nodal tissue: the sino-atrial node (SAN) in the right upper corner of the right atrium; the atrio-ventricular node (AVN) in the lower left corner of the right atrium near the AV septum; the AV bundle passes through the septa and divides into right and left bundles giving Purkinje fibres (the bundles with Purkinje fibres form the bundle of His). Nodal tissue is autoexcitable. The SAN generates the most action potentials (70 to 75 per minute) and is the pacemaker.

example.q: Trace the impulse from the pacemaker to the ventricular muscles.
steps: SAN (pacemaker) fires and the atria contract.
The impulse reaches the AVN.
It travels through the AV bundle, right and left bundles and Purkinje fibres.
The ventricular muscles contract.
example.answer: SAN → AVN → AV bundle → right and left bundles → Purkinje fibres → ventricles

topics.title: The cardiac cycle, cardiac output and heart sounds

learn.hook: 'Lub-dub, lub-dub': each beat your doctor hears through a stethoscope is the sound of heart valves snapping shut.
points: Joint diastole: all four chambers relaxed; tricuspid and bicuspid valves open; blood flows from the pulmonary veins and vena cava through the atria into the ventricles; semilunar valves closed.
Atrial systole: the SAN fires, both atria contract, increasing ventricular filling by about 30%. The impulse passes via the AVN, AV bundle and bundle of His to the ventricles.

Ventricular systole (atria relax): ventricular pressure rises, closing the tricuspid and bicuspid valves; further rise opens the semilunar valves and blood flows into the pulmonary artery and aorta. Ventricular diastole: pressure falls, semilunar valves close; AV valves open as atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure; joint diastole again.

At 72 beats per minute, one cardiac cycle lasts about 0.8 s. Each ventricle pumps about 70 mL per beat (stroke volume). Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate, about 5000 mL (5 L) per minute; it is much higher in athletes.
First heart sound (lub): closure of tricuspid and bicuspid valves. Second heart sound (dub): closure of semilunar valves. These sounds have clinical diagnostic significance.

topics.title: ECG and double circulation

learn.hook: An ECG strip in an emergency ward is a story in waves: P, QRS and T tell a doctor exactly what the heart's electrical system is doing.
points: An electrocardiograph records the electrical activity of the heart during the cardiac cycle as an ECG. A standard ECG uses three leads: one to each wrist and one to the left ankle; more chest leads give detail.

P wave: electrical excitation (depolarisation) of the atria, leading to atrial contraction. QRS complex: depolarisation of the ventricles, initiating ventricular contraction; contraction starts shortly after Q and marks the beginning of systole. T wave: return of ventricles to normal (repolarisation); the end of T marks the end of systole.

Counting QRS complexes in a given time gives the heart rate. Since ECGs have roughly the same shape for a given lead setup, deviations indicate possible abnormality, so the ECG has great clinical significance.

Pulmonary circulation: right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium. Systemic circulation: left ventricle → aorta → arteries, arterioles, capillaries → tissues → venules, veins, vena cava → right atrium.

The hepatic portal system carries blood from the intestine to the liver through the hepatic portal vein before it enters systemic circulation. The coronary system circulates blood to and from the heart muscle.

topics.title: Regulation of the heart and circulatory disorders

learn.hook: India has one of the world's largest numbers of people with high blood pressure, and many don't know it. A simple BP check can save lives.
points: The heart is myogenic: its activity is auto-regulated by nodal tissue. A neural centre in the medulla oblongata moderates it through the autonomic nervous system: sympathetic signals increase heart rate, strength of ventricular contraction and cardiac output; parasympathetic signals decrease heart rate, conduction speed and cardiac output. Adrenal medullary hormones also increase cardiac output.

Hypertension: blood pressure higher than normal (120/80 mm Hg; 120 is systolic or pumping pressure, 80 is diastolic or resting pressure). Repeated readings of 140/90 or higher indicate hypertension, which leads to heart disease and affects the brain and kidneys.

Coronary artery disease (atherosclerosis): deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue narrow the lumen of arteries supplying the heart muscle. Angina (angina pectoris): acute chest pain when not enough O₂ reaches the heart muscle; more common in middle-aged and elderly people.

Heart failure: the heart cannot pump blood effectively enough to meet the body's needs; also called congestive heart failure because lung congestion is a main symptom. It is not the same as cardiac arrest (heart stops beating) or heart attack (heart muscle suddenly damaged by inadequate blood supply).

Quick recap for exams: ABO compatibility depends on antigens and antibodies; the SAN is the pacemaker; open circulation uses sinuses while closed uses vessels; ECG waves P, QRS and T reflect atrial and ventricular electrical events.

topics.title: Nitrogenous wastes and excretory structures in animals

learn.hook: A pigeon's white droppings and a fish's invisible ammonia are both ways of getting rid of nitrogen. The choice depends on how much water an animal can spare.
points: The major nitrogenous wastes are ammonia, urea and uric acid. Ammonia is the most toxic and needs a large amount of water for removal; uric acid is the least toxic and can be removed with minimum water loss.

Ammonotelism (excreting ammonia): many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects. Ammonia, being readily soluble, diffuses out across body or gill surfaces as ammonium ions; kidneys play no significant role.

Ureotelism (excreting urea): mammals, many terrestrial amphibians and marine fishes. Ammonia is converted to urea in the liver, released into blood and excreted by kidneys; some urea may be retained in the kidney matrix to maintain osmolarity.
Uricotelism (excreting uric acid as pellet or paste with minimum water loss): reptiles, birds, land snails and insects. Terrestrial life favoured less toxic wastes to conserve water.

Excretory structures: protonephridia or flame cells (Platyhelminthes such as Planaria, rotifers, some annelids, Amphioxus; mainly osmoregulation); nephridia (earthworm and other annelids); Malpighian tubules (most insects, including cockroaches); antennal or green glands (crustaceans such as prawns).

example.q: Why do birds excrete uric acid instead of ammonia?
steps: Ammonia is very toxic and needs a lot of water to remove.
Uric acid is the least toxic and can be removed as a paste with minimum water loss.
This conserves water on land and during flight.
example.answer: To conserve water; uric acid needs very little water.

topics.title: The human excretory system and the kidney

learn.hook: Your two kidneys are each about the size of your fist and weigh only 120 to 170 g, yet they filter about 180 litres of fluid a day.
points: The human excretory system has a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra.

Kidneys are reddish-brown, bean-shaped, between the last thoracic and third lumbar vertebrae, close to the dorsal inner wall of the abdominal cavity. Each adult kidney is 10 to 12 cm long, 5 to 7 cm wide, 2 to 3 cm thick and weighs 120 to 170 g.
The hilum is a notch on the inner concave surface through which the ureter, blood vessels and nerves enter. Inner to it is the funnel-shaped renal pelvis with projections called calyces.
The outer layer is a tough capsule. Inside are the outer cortex and inner medulla; the medulla forms conical medullary pyramids projecting into the calyces.
The cortex extends between medullary pyramids as renal columns, the columns of Bertini.

example.q: List the path of urine from the kidney to the outside.
steps: Urine collects in the calyces and renal pelvis.
It passes down the ureter.

topics.title: The nephron: the kidney's working unit

learn.hook: Each of your kidneys has about a million nephrons. Laid end to end, the tubules would stretch for kilometres.
points: Each kidney has nearly one million nephrons, the functional units. Each nephron has a glomerulus and a renal tubule.
The glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries formed by the afferent arteriole (a branch of the renal artery); blood leaves it by the efferent arteriole.

The renal tubule begins as the double-walled, cup-like Bowman's capsule enclosing the glomerulus; together they form the Malpighian body (renal corpuscle). Then come the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), the hairpin-shaped Henle's loop (descending and ascending limbs), the distal convoluted tubule (DCT), and collecting ducts into which many DCTs open; collecting ducts open into the renal pelvis through medullary pyramids.

The Malpighian corpuscle, PCT and DCT lie in the cortex; Henle's loop dips into the medulla. Cortical nephrons have a short loop barely reaching the medulla; juxtamedullary nephrons have a very long loop running deep into the medulla.

The efferent arteriole forms peritubular capillaries around the tubule; a minute vessel running parallel to Henle's loop forms the U-shaped vasa recta, which is absent or highly reduced in cortical nephrons.

example.q: Trace the path of filtrate through a nephron.
steps: Filtrate forms in Bowman's capsule.
It flows through the PCT.
Then through the descending and ascending limbs of Henle's loop.
Then the DCT, and into the collecting duct.
example.answer: Bowman's capsule → PCT → Henle's loop → DCT → collecting duct
